1. I, the Chairman of the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development,
having been authorised by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf this Hundred-Fifty Third Report of the
Committee on 'Gender Budget Analysis.
 
2. Gender Budgeting being a new concept, the Committee had to largely depend on the documents/papers received from
the Department of Women and Child Development, which is the nodal agency for the purpose of Gender Budgeting in
Govt. of India. Publications brought out on the subject by the National Institute of Public Finance & Policy and United
Nations Development Fund for Women were also consulted.
 
3. The Committee heard the Secretary and other Officials of the Department of Women & Child Development on the
subject.
 
4. The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on 17
th December, 2004. 
 
NEW DELHI;
December 17 , 2004__
Agrahayana 26, 1926 (Saka)
VAYALAR RAVI
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Human Resource Development
 
R E P O R T
 
I           Introduction
 
1.1       The words 'gender' and 'sex' are commonly referred to in respect of women and men.  While sex is a biological
concept, gender is mainly a social and cultural concept; it refers not only to women and men but also to the relations of
social, economic and political powers enjoyed by them in a society.  This distribution of power had never been even in
any society.  Gender equality, therefore, has been made an integral part of the developmental planning and efforts, by
not only the national governments but by multinational agencies as well.  Efforts made by the UN during the 1990s, led
to a global consensus in integrating a gender perspective in all policies and budgetary dimensions of different countries.
 
1.2       For achieving the goal of gender equality, Governments take affirmative actions in favour of women and girl
children with a view to enabling them not only to share the benefits of development proportionately but also contribute
their bit to national construction.  Any effort of gender empowerment cannot succeed, unless there is an effective
targeting of national resources to women's cause.  And this will be possible only if we know precisely how much of our
resources are being spent on women and girl children, both scheme-wise and Ministry-wise.   
 
1.3       Generally, budgeting involves four components: (i) the budgetary allocation of resources to various heads, (ii)
the actual Government outlays on various heads, (iii) an accounting of how resources are utilised for a particular
purpose and (iv) an evaluation of the effectiveness of the resources utilised in delivering the intended results.  Gender
Budgeting involves looking at all the four components from the point of view of women as beneficiaries.
 
1.4       Gender Budgeting thus refers to the process aimed not only at capturing/highlighting gender sensitivities of
budgetary allocations but also to help identify gaps in access to and distribution of resources on gender basis. 

153rd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/153rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:27]
Budgeting allocations using traditional macro-economic practices with no regard to different needs and requirements
that men and women may have in a society transmit and breed gender biases in that society.  Gender budget analysis,
therefore, is critical in fostering a more open democratic and just society where government's accountability and
transparency in its working are more real than apparent.  Gender aware budgets, in fact, promote equity as well as
efficiency.
 
1.5       Gender Budgeting also involves carrying out an impact analysis of Government programmes and its budgetary
allocation on the overall socio-economic status of women in the country with a view to targeting of public spending and
offsetting any undesirable gender-specific consequences of previous budgetary measures.
 
1.6       The aim of gender budgeting is thus not to have a separate budget for women but to look at public expenditure
for assessing relative benefits/costs accruing to men and women.  Apart from the public expenditure and its impact on
gender balance, it also concerns about the adequacy, affectivity and implementation etc. of public policies from gender
perspective.
 
II         International Initiatives
 
2.1       Gender Budgeting is gaining increasing acceptance as a tool for engendering macro-economic policy-making. 
The Fourth World Conference of Women was held in Beijing  in September 1995 and the 'Platform for Action' that it
adopted called for a gender perspective in all macro-economic policies and their budgetary dimensions.  The Outcome
Document of the UN General Assembly Special Session on Women held in June 2002, also called upon all the nations
to mainstream a gender perspective into their key macro-economic and social development programmes.  Emphasis on
gender budgeting was also placed by the Sixth Conference of Commonwealth Ministries of Women's Affairs held in
New Delhi in April 2002.
 
2.2       Many countries, both in the developed and the developing world have undertaken the exercise of gender budget
analysis.  Australia , Canada, UK, South Africa, Sri Lanka  and some of the African nations such as Tanzania and
Mozambique - are practicing gender budgeting in different forms.  The practices vary from gender audit in Australia  to
cross-sectoral gender sensitive analysis of expenditure in South Africa and to gender conscious planning and gender-
segregated data collation in Sri Lanka and presentation of Gender Impact Statement alongwith the budget in the U.K. 
Gender budget initiatives are currently being attempted in 35 countries following diverse trajectories in terms of the
process and partners involved in undertaking the activity. 
 
III        Gender Budgeting in India
3.1       In India, women constitute about half of the population who have traditionally been at disadvantage in any area
of life.  Efforts for removing this disparity, no doubt, has been made from the beginning by the government as well as
by the civil society in one form or the other.  The Planning Commission of India has always focused on women's issues
as per the perceptions of their members on the status of women in the country.  The Central Social Welfare Board
(1953) was the first major step in this direction during the period of First Five Year Plan.  The Second Five-Year Plan
(1956-1960) adopted the development of mahila mandals to undertake work at the grassroots level i.e. upto village
level. The Third, Fourth and Interim Plans (1961-74) carved out a special provision for women's education, pre-natal
and child health care, supplementary feeding for children and nursing of expectant mothers. The Fifth Five-Year Plan

153rd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/153rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:27]
(1974-1978) marked a major shift in the approach towards women, from welfare to development. The Sixth Five-Year
Plan (1980-85) accepted women's development as a separate economic agenda. It took a multi-disciplinary approach
with a three-pronged thrust on health, education and employment. The Seventh Five-Year Plan (1985-1990) declared as
its objective of bringing women into the mainstream of national development. Another landmark was the enactment of
73
rd & 74 th Amendment Bill providing reservation of 1/3 rd of seats for women in the units of local self-Government
across the country.
 
3.2       The Eighth Five-Year Plan (1992-1997), in fact, marked a paradigm shift from development to empowerment of
women and promised to ensure the flow of benefits to women in the core sectors like education, health and employment.
The outlay for women was raised substantially to Rs 2,000 crore in this Plan. The Eight Plan highlighted for the first
time the need to ensure a definite flow of funds from the general developmental sectors to the area of women
development.  The Plan document made an explicit statement that "the benefits of development from different sectors
should not by pass women and special programmes on women should complement the general development
programmes.  The latter, in turn, should reflect greater gender sensitivity".  Although this approach could not make
much dent in ensuring adequate flow of funds and benefit to women, the Eighth Plan marked the beginning of a gender
based budgeting, which for the first time, stressed upon the need for a gender sensitive perspective in the planning
process. 
 
3.3       The Ninth Plan (1997-2002) adopted 'Women Component Plan' as one of the major strategies and directed both
the Central and State Governments to ensure "not less than 30 per cent of the funds/benefits are earmarked in all the
women related sectors.  Special vigil advocated on the flow of the earmarked funds/benefits through an effective
mechanism to ensure that the proposed strategy brings forth a holistic approach towards empowering women.  The
National Policy for Empowerment of Women 2001 envisaged introduction of a gender perspective in the budgeting
process as an operational strategy.
 
3.4       Tenth Plan reinforces commitment to gender budgeting to establish its gender-differential impact and to translate
gender commitments into budgetary commitments.  Therefore, the Tenth Plan will initiate immediate action in tying up
these two effective concepts of Women Component Plan (WCP) and Gender Budgeting to play a complementary role to
each other, and thus ensure both preventive and post-facto action in enabling women to receive their rightful share from
all the women-related general development sectors.
 
3.5       In the context of India, where the gender bias is inherent in a male-dominated society, Gender Budgeting
becomes all the more relevant.  The Committee observes that the trends in sex ratio and other socio-economic indicators
clearly show, how the bias is getting accentuated in many parts of the country.  Over the years, during the course of
examination of various women and girl child related programmes/schemes, one factor which has been constantly
drawing the attention of the Committee is that inspite of well-conceived programmes and the funds allocated, there has
been no noticeable improvement in the status of women/girls.  Recently released State specific sex ratio figures of
Census 2001, do not leave any doubt in this regard.  The Committee is of the view that it is high time that the Budget of
the Government provides a clear indication of how much is earmarked specifically for the benefit of women so as to
ensure effective implementation of women/girl related programmes.  Department of Women & Child Development is
not only the nodal agency for such programmes but also the nodal Department assigned with carrying out the task of

153rd Report of HRD

Gender Budgeting, the Committee, accordingly decided to make a study on work done so far in this emerging area.
 
3.6       The Committee noted from the Economic Survey 2003-04, that a Task Force on Women and Children was
constituted in August 2000 under the Chairmanship of Shri K.C. Pant.  In its report submitted in April 2002, the Task
force inter-alia recommended the setting up of an Inter-Ministerial Standing Committee in the Department of Women
and Child Development, composed of officials and non-officials experts to review and monitor gender mainstreaming in
Government.  The Task Force also reviewed the whole gamut of legislations concerning women and recommended
amendment of 22 laws to make them more effective.  The concerned Ministries and Departments in the Government
have initiated necessary action for amending these laws.  The Department of Women & Child Development acts as a
watchdog on their actions.
 
3.7       The Committee was informed that the Government had recently constituted an Expert Group on "Classification
System of Government Transactions" whose terms of reference included examining the feasibility of and suggesting the
general approach to gender budgeting and economic classification.  The Expert Group has since submitted their report. 
As recommended by the Expert Group, some Ministries/Departments had been identified for gender budgeting, a
"tentative list" of which is given below:-
 
1.
                  Agriculture
2.                  Agro and Rural Industries
3.                  Communications and Information Technology
4.                  Environment and Forests
5.                  Food Processing Industries
6.                  Health and Family Welfare
7.                  Home Affairs
8.                  Human Resource Development
9.                  Labour
10.              Law and Justice
11.              Non-conventional Energy Resources
12.              Rural Development
13.              Science and Technology
14.              Social Justice and Empowerment
15.              Small Scale Industries
16.              Tribal Affairs
17.              Urban Employment and Poverty Alleviation
18.              Youth Affairs and Sports
 
3.8       The Expert Group has also recommended the classification of Government expenditure into three categories: a)
Women-centric programmes/schemes with 100 per cent pro-women allocation; b) Schemes/programmes that have a
significant (over 30 per cent) allocation for women; and c) Schemes/Programmes that cannot have gender sensitive
elements.
 
3.9
              These have been further divided into i) Protective and Welfare Services; ii) Regulatory Services; iii) Economic
Services; and iv) Social Service.
 
IV        Issues for Gender Budgeting
 
4.1       The Committee is of the opinion that in view of integration of gender equality with sustainable development,

153rd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/153rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:27]
need and importance of gender budgeting can hardly be over emphasised.  The aim of gender budgeting is to
generate/capture the gender based data/information, which will be relevant input for assessing the gender specific
impact of budgetary allocations.  The Committee found that currently gender segregated macro-economic data were not
available in India.  In the absence of such data from different sectors of our economy, the Committee feels, it will be
difficult to analyse the budgetary allocations on the basis of gender.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
process of gender budgeting should necessarily contain not only the segregation of gender based data but also aspects
like quantification of contribution of women in the economy; impact of Government budget on women; and policy
alternatives for evolving a gender sensitive social order.
 
V         Role of Department of Women and Child Development
 
5.1       The Committee heard the Secretary, Department of Women and Child Development, which has the mandate to
monitor the actions taken by different government agencies for the promotion of gender equality.  The Committee was
informed that the Department had taken the following initiatives in the recent years to advocate gender sensitivity in
planning and budget-making:-
 
q                   Consultations with State and Union territory Administrations through a workshop on 'Gender Issues and
Indicators' in November 1998, followed by another workshop on 'Developing Gender Development Index' (GDI)
and 'Gender Empowerment Measures' (GEM) and Establishing Indicators for States and Districts held on
December, 1998.
q                   A workshop on 'Engendering National Budgets in the South Asia Region' was held in July 2000 in New Delhi
in collaboration with the UNIFEM in which government representatives, UN agencies, media, NGOs, research
institutions, civil society and members of the Planning Commission participated.
q                   National Institute of Public Finance and Policy (NIPFP) was commissioned to study the gender-related
economic policy issues.  Based on the interim report of the Institute, the Economic Survey 2000-2001
highlighted for the first time aspects like, gender inequality and status of women, to be continued in its future
editions.  The NIPFP analyzed the Union Budget 2001-2002 from a gender perspective.
q                   Follow up Workshops in October and December, 2001 were organized, culminating in initiation of measures to
undertake analysis of State Budgets broadly adopting the methodology suggested by the NIPFP report on the
Union Budget.
q                   Taking the study done by NIPFP as a base, the Department of Women and Child Development carried out
concurrent Gender analysis of Union Budget for the financial years 2002-2003 and 2003-2004.
 
5.2       The Department of Women and Child Development informed the Committee that after extensive consultations
with gender experts and research institutions, it has initiated an exercise for State Gender Budget Analysis under the
coordination of the National Institute for Public Cooperation and Child Development.  Gender Budget studies have been
commissioned for 25 States through 19 social research scientists and research organizations to provide an analysis of the
changing status of women in the selected areas.  The exercise covers the years: 2000-2001, 2001-2002 and 2002-2003.
 
5.3       After looking at these efforts made by the Department, the Committee notes that so far, this exercise had
remained confined mainly to holding Seminars/Workshops since November, 1998.  The Committee is of the opinion

153rd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/153rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:27]
that the exercise of gender budgeting was not being carried out with the seriousness that it deserved.  The Committee
feels that the exercises undertaken by the Department so far, were hardly enough to sensitize the other Ministries and
Departments of the Government of India for undertaking this important activity.  Perhaps, the idea of making the
Department of Women & Child Development as a nodal agency for undertaking this exercise was to do the ground
exercise and evolve methodologies, etc.  to be later on adopted by other Ministries/Departments for gender budgeting in
an organized and comprehensive manner.  The Committee is constrained to say that unfortunately this has not happened
and we have not been able to evolve till today the required tools, methodologies and institutional mechanisms for
segregating gender based data, leave alone the quantification of contribution of women in the economy and the impact
of budgetary allocations on the women in our society.  Unless it is done, the Committee firmly believes, the goal of the
gender budgeting shall remain elusive.
 
5.4       The Committee in this regard would like to point out that the Department of Women and Child Development
which had started publishing a separate chapter titled "Gender Budget Initiatives" in its Annual Reports from the year
2001-02, has discontinued the same in 2003-04.  The Annual Report of the Department for the year 2003-04, in other
words, did not contain that chapter.  This fact was pointed out to the Secretary of the Department who explained that she
had joined the Department after the Annual Report had been published.  She, however, assured the Committee that not
only an explanation in writing would be taken from those responsible, but also the entire information for the current
year as well as for the year 2003-04 would be included in the Annual Report for 2004-05. 
 
5.5       It is not clear to the Committee, whether the decision to discontinue the chapter on Gender Budget Initiatives
was advertent or inadvertent.  If it was advertent, the Committee would like to know the reasons for this; and if it was
inadvertent, the Committee expresses its unhappiness in the matter.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
chapter on Gender Budget Initiatives should be restarted in the Annual Report from the year 2004-05, which should also
list the developments/steps taken in the year 2003-04.
 
VI        Gender Budgeting in other Ministries/Departments
 
6.1       The Committee was informed that the Cabinet Secretary had directed all the Ministries and Departments to
devote a chapter on gender issues in their Annual Reports. The Committee, however, observes that hardly any Ministry
and Department had started this exercise so far.  The Committee feels that the Department had not pursued this matter
with other Ministries and Departments effectively. The Committee recommends that the Department should make all
out efforts to persuade the other Ministries and Departments to include a chapter on gender budgeting in their Annual
Reports highlighting new initiatives/policies on gender related issues, resources available and their utilization and
gender disaggregated statistics for promoting gender awareness within and outside Government.
 
6.2       The Committee was informed that 18 Ministries /Departments which have women related specific schemes have
been identified to monitor for effective gender budgeting and expenditure. To a specific query as to the rationale behind
identifying only 18 Ministries for gender budgeting, the Department informed that bulk of the government's budget goes
to these 18 Ministries/Departments identified by it. 
 
6.3       The Committee appreciates the idea of identifying some Ministries/Departments for impressing upon them to
undertake the process of gender budgeting on a wider scale.  The Committee, however, feels that to the best of its

153rd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/153rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:27]
knowledge, the identified Ministries/Departments have apparently not been able to take up the exercise of gender
budgeting in their respective areas.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take up with
these Ministries/Departments to start the exercise of gender based analysis of their allocations/expenditure from the next
year 2005-06 positively.
 
6.4       The Committee is of the opinion that gender based analysis of allocations should be done for the entire Budget
of the government. This exercise, therefore, will have to be taken up by all the Ministries/Departments of the
Government of India, not only by those identified for this purpose so far.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the remaining ones should also be sensitized to infuse gender aspects into their allocations/expenditure without further
delay.  This is necessary to have holistic idea about gender based allocations of the entire Budget of the Government of
India. The Department of Women and Child Development being a nodal agency should assume greater responsibilities
for undertaking this exercise of the gender budgeting by all the Ministries/Departments without further delay.
 
6.5       The Committee notes that the objective of gender budgeting is there, the Ministries/Departments are identified,
but the results are not forthcoming in absence of any guidelines for this purpose.  The Committee fails to understand the
Department’s limitations in this regard.  The Committee recommends to have specific guidelines laid down regarding
gender budgeting to be followed by all the Ministries/Departments.  This would still be quite possible on the basis of
experiences/feedback received on the problems being faced in implementation of gender budgeting.
 
VII      Lack of Inter-Ministerial Coordination
 
7.1       The Committee notes that creation of an inter-ministerial body has been recommended by a Task Force headed
by Shri K.C. Pant in April 2002.  Creation of an Inter-Departmental Steering Committee has also been suggested by the
Expert Group on Gender Budgeting.  Main task of such a Committee will be to develop an overall time-bound
programme for Gender Budgeting in identified Ministries and also to monitor and review the progress.  The Task Force
has also suggested that the Secretary, Department of Women & Child Development should be the Chairperson of the
Inter-Departmental Steering Committee.
 
7.2       The Committee appreciates the idea of having a monitoring and coordination mechanism for the purpose of
gender budgeting exercise.  Such a machinery assumes greater relevance in view of the fact that gender budgeting has to
be ultimately taken up not only by all the Departments/Ministries but by the State governments and local bodies as
well.  The Committee, however, fails to understand as to why no such inter-ministerial body could be created so far,
despite the specific suggestions made by the two important groups mentioned above.  The Committee is not aware
whether any initiative has been taken by the Department so far.  In view of the importance and urgency of such inter-
ministerial coordinating mechanism, the Committee urges upon the Government to take immediate steps to put such a
machinery in place.
 
7.3       The Committee feels that apart from having an inter-ministerial body for coordinating and monitoring, it is
equally important to have intra-ministerial/Departmental cells for coordinating/facilitating this exercise within each
Ministry/Department.  Such cells would certainly provide required impetus for this exercise.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that such monitoring cell should be created in all the Ministries/Departments.
 

153rd Report of HRD

VIII     Developing suitable Methodology
 
8.1       The Committee notes that we are yet to evolve suitable methodologies, tools, etc. for doing an effective Gender
Budget Analysis.  The Department of Women & Child Development has, with the help of NIPFP, undertaken some
exercise in this regard, which is limited to only few Departments/Ministries.
 
            The Committee emphasizes the need for developing/refining methodologies and gender tools like gender audit,
gender impact assessment, gender analysis and gender budgeting to monitor implementation and impact of gender
policies. 
 
8.2       The Committee also emphasizes the urgent need for undertaking research activities in different aspects of gender
budgeting including gender benefit incidence analysis.
 
IX        Need for Training/Capacity Building
 
9.1       The Committee notes that the exercise of Gender Budgeting, which is in the process of evolving suitable tools,
techniques and methodologies pre-supposes the need for orientation/training for the officials responsible for the job in
different Ministries/Departments.  They can undertake this exercise effectively and efficiently only if they are familiar
or have been adequately trained for the purpose.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the training and capacity-
building efforts should be made for the officials working in the Government Departments both at the Centre as well as
in States.  Possibility of arranging orientation/training for the people's representatives in local bodies should also be
considered.
           
9.2       The Committee recommends that government functionaries and financial specialists should be sensitized since it
is with the help of theses people that budget is made and auditing of expenditure is done at the end of financial year. If
they would do their job effectively, it will help in further streamlining the gender budget analysis. This should,
therefore, be specifically trained/sensitized to the importance of the task as their knowledge and motivation becomes
critical in determining the accuracy and validity of such an exercise.
X         Need for Impact Assessment
 
10.1     The Committee notes that there are still a number of core issues like the increasing burden of poverty on women;
inaccessibility and unequal access to health, family welfare and educational services; inequality in access and control
over assets and resources, both within and outside the family; inequality and inaccessibility to work, employment and
decision-making; and violence against women including domestic and otherwise, which have apparently some direct or
indirect bearing on framing policy relating to gender budgeting.
 
10.2     In view of this, the need for impact assessment of gender allocations, the Committee feels, assumes greater
importance. This impact assessment should not only be restricted to women-specific and pro-women programmes but
also should extend to impact of mainstream expenditure on women. 
 
10.3     The integration of gender in budgeting policies, Committee feels, would not only ensure better transparency and
accountability in the allocations meant for women, it would, at the same time, help evaluate the effectiveness of
resources utilized in delivering the intended results.  Simply focusing on how much money has been allocated for

153rd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/153rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:27]
women-specific and pro-women schemes could be counter-productive, if the outcome and performance of schemes were
far from the desired level.  This would, in fact, help us monitor output as well as input.
           
10.4     The Committee, therefore, would like the Department to explore the possibility of including a comparative
'Gender Impact Statement' as a separate part in Annual Budget of the government.
 
XI        Gender Budgeting in States
 
11.1     The exercise of gender budgeting, the Committee is of the view, would remain woefully incomplete without
extending it to State Budgets as well, because the States and Union territories account for bulk of expenditure on social
sector which relate to welfare/empowerment of women.  The Committee is happy to note that the exercise of State
budget from gender perspective was already on.  The Committee was informed that data from only ten States- Assam,
Bihar, Meghalaya, Gujarat, J&K, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, M.P. Orissa and Manipur were received.  The Committee has
learnt that due to wide variation in nomenclature of schemes/programmes across the States and discrepancies in data,
which require further validation, authentic collection of results and a comparative analysis is difficult to be made.  The
Committee, therefore, urges upon the government to formulate uniform procedures pertaining to gender budgeting and
analysis and disseminate these to the States.  The Committee also emphasizes the need for standardizing nomenclature,
terms, etc. with a view to avoiding possible ambiguities and confusions across the States.
 
11.2     The Committee is aware of the practical difficulties involved in having a meaningful analysis of State budgets,
but at the same time, it cannot ignore to emphasize about the necessity of undertaking and refining the exercise of State
budget analyses.
 
11.3     The Committee notes that of all the States and UTs, only ten have supplied data regarding their budgets, which is
not a very encouraging sign in this regard.  The Committee does not know the reasons behind it.  The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the States, which have not responded should be approached and persuaded to undertake/start
the exercises at the earliest.  The Department should act as a facilitator and provide necessary help, expertise, etc. for
this purpose to the States.
 
XII      Gender Budgeting in Local Bodies
 
12.1     The Committee emphasizes the need for taking up gender based analysis not only for the States but also for local
bodies - nagarpalikas, panchayats, etc. which also undertake social expenditure having gender specific benefits. 
 
XIII     Gender Budgeting in Private Sector
 
13.1     The Committee emphasizes the need for undertaking the exercise of gender analysis of allocations/expenditure
in private sector also.  The Committee would like to point out that of the total women workforce, their share in private
sector is far larger than those in the public sector.  In unorganized sector, there are no legitimate and other safeguards
even to claim minimum wages, leave aside other benefits.   In view of this situation, the Committee feels that no
realistic assessments and conclusions can be made about gender budgeting at the national level without involving
private sector. The Committee is aware of the practical limitations involved in taking up such exercise, it still

153rd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/153rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:27]
emphasizes the greater need for starting gender budgeting in private sector also.
 
XIV     Strengthening Statutory Support for Women
 
14.1     The Committee notes that the Task Force had reviewed the whole gamut of legislations concerning women and
had recommended amendment to 22 laws with a view to making them more effective.  The Committee is also of the
view that existing Statutes concerning women and girl child need to be reviewed minutely by the experts in the light of
latest developments and emerging scenario with a view to amending them to make them relevant and effective.  This
Committee has emphasised this aspect in several of its earlier reports submitted to the Government.  But the Committee
is of the opinion that the Department of Women & Child Development has not been able to act timely and sufficiently in
having the exercise of getting these laws amended expedited.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Department should submit a Status Report on those 22 laws identified alongwith latest position regarding the actions so
far taken for amending those laws.  The Committee further feels that the Department should try and fix a time schedule
for amending every law and impress upon the concerned Ministries alongwith Ministry of Law & Justice to accomplish
the work within that time.

OBSERVATIONS/ RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
III        GENDER BUDGETING IN INDIA
 
3.5       In the context of India, where the gender bias is inherent in a male-dominated society, Gender Budgeting
becomes all the more relevant.  The Committee observes that the trends in sex ratio and other socio-economic indicators
clearly show, how the bias is getting accentuated in many parts of the country.  Over the years, during the course of
examination of various women and girl child related programmes/schemes, one factor which has been constantly
drawing the attention of the Committee is that inspite of well-conceived programmes and the funds allocated, there has
been no noticeable improvement in the status of women/girls.  Recently released State specific sex ratio figures of
Census 2001, do not leave any doubt in this regard.  The Committee is of the view that it is high time that the Budget of
the Government provides a clear indication of how much is earmarked specifically for the benefit of women so as to
ensure effective implementation of women/girl related programmes.  Department of Women & Child Development is
not only the nodal agency for such programmes but also the nodal Department assigned with carrying out the task of
Gender Budgeting, the Committee, accordingly decided to make a study on work done so far in this emerging area.
 
IV        Issues for Gender Budgeting
 
4.1       The Committee is of the opinion that in view of integration of gender equality with sustainable development,
need and importance of gender budgeting can hardly be over emphasised.  The aim of gender budgeting is to
generate/capture the gender based data/information, which will be relevant input for assessing the gender specific
impact of budgetary allocations.  The Committee found that currently gender segregated macro-economic data were not
available in India.  In the absence of such data from different sectors of our economy, the Committee feels, it will be
difficult to analyse the budgetary allocations on the basis of gender.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the

153rd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/153rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:27]
process of gender budgeting should necessarily contain not only the segregation of gender based data but also aspects
like quantification of contribution of women in the economy; impact of Government budget on women; and policy
alternatives for evolving a gender sensitive social order.
 
V         Role of Department of Women and Child Development
 
5.3       After looking at these efforts made by the Department, the Committee notes that so far, this exercise had
remained confined mainly to holding Seminars/Workshops since November, 1998.  The Committee is of the opinion
that the exercise of gender budgeting was not being carried out with the seriousness that it deserved.  The Committee
feels that the exercises undertaken by the Department so far, were hardly enough to sensitize the other Ministries and
Departments of the Government of India for undertaking this important activity.  Perhaps, the idea of making the
Department of Women & Child Development as a nodal agency for undertaking this exercise was to do the ground
exercise and evolve methodologies, etc.  to be later on adopted by other Ministries/Departments for gender budgeting in
an organized and comprehensive manner.  The Committee is constrained to say that unfortunately this has not happened
and we have not been able to evolve  till today the required tools, methodologies and institutional mechanisms for
segregating gender based data, leave alone the quantification of contribution of women in the economy and the impact
of budgetary allocations on the women in our society.  Unless it is done, the Committee firmly believes, the goal of the
gender budgeting shall remain elusive.
 
5.5       It is not clear to the Committee, whether the decision to discontinue the chapter on Gender Budget Initiatives
was advertent or inadvertent.  If it was advertent, the Committee would like to know the reasons for this; and if it was
inadvertent, the Committee expresses its unhappiness in the matter.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
chapter on Gender Budget Initiatives should be restarted in the Annual Report from the year 2004-05, which should also
list the developments/steps taken in the year 2003-04.
VI        Gender Budgeting in other Ministries/Departments
 
The Committee, however, observes that hardly any Ministry and Department had started this exercise so far. 
The Committee feels that the Department had not pursued this matter with other Ministries and Departments effectively.
The Committee recommends that the Department should make all out efforts to persuade the other Ministries and
Departments to include a chapter on gender budgeting in their Annual Reports highlighting new initiatives/policies on
gender related issues, resources available and their utilization and gender disaggregated statistics for promoting gender
awareness within and outside Government. (Para 6.1)
 
6.3       The Committee appreciates the idea of identifying some Ministries/Departments for impressing upon them to
undertake the process of gender budgeting on a wider scale.  The Committee, however, feels that to the best of its
knowledge, the identified Ministries/Departments have apparently not been able to take up the exercise of gender
budgeting in their respective areas.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take up with
these Ministries/Departments to start the exercise of gender based analysis of their allocations/expenditure from the next
year 2005-06 positively.
 
6.4       The Committee is of the opinion that gender based analysis of allocations should be done for the entire Budget
of the government. This exercise, therefore, will have to be taken up by all the Ministries/Departments of the

153rd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/153rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:27]
Government of India, not only by those identified for this purpose so far.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the remaining ones should also be sensitized to infuse gender aspects into their allocations/expenditure without further
delay.  This is necessary to have holistic idea about gender based allocations of the entire Budget of the Government of
India. The Department of Women and Child Development being a nodal agency should assume greater responsibilities
for undertaking this exercise of the gender budgeting by all the Ministries/Departments without further delay.
 
6.5       The Committee notes that the objective of gender budgeting is there, the Ministries/Departments are identified,
but the results are not forthcoming in absence of any guidelines for this purpose.  The Committee fails to understand the
Department’s limitations in this regard.  The Committee recommends to have specific guidelines laid down regarding
gender budgeting to be followed by all the Ministries/Departments.  This would still be quite possible on the basis of
experiences/feedback received on the problems being faced in implementation of gender budgeting.
 
VII      Lack of Inter-Ministerial Coordination
 
7.2       The Committee appreciates the idea of having a monitoring and coordination mechanism for the purpose of
gender budgeting exercise.  Such a machinery assumes greater relevance in view of the fact that gender budgeting has to
be ultimately taken up not only by all the Departments/Ministries but by the State governments and local bodies as
well.  The Committee, however, fails to understand as to why no such inter-ministerial body could be created so far,
despite the specific suggestions made by the two important groups mentioned above.  The Committee is not aware
whether any initiative has been taken by the Department so far.  In view of the importance and urgency of such inter-
ministerial coordinating mechanism, the Committee urges upon the Government to take immediate steps to put such a
machinery in place.
 
7.3       The Committee feels that apart from having an inter-ministerial body for coordinating and monitoring, it is
equally important to have intra-ministerial/Departmental cells for coordinating/facilitating this exercise within each
Ministry/Department.  Such cells would certainly provide required impetus for this exercise.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that such monitoring cell should be created in all the Ministries/Departments.
 
VIII     Developing suitable Methodology.
 
8.1       The Committee notes that we are yet to evolve suitable methodologies, tools, etc. for doing an effective Gender
Budget Analysis.  The Department of Women & Child Development has, with the help of NIPFP, undertaken some
exercise in this regard, which is limited to only few Departments/Ministries.
            The Committee emphasizes the need for developing/refining methodologies and gender tools like gender audit,
gender impact assessment, gender analysis and gender budgeting to monitor implementation and impact of gender
policies.  
8.2       The Committee also emphasizes the urgent need for undertaking research activities in different aspects of gender
budgeting including gender benefit incidence analysis.
IX        Need for Training/Capacity Building
9.1       The Committee notes that the exercise of Gender Budgeting, which is in the process of evolving suitable tools,
techniques and methodologies pre-supposes the need for orientation/training for the officials responsible for the job in
different Ministries/Departments.  They can undertake this exercise effectively and efficiently only if they are familiar

153rd Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/153rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:27]
or have been adequately trained for the purpose.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the training and capacity-
building efforts should be made for the officials working in the Government Departments both at the Centre as well as
in States.  Possibility of arranging orientation/training for the people's representatives in local bodies should also be
considered.
           
9.2       The Committee recommends that government functionaries and financial specialists should be sensitized since it
is with the help of theses people that budget is made and auditing of expenditure is done at the end of financial year. If
they would do their job effectively, it will help in further streamlining the gender budget analysis. This should,
therefore, be specifically trained/sensitized to the importance of the task as their knowledge and motivation becomes
critical in determining the accuracy and validity of such an exercise.
X         Need for Impact Assessment
10.1     The Committee notes that there are still a number of core issues like the increasing burden of poverty on women;
inaccessibility and unequal access to health, family welfare and educational services; inequality in access and control
over assets and resources, both within and outside the family; inequality and inaccessibility to work, employment and
decision-making; and violence against women including domestic and otherwise, which have apparently some direct or
indirect bearing on framing policy relating to gender budgeting.
 
10.2     In view of this, the need for impact assessment of gender allocations, the Committee feels, assumes greater
importance. This impact assessment should not only be restricted to women-specific and pro-women programmes but
also should extend to impact of mainstream expenditure on women. 
 
10.3     The integration of gender in budgeting policies, Committee feels, would not only ensure better transparency and
accountability in the allocations meant for women, it would, at the same time, help evaluate the effectiveness of
resources utilized in delivering the intended results.  Simply focusing on how much money has been allocated for
women-specific and pro-women schemes could be counter-productive, if the outcome and performance of schemes were
far from the desired level.  This would, in fact, help us monitor output as well as input.
           
10.4     The Committee, therefore, would like the Department to explore the possibility of including a comparative
'Gender Impact Statement' as a separate part in Annual Budget of the government.
 
XI        Gender Budgeting in States
 
11.1     The exercise of gender budgeting, the Committee is of the view, would remain woefully incomplete without
extending it to State Budgets as well, because the States and Union territories account for bulk of expenditure on social
sector which relate to welfare/empowerment of women.  The Committee is happy to note that the exercise of State
budget from gender perspective was already on.  The Committee was informed that data from only ten States- Assam,
Bihar, Meghalaya, Gujarat, J&K, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, M.P. Orissa and Manipur were received.  The Committee has
learnt that due to wide variation in nomenclature of schemes/programmes across the States and discrepancies in data,
which require further validation, authentic collection of results and a comparative analysis is difficult to be made.  The
Committee, therefore, urges upon the government to formulate uniform procedures pertaining to gender budgeting and
analysis and disseminate these to the States.  The Committee also emphasizes the need for standardizing nomenclature,
terms, etc. with a view to avoiding possible ambiguities and confusions across the States.

11.2     The Committee is aware of the practical difficulties involved in having a meaningful analysis of State budgets,
but at the same time, it cannot ignore to emphasize about the necessity of undertaking and refining the exercise of State
budget analyses.
 
11.3     The Committee notes that of all the States and UTs, only ten have supplied data regarding their budgets, which is
not a very encouraging sign in this regard.  The Committee does not know the reasons behind it.  The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the States, which have not responded should be approached and persuaded to undertake/start
the exercises at the earliest.  The Department should act as a facilitator and provide necessary help, expertise, etc. for
this purpose to the States.

PREFACE
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development, having
been authorized by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf this Hundred-Fifty Fourth Report on the ‘Functioning of
Navodaya Vidyalayas’.
2.         The Navodaya  Vidyalayas were set up by the Government primarily with the view to providing quality education upto
the secondary level to the children predominantly from the rural areas at an affordable cost.  These Vidyalayas, after several years
of their existence, have no doubt, shown good results but their functioning leaves a lot to be desired. Concerns have been
expressed on different aspects of their working by all concerned ¾ students, teachers, parents, educationists and the general
public as well.  The Committee also had invariably been emphasising the need for taking remedial measures for addressing those
concerns, but with no signs of visible improvement. 
3.         The Committee decided to make an indepth study of this unique and premier school system covering all aspects of its
functioning with a view to identifying the problem areas and suggesting measures for tackling them.
4.         The Committee visited several Navodaya Vidyalayas in different parts of the country and held discussions with the
teaching/non-teaching staff, students, parents, State Government authorities and also the general public.
5.         The Committee sought written replies on detailed questionnaire prepared on the basis of various documents/papers
furnished by the Department of Secondary and Higher Education and also on issues/problem areas highlighted during its on-the-
spot visits to some of  the Vidyalayas and deliberations held there.  The Committee also held extensive discussions with the
Secretary, Department of Secondary and Higher Education and Commissioner, Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti and other concerned
officials on a number of occasions.

REPORT
 
I           INTRODUCTION
 
1.1       The National Policy on Education-1986 envisaged establishment of a Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya (JNV) in each district
of the country. The Navodaya Vidyalayas (NVs) are fully residential, co-educational institutions covering classes VI to XII. The
Navodaya Vidyalaya Scheme started with two model schools in 1985-86 at present, covers 509 Districts in 34 States/UTs of the
country.
 
OBJECTIVES
 
            The main objectives of the JNVs as set forth are:
 
1.         To provide good quality modern education including a strong component of culture, inculcation of values, awareness of
the environment, adventure activities and physical education to the talented children predominantly from the rural areas
irrespective of their family’s socio economic condition;
2.          To serve the objectives of excellence coupled with equality and social justice.
3.          To ensure that all students of Navodaya Vidyalayas attain a reasonable level of competence in three languages as
envisaged in Three Language Formula;
4.          To promote national integration by providing opportunities to talented children, largely from rural areas of the country to
live and learn together and develop their full potential, and
5.         To serve, in each district, as focal points for improvement in the quality of school education in general, through sharing of
experiences and facilities.
 
           SALIENT FEATURES
 
The following features establish the separate identity of JNVs: -
           
(i)                  Good quality modern education for talented children predominantly from rural areas.
(ii)                Ratio/class of candidates  - 
Rural, atleast   75%, Urban at the most    25%
(iii)               Reservation of seats for students from SC/ST categories in proportion to their population in the district subject to the
national minimum.
(iv)              Reservation of seats for girls - 33%.
(v)                Co-educational and fully residential, upto Class-XII.
(vi)              Location- usually in rural areas on the basis of offer of cost free land and rent free temporary buildings by State/UT
Governments.
(vii)             Free education including boarding and lodging as well as expenses on uniforms, text books, and stationery etc.
(viii)           Affiliated to CBSE.
(ix)              Admission in only Class-VI through objective type test designed and conducted by CBSE.
(x)                Implementation of three-language formula.
(xi)              Regional language as medium of instruction for first three years and Hindi/English afterwards.
(xii)30% of students in Class IX from a Vidyalaya located in one linguistic area spend one academic year in a Vidyalaya in a
different linguistic region to promote national integration through understanding of the diversity and plurality of
country’s culture and people.
 
II    Organizational set-up
 
2.1       The Navodaya Vidyalayas are managed by Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti (NVS) which is an autonomous organization of

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
the Ministry of Human Resource Development, Department of Secondary and Higher Education.  The Samiti functions through an
Executive Committee under the Chairmanship of the Union Minister of Human Resource Development. Union Minister of State
of Education is normally the Vice-Chairman of the Samiti.  Members of Parliament, representatives from industry, representatives
from State Governments and eminent educationists are nominated as Members of the Samiti. The Executive Committee is assisted
by Finance Committee and Academic Advisory Committee in its functions.
 
2.2       For each Vidyalaya, there is a Vidyalaya Advisory Committee and a Vidyalaya Management Committee for the general
supervision of the Vidyalaya. District Magistrate of the concerned district is the Chairman of these Committees with local
educationists, public representatives and officials from the district as members.
 
III        Norms for opening of Navodaya Vidyalayas 
3.1       As envisaged in the scheme, one Navodaya Vidyalaya each is to be established in all the districts, which were in existence
in the country at the commencement of Eighth Five Year Plan. However, due to reorganization/creation of new districts
subsequently during the Ninth Five Year Plan and thereafter, several new districts have been created in many States and proposals
have been received from the State Governments for opening more JNVs. Accordingly, it has been decided to cover 574 districts
existing in the country (excluding Tamil Nadu which has not yet accepted the Scheme). As on 31.8.04, JNVs have been
sanctioned in 509 districts of the country. Remaining 65 districts are proposed to be covered by the end of Tenth Plan Period.
 
3.2       The Committee was given to understand that out of 509 sanctioned JNVs, 485 JNVs are functional.  Out of the remaining
24 non-functional JNVs, 9 have been sanctioned only during the years 2003-04 and 2004-2005 and are likely to start functioning
from the next academic year.  The Committee is, however, constrained to note that out of the remaining 15 non-functional JNVs,
three JNVs, one each in Bihar, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh were sanctioned in 2001-2002, ten JNVs, one each in Gujarat,
Haryana, Jharkhand, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Tripura, UP and Uttaranchal and two in Mizoram were sanctioned in 2002-2003.  In
all these cases, temporary accommodation has not been made available by the concerned State Governments so far.  The
Committee fails to understand the reasons behind the inability of the State Governments in fulfilling the minimum requirements
for proposals initiated by them. The Committee observes that majority of these districts are located in remote and tribal areas
where JNVs are primarily required to be opened. The Committee is particularly disturbed by the situation in Mizoram. The
Committee finds that out of the six JNVs sanctioned in Mizoram, two JNVs opened – one in 1987-1988 in Lungli District and the
other in Chimtupui District in 1992-93 had to be closed down due to less enrolment and administrative reasons. In respect of three
JNVs sanctioned in 2002-2003, temporary accommodation is yet to be made available.  At present, only one JNV is functional.
The remaining two districts of the State are yet to be covered. The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for the
Department for taking up such cases at the highest level.  The Committee feels that given the peculiar geographical location and
the overall backwardness of the North-East region, the Central Government should make special efforts on meeting all the
requirements to make JNVs functional at the earliest.
 
3.3.      The Committee recommends that concerted efforts should be made to expedite not only the sanctioning of all the 574
JNVs, but also to make them functional in a time bound manner. The Committee would like the Ministry to play the role of a
facilitator in clearing the proposals received as well as in encouraging other proposals to be put up for opening new schools in the
remaining districts.
 
3.4       As per the information made available to the Committee, out of the 485 functioning JNVs, only 368 JNVs are functioning
in permanent sites and 117 JNVs are functioning at temporary sites.  The Committee was given to understand that 35 JNVs are
likely to be completed by 31
st March 2005, 6 JNVs by 31st March 2006, 1 by 31st August, 2006, in respect of 13 JNVs, land is yet
to be transferred, and land allotted to 2 JNVs was under dispute.
 

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
3.5       The Committee is not aware about the latest position in all such cases.  The Committee, however, apprehends that no
significant progress would be there in most of the cases.  The Committee observes that different construction agencies both state
and national level are involved in the construction of school buildings.  The Committee, however, finds that civil construction in
the schools was generally running much behind the schedule, because of one reason or the other.  Apart from non-availability of
funds in time, the Committee found that long procedures and lack of proper coordination between different agencies involved in
the exercise were responsible for such delays resulting in time and cost over-run, which must be avoided.  The Committee
strongly feels that there should be a mechanism at central level working in co-ordination with all concerned state authorities which
would constantly monitor all such cases as per time bound action plan. The Committee would also like the Ministry to prepare a
consolidated estimate required for construction of pending buildings and plead strongly for that fund with the Ministry of Finance.
 
3.6       The Committee was informed that opening of JNVs depends upon receipt of the proposals from the concerned States/UT
Governments offering 30 acres of suitable land free of cost with sufficient temporary buildings and other infrastructure free of rent
or on permanent basis to accommodate 240 students and staff for three to four years or till the Samiti constructs its own buildings
at the permanent site. The Committee notes that the Samit is, however, not very rigid about the criteria of 30 acres of land which
can be relaxed to the extent of 10 acres of land in hilly areas or wherever there is extreme scarcity of land on case to case basis. 
 
 
3.7       The Committee was informed that 104 JNVs are located in less than 30 acres of land, { with the minimum area of land
(9.5 acres)  in JNV Bhadoi district, UP } out of which maximum number of 29 JNVs are located in Chandigarh region; as many as
26 JNVs do not have any play field; and most of the JNVs in J&K are not having even a permanent school building. The
Committee appreciates the compulsions to relax the condition of 30 acres of land in selective cases where land is scarce. 
However, the Committee recommends that the relaxation should be granted only after carefully examining the interests of the
students and their development.  For example, the paucity of land should not be a constraint for games & sports facilities and for
this the sports facilities available in nearby schools, institutions, clubs etc, could be shared so that the students are not deprived of
their educational and developments needs.  The Committee would also emphasise that all efforts should be made to provide
required facilities in JNVs   which can be made available in less than 30 acres of land area at the earliest.
 
IV        INFRASTRUCTURE
4.1       Every Navodaya Vidyalaya is stipulated to have a school building on 2000 sq. meters of space, having 30 classrooms, a
library, a computer room, a staff room, laboratory, six dormitories, boys and girls hostels, dining & kitchen facility, residence for
faculty & staff with ample open spaces for play and recreation.  A Smriti Van in the memory of late Sh. Rajiv Gandhi, former
Prime Minister of India, forms an integral part of all the Navodaya School campuses.  Besides, the provision for underground
water tank, one tubewell, a sub-station building, proper sewerage system, water supply and boundary wall for the entire building
also forms the components of the scheme.
 
4.2       The Committee during its visits observed general lack of or poor infrastructure in the Navodaya Vidyalayas. Same was the
report given by many witnesses with whom the Committee held discussions.  Upkeep of the buildings and facilities both in
schools and in hostels were found not upto the mark.  Less said is better about the infrastructure of Smriti Vans. 
 
4.3       The Committee was given to understand that out of 485 functional JNVs as on 31.8.2004, 368 JNVs are functioning in
permanent site.  The Committee, however, observes that out of these 368 JNVs, 104 are having land area less than the prescribed
areas of 30 acres.  And out of these JNVs, 11 JNVs are having less than 18 acres, 9 JNVs are having temporary buildings,
situation is really bad in J&K as out of 13 JNVs, 4 are running in S.P. sheds and 1 in temporary building.  The Committee is not

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
satisfied about the buildings and infrastructure available in the remaining JNVs in the state, as exact details have not been made
known to the Committee. Actual status of buildings and infrastructure of JNVs in Chandigarh, Hyderabad and Jaipur Region has
also not been made available to the Committee.  The Committee apprehends that these JNVs must be in a bad state, totally lacking
the minimum requirements.  The Committee is also not aware about the status of JNVs having 30 acres of land and functioning
from permanent sites.  The Committee feels that JNVs functioning from permanent site does not seem to make much difference. 
The Committee wonders about the factors delaying the provision of required infrastructure once land is made available.  The
Committee recommends that all JNVs having permanent site should be provided required buildings and infrastructure without any
delay.  The Committee strongly feels that an effective monitoring mechanism should be evolved for accomplishing this over
delayed task.  The Department/NVS should work out a time bound action plan in this regard in active coordination with Regional
Offices, State authorities and district administration.  Funds as and when required should be provided for this purpose but on the
condition that all works are implemented at the earliest.
 
4.4       The Committee further recommends that apart from providing the requisite basic infrastructure, provision for fire safety
should also be made on priority basis to make the buildings safer. Regular inspections should be made to see that buildings etc
were properly maintained.  The school authorities should also discuss the problem of maintenance of building in the Parents
Teachers Meetings, so that the local authorities could be pressurized to do the job.
 
V         STUDENT INTAKE
 
5.1       Prescribed student intake per Navodaya Vidyalaya is 600 students i.e. 400 boys and 200 girls.  The Committee is,
however, surprised to note that only 33 NVs have student intake ranging from 502 to 572.  Student strength as on 31.3.04 is much
below the prescribed limit in the remaining functional 452 NVs.  Position in some Regions is very disturbing.  Details as indicated
below are self-revealing: -
 
Region No. of JNVs Average student strength
Shillong 58 262
Pune 53 324
Chandigarh 42 328
Patna 50 343
Lucknow 66 350
Bhopal 75 351
Jaipur 47 379
 
           
Some of the state-wise figures are a cause for serious concern. The Committee apprehends that school-wise position would
be even more damaging. The Committee fails to understand the factors responsible for overall student intake in JNVs remaining
much below the prescribed limit.  Either JNVs have failed to attract students or adequate infrastructure for required student
capacity is not there.  Both the situations are very discouraging.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department
should take steps for conducting a survey for analyzing the reasons for low intake of student in JNVs with particular focus on the
JNVs having very low figures and based on the findings of the survey, take remedial action.  The Committee feels that except
under unavoidable circumstances, the seats must not be allowed to remain vacant.  The Committee opines that a merit list of all
the students aspiring for the admission may be prepared and the vacancies, if any, may be filled up from amongst the candidates in
the list after relaxing the qualifying forms.  The candidates belonging to weaker section of the society should be given preference
while filling up such vacancies.
 
VI        COMPUTER EDUCATION IN NAVODAYA VIDYALAYAS
 

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
6.1       JNVs being model pace-setting institutions in the district are equipped with required educational technology including
computers.  The Committee was given to understand that computers have been provided to 454 JNVs.  Under the Computer
Education Programme, each Vidyalaya is equipped to develop a Computer lab with minimum 7 P-III computers.  The main
objectives of Computer Education Programme of the Vidyalayas are to:
 
·                    Facilitate the students to learn computer literacy and hands on experience from class VI to XII.
·                    Create computer culture and consciousness among the young rural students.
·                    Familiarize the students with different range of computer applications and help them to understand the potential of
Information Technology in learning process.
·                    Integrate Information Technology with classroom transaction.
·                    Improving the capacities of the children in terms of their performance in scholastic and non-scholastic activities.
·                    Empower the teachers to use computers as one of their important teaching aid.
·                    Extending the facility of Computer Literacy to the students of neighborhood schools.
 
6.2       The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Samiti in the field of Computer education.  It, however, notices that
a large number of schools were yet to have this facility. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all the JNVs should be
covered under this scheme at the earliest. The Committee opines that the maintenance and connectivity with Internet should be
ensured to get optimum utilization of computers.  The Committee recommends that all the teachers should be encouraged and
suitably trained to work on computers.
 
VII      SMART SCHOOLS SCHEME
 
7.1       33 Vidyalayas have been identified as SMART Schools with one JNV from each State/UT.  Computer Equipment
comprising 34 computers (2 Server Computers, and 32 Node Computers), one Multimedia LCD Projector, one Laser Printer, one
Scanner, one CD Writer, one Modem, 6 UPSs (2 UPSs for Server Computers and 4 UPSs for Node Computers) are supplied to
each JNV selected as Smart School in addition to existing quota of computer equipment.  These Vidyalayas have developed
Computer Lab(s) with LAN facility.
7.2       The Committee recommends that more Vidyalayas may be covered under the scheme.  Local M.P. and MLA can be
associated for extending funds to such Vidyalayas for purchasing computers.

IX        CRITERIA FOR ADMISSION IN NAVODAYA VIDALAYAS
9.1       Admission to NVs is done on the basis of a Selection Test, for which a candidate has to fulfill the following eligibility
conditions: -

(a)    A candidate appearing for the Selection Test must be studying in Class V in a recognized school in that district where
he/she is seeking admission. Actual admission in Class VI is given subject to the condition of having passed Class V
before admission.
 
(b)   A candidate seeking admission must be between the age group 9-13 years on 1 st May of the year for which the Selection
Test is conducted.
 
(c)    A candidate must have studied and passed Class III, IV & V from recognized school/schools in the preceding three
continuous academic session for which the Selection Test is conducted spending one full academic session in each class
through the formal system of education, without any repetition of class, gap and/ or break in attendance.
 
(d)   A candidate who is not promoted to Class V before November of the preceding academic year, for which the test is
conducted, is not eligible to apply.
 
(e)    A candidate is not allowed second attempt to appear in the selection test under any circumstances.
 
(f)     A candidate seeking admission under the rural quota must have studied and passed III, IV & V from recognized school (s)
located in the rural areas.
 
            The above conditions are applicable to all the candidates irrespective to their caste or gender.  Efforts are made to ensure
that one-third of the total seats are filled up by girls.
 
9.2       The Samiti has given the following figures about the percentage of students belonging to SC/ST categories, girls and rural
areas in the Navodaya Vidayalayas, which is well above national norms (15% SC & 7.5% ST):

9.3      The Committee appreciates the adequate representation of SCs, STs and girls in Navodaya Vidyalayas. It still feels that
there is scope for further increase in percentages of girls as well as students from rural areas. The Committee, however, expresses
its reservation about the eligibility condition requiring a rural candidate to pass class III, IV and V from recognized
school/schools, without any repetition of class, gap or break in attendance.  The Committee feels that it is not in consonance with
the ground realities and hardships faced in rural India. In villages, many times, parents are forced to take their children off the
school due to financial or personal reasons, resulting in break in studies. Consequently, many deserving children would stand
disqualified for the test.  The Committee feels that such restrictions for taking the test do not appear to be justified which might
deprive the poor children from getting quality education.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that this condition should be
reconsidered with a view to enabling those students who are talented, but are unable to afford continuous education. Such
students may be given remedial coaching, if need be.
 
9.4       During its study visits, the Committee was given to understand that admission process for NVs is a prolonged affair as the
admission tests are conducted in early May and the admission process is completed only by December.  However, the Samiti has
claimed that from the academic year 2001-2002 onwards, the system has been streamlined.  By and large, now the main admission
process is completed by July.  Only in case of new Vidyalayas, which are running in temporary accommodation, the admission
gets delayed mainly due to lack of necessary facilities.
 
9.5       The Committee recommends that all out efforts should be made to complete the admissions in time so that the studies of
children do not suffer.

X         PROBLEM OF DROPOUT
 
10.1     The Committee’s attention has been drawn towards the problem of drop-out in different classes of JNVs.  On a specific
query, various reasons were identified by the JNVs, which can be broadly classified as follows: -
-
                     medical ground, personal problem, family problem, transfer of parents to other station;
-                     non-eligibility of students for admission in science stream in class XI;
-                     Shifting to State Government Schools after passing class X for getting the benefit of State Quota in professional
courses.
-                     Unwillingness to move on migration in class IX.
 
10.2     The Committee was given to understand that the vacancies arising in classes upto VIII are not being filled up in view of
special identity of JNVs which are meant to provide quality education to children predominantly from rural areas.  Periodical
intake of students against the vacancies would create two types of children – those who have already adjusted to the system and
the newly admitted students not able to adapt themselves. Lateral entry is allowed only in class IX which is a stage when the
children are grown up, and special orientation programmes are conducted for them after their admission, with a view to bring
them on par with the regular students.
                  
10.3     The Committee is not inclined to accept this reasoning. The Committee is of the opinion that vacancies, if continued for a
long time, do result in wastage of scarce resources. It also results in denial of opportunity to students who badly need quality
education.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts be made for filling the seats at first opportunity. Preference to girl
students of the area may be given in filling these vacant seats, as their adaptability to any situation is more than the boys. 
Regional offices of NVS may be empowered to fill up those vacancies under intimation to the headquarters.
 
10.4     The Committee notes with serious concern the tendency of most of the NV students, particularly in Maharashtra,
Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh leaving the school after class X to join schools run by State Governments with a view to get the
benefit of State quota in professional courses. The Committee finds that the percentage of students leaving the Vidyalayas after
class X in some of the states like Andhra Pradesh (43.75%) Karnataka (37.68%) and Maharashtra (45.91%) is very high.
           
10.5     The Committee was informed that the possibility of giving the option to the students to choose either CBSE or State Board
was explored by the Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti and the matter was taken up with the CBSE also. The CBSE, however, has not
agreed for the affiliation from both the Boards. The matter was also referred for further review to the Expert Committee
nominated by the Government for review of Management Structure and Operation Mechanism of JNVs which has given the
following recommendation:-
“The possibility of some or all Navodaya Vidyalayas offering affiliation both to the State Board and Central Board
simultaneously has been considered and has been found to be devoid of merit.  It is felt that such dual affiliation will
seriously undermine the concept of national identity and national uniformity in regard to teaching and learning in

Navodaya Vidyalayas.  Dual affiliation will also pose problem about the medium of instruction and it is likely to require

10.6     The Committee notes that while the students of Kendriya Vidyalayas in states like Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu have
the options to choose between CBSE and State Boards, this facility of dual affiliation is not available in Navodaya Vidyalayas. 
The Committee also notes the concerns expressed by the Expert Committee nominated by the Government, which has been
quoted above.  The only concern of the Committee is that selective application of the principle of dual affiliation between KVS
and JNVs seems to be controversial.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that this issue should be reviewed by the
Department at the earliest with a view to have uniform policy in this regard.

inform students about various courses and other career guidance information.
 
11.2     The Committee opines that outside agencies should also be roped in for specialized counselling on the career options

professional and career oriented options to the students.

XIII     HOSTEL FACILITY
 
13.1     The Committee notes that out of 485 JNVs functioning as on 31.8.04, 368 JNVs are functioning in permanent site and 117
JNVs are functioning at temporary sites.  The Committee presumes that all 368 JNVs functioning in permanent site must be
having hostel facilities.  If that be so, the Committee is surprised to note that out of 339 posts of Matron sanctioned as on 30.6.04,
only 36 were in place.  In Bhopal, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow and Pune regions, not even one post of Matron has been filled up.
The Committee is unable to understand how the hostels can function properly without Matron.
 
13.2     The Committee was given to understand that teachers are also entrusted with the responsibility of supervising the hostels. 
The Vidyalayas being residential schools, a great deal of regular support in terms of care, counseling, guidance and emotional
attachment is to be developed among the students.  The parental care, which is otherwise not available, is to be provided by the
teachers.  In view of this, the hostel supervision is at time entrusted to the teachers.  The Committee is, not inclined to agree with
this approach. Engaging teachers for Matron’s job, the Committee is of the view, could be only a stopgap arrangement.  Teachers
are already over-burdened with their present assignment of teaching.  They can, at best, help the matron in smooth running of the
hostels.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that recruitment for the post of matron should be expedited within a stipulated
time frame.

15.1     The Committee was informed that against sanctioned posts of 2972 PGT Teachers as on 30.6.04, 2550 posts were filled up

opting for “Hard Stations”. However, the Committee is constrained to observe that these initiatives do not seem to be having the

15.7     The Committee feels that the vacancies in the teaching staff adversely affects the overall performance of Navodaya

XVII    POSTING IN HARD STATIONS
17.1     With a view to motivate employees for accepting posting in Navodaya Vidyalayas located in North East Region and other
hard and difficult stations, as identified by the Samiti provides the following incentives:
 
a)
                  On completion of mandatory tenure Category-I employees will be posted to station of their choice. Choices in respect of

b)
                  Orders for posting outside the NE Region in respect of category-I employees will be issued two months before the

mandatory tenure, they shall stand relieved automatically and report for duty to the Regional Office having the jurisdiction

c)
                  Category-I employees will further be assured of posting of their choice in the NE Region from within the available

posting to NE Region under these instructions, would be due for transfer out of hard and difficult stations only in the year 2006-07
