17.3     The Committee was informed that there has been very significant response to the incentives given by the Samiti for the
employees opting hard and difficult stations including North East Region. During the year 2003-04 and 2004-05, 260 teachers
have willingly opted for posting to these stations and are continuing at present.
 
17.4        The Committee recommends that the NVS should ensure a more transparent transfer policy for teachers.  The teachers
should be posted at hard stations only on rotational basis and should be transferred soon after completing their tenure. The

and stay back particularly in the areas like North East and Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
 
XVIII              PENSIONARY BENEFITS TO NVS EMPLOYEES
 
           
18.1     The Committee notes that the employees of NVs do not get pensionery benefits whereas employees of KVS, NCERT and
other similar autonomous organizations under the Department of Secondary and Higher Education enjoy the benefit of pension.
The Committee was informed thata proposal for introduction of pension scheme for the employees of the Samiti was referred to
the Ministry of Finance, Department of Expenditure in July 1989 which did not support the proposal on the ground that the
pension provision would increase the expenditure of the Government as pension scheme is costlier than the Contributory
Provident Fund scheme.  Since then the proposal has been taken up with the Ministry of Finance at various levels on several
occasions but with no success.  The Ministry of Finance on different occasions advised the Samiti either to work out a suitable
annuity scheme through the Life Insurance Corporation based on voluntary contributions of the employees without any liability on
the Government or to consider opting for pension scheme notified by Ministry of Labour.  The Samiti had taken up this matter
with the Life Insurance Corporation but the schemes offered by LIC or the pension scheme notified by Ministry of Labour were

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
not accepted by the employees of the Samiti as they were not found comparable to the GPF/Pension Scheme in vogue in the
Government and other autonomous organizations.
 
18.2     Another initiativeat HRM level in 1998 was grounded down by the Ministry of Finance on the plea that there would be
similar demands from other autonomous organizations receiving grants-in-aid from the Government, which may be difficult to
resist. The Finance Ministry advanced the following reasons for rejecting the proposal: -
 
(a)    The cost of introduction of pension scheme is much higher than the CPF Scheme.  While CPF is an one-time
settlement, pension is a life-long commitment not only in respect of the pensioner but his family also.  The liability on
account of pension keeps on increasing with every increase/revision in pay/pensionary benefits on the basis of the
recommendations of the successive Pay Commissions, revision in the rates of dearness relief etc.  As most of the
autonomous organizations are fully funded through grants-in-aid received from the Government, Government’s
liability will increase to that extent if pension scheme is introduced.
 
(b)
   For servicing the pension scheme, a pension fund is required to be set up to be managed by a Trust.  Difficulties may
be experienced in judicious administration of the fund.
 
(c)    Under the Employees’ Provident Fund Act, the accretions to the Provident Fund are to be invested as per the pattern of
investment laid down by the Government.  With the formation of a Pension Fund, if accretions are invested elsewhere,
the Government will loose resources to that extent.
 
(d)
   In case the organization is wound up for one reason or the other, the Government may have to take over the entire
liability for pension.
 
 
18.3     The Committee takes note of the reservations of the Ministry of Finance in providing Pensionary benefit to employees of
NVS.   The Committee fails to comprehend the reasons for having different approach of mind for employees working in two
organisations doing similar work under a similar set up and conditions.   The Committee would like to point out when employees
of Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan can enjoy the pensionary benefits on their retirement, what deters the Government in providing
similar facility for employees of Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti, many of them away from their families serving in residential
schools located in rural areas.  The Committee, therefore, strongly feels that the position may be reviewed again and a decision
acceptable to employees of JNVs may be reached at the earliest.

XXI     REGIONAL OFFICES
 
21.1     The Samiti has eight Regional Offices located at Bhopal, Chandigarh, Hyderabad, Patna, Pune, Lucknow, Jaipur and
Shillong for administration of Vidyalayas under their respective regions. Out of these eight Regional Offices, only Regional
Office at Chandigarh is functioning in its own permanent building.  All other Regional Offices are functioning in rented
buildings.   The Committee was informed that the efforts of Samiti to acquire some suitable piece of land for construction of its
own Regional Office buildings through the State Government authorities have not evoked encouraging response.
 
21.2     The Committee notes with concern that the Regional Offices are functioning in rented buildings.  The Committee
recommends that concerted efforts with the concerned State Governments should be made to get suitable land so that Regional
Offices could be shifted to their own permanent buildings.  The Committee would like the Department to accord due importance
to the Regional Offices, which are instrumental in managing the affairs of the JNVs in that particular region more effectively and
efficiently.  The Ministry of HRD should take the lead and pursue the State Government, if possible at the Minister’s level. 
 
21.3     Each Regional Office has been provided with one Deputy Director, 5 Assistant Directors, 1 Accounts Officer and 2
Section Officers along with supporting secretariat staff.  For monitoring and supervision of construction of Vidyalaya buildings,
one Executive Engineer and one Junior Engineer has been provided to each Regional Office by internal adjustment.  This staff
pattern was approved by the Government during 1988-89 and there has been no increase in the staff strength thereafter. On the
contrary 10% of secretarial posts have been reduced under economy instructions of the Government.  
 
21.4     The Committee notes that in spite of expansion of JNVs from 2 Vidyalayas started in 1985-86 to 509 at present, the staff
strength at Regional Offices has not increased proportionately.  These eight Regional Offices with the meagre sanctioned staff
strength, functional strength may be even less, are supposed to supervise the functioning of 509 sanctioned NVs (485 NVs being
functional), many of them located in remote and inaccessible areas.   The Committee can well imagine the state of affairs.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends to have an O&M study done urgently for the evaluation of the work & staff in ROs, so that the
requisite number of posts could be created for smooth functioning of NVs.

XXV    SURVEY OF JNVs
 
25.1
          The Navodaya Vidyalaya System is a unique experiment in the annals of school education in India.  Its significance lies in
the selection of talented rural children to provide them with quality education comparable to the best, in a residential schools
system irrespective of their capacity to pay for it. Scheme of Navodaya Vidyalayas started in 1985-86 now covers almost all parts
of the country.   Over the years, these Vidyalayas have played a major role in providing qualify school education with special
focus on students from rural background.  
 
25.2
          The Committee feels that there is an urgent need for conducting a survey of all the JNVs so as to assess the shortfall in
required infrastructure, condition of school/hostel buildings, availability/non-availability of proper hostel facilities in all respects.

recommendations/observations on various aspects of functioning of JNVs should lead to corrective action by JNVs/Department.

III        NORMS FOR OPENING OF NAVODAYA VIDYALAYAS 
 
            The Committee was given to understand that out of 509 sanctioned JNVs, 485 JNVs are functional.  Out of the remaining
24 non-functional JNVs, 9 have been sanctioned only during the years 2003-04 and 2004-2005 and are likely to start functioning
from the next academic year.  The Committee is, however, constrained to note that out of the remaining 15 non-functional JNVs,
three JNVs, one each in Bihar, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh were sanctioned in 2001-2002, ten JNVs, one each in Gujarat,
Haryana, Jharkhand, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Tripura, UP and Uttaranchal and two in Mizoram were sanctioned in 2002-2003.  In
all these cases, temporary accommodation has not been made available by the concerned State Governments so far.  The
Committee fails to understand the reasons behind the inability of the State Governments in fulfilling the minimum requirements
for proposals initiated by them. The Committee observes that majority of these districts are located in remote and tribal areas
where JNVs are primarily required to be opened. The Committee is particularly disturbed by the situation in Mizoram. The
Committee finds that out of the six JNVs sanctioned in Mizoram, two JNVs opened – one in 1987-1988 in Lungli District and the
other in Chimtupui District in 1992-93 had to be closed down due to less enrolment and administrative reasons. In respect of three
JNVs sanctioned in 2002-2003, temporary accommodation is yet to be made available.  At present, only one JNV is functional.
The remaining two districts of the State are yet to be covered. The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for the
Department for taking up such cases at the highest level.  The Committee feels that given the peculiar geographical location and
the overall backwardness of the North-East region, the Central Government should make special efforts on meeting all the
requirements to make JNVs functional at the earliest. (Para 3.2)
 
            The Committee recommends that concerted efforts should be made to expedite not only the sanctioning of all the 574
JNVs, but also to make them functional in a time bound manner. The Committee would like the Ministry to play the role of a
facilitator in clearing the proposals received as well as in encouraging other proposals to be put up for opening new schools in the

IX        CRITERIA FOR ADMISSION IN NAVODAYA VIDALAYAS
 
           The Committee appreciates the adequate representation of SCs, STs and girls in Navodaya Vidyalayas. It still feels that
there is scope for further increase in percentages of girls as well as students from rural areas. The Committee, however, expresses
its reservation about the eligibility condition requiring a rural candidate to pass class III, IV and V from recognized
school/schools, without any repetition of class, gap or break in attendance.  The Committee feels that it is not in consonance with
the ground realities and hardships faced in rural India. In villages, many times, parents are forced to take their children off the
school due to financial or personal reasons, resulting in break in studies. Consequently, many deserving children would stand
disqualified for the test.  The Committee feels that such restrictions for taking the test do not appear to be justified which might
deprive the poor children from getting quality education.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that this condition should be
reconsidered with a view to enabling those students who are talented, but are unable to afford continuous education. Such
students may be given remedial coaching, if need be. (Para 9.3)

appointments well before the start of next academic session. (Para 15.7)
 
 
            Although the concept of appointing teachers on contract basis is a practical and need-based idea, however, the Committee
has reservations about performance and accountability of these teachers.  The Committee opines that the performance of teachers
appointed on contract basis should be reviewed regularly who may be relieved, if found wanting. (Para 15.8)
 
XVI     THREE LANGUAGE FORMULA
 
            The Committee notes that 25% vacancies of regional language teachers reflect the extent to which the regional languages
are being ignored.  The situation is more alarming in the North Eastern Region which needs to be brought more seriously into the
mainstream of our educational reforms in an acceptable mode of communication and which is possible only when we nurture the
regional languages properly.   The Committee thus opines that the posting of language teachers needs to be streamlined to ensure
a proper academic atmosphere throughout the year.  At the time of appointment of teachers, a clause may be added that rotational
transfers are a part of job and no request for stay of transfer will be entertained. (Para 16.4)
 
XVII    POSTING IN HARD STATIONS
 
               The Committee recommends that the NVS should ensure a more transparent transfer policy for teachers.  The teachers
should be posted at hard stations only on rotational basis and should be transferred soon after completing their tenure. The

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
transfers/postings should be effected in the beginning of the academic year and the process of relieving/joining should be
streamlined. The Government may also consider extending additional facilities and allowances to motivate more teachers to join
and stay back particularly in the areas like North East and Andaman & Nicobar Islands. (Para 17.4)
 
XVIII              PENSIONARY BENEFITS TO NVS EMPLOYEES
 
            The Committee takes note of the reservations of the Ministry of Finance in providing Pensionary benefit to employees of
NVS.   The Committee fails to comprehend the reasons for having different approach of mind for employees working in two
organisations doing similar work under a similar set up and conditions.   The Committee would like to point out when employees
of Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan can enjoy the pensionary benefits on their retirement, what deters the Government in providing
similar facility for employees of Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti, many of them away from their families serving in residential
schools located in rural areas.  The Committee, therefore, strongly feels that the position may be reviewed again and a decision
acceptable to employees of JNVs may be reached at the earliest. (Para 18.3)
 
XIV     TRAINING OF TEACHERS
 
            Training is an integral part of any organization. Training gives a chance of interacting with fellows of same profession and
gives them exposure to learn many new things.        The Committee notes that the training aspect for NVS staff leaves much to be
desired.  There is not even sufficient number of trainers in training centres.  The Committee feels that training aspect is being
neglected badly.  Even the post of Directors, in the training institutes, was not approved and the Regional officers were entrusted
with the job to look after the training institutes. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should make urgent efforts for
strengthening and streamlining the process of training for the teachers by providing necessary infrastructure and manpower. (Para
19.3)
 
            The Committee notes that utility of six training centres established in 2001-2002 was analysed by the Samiti in 2002-2003
and Mangalore Training Centre was closed.   The Committee finds that these training centres are not evenly spread covering all
parts of the country.   While two of the centres are located in Andhra Pradesh, no training centre has been set up in the North-
eastern region.  Northern region also does not seem to be adequately covered.   The Committee feels that these centres could have
been easily set up in the eight Regional Offices of NVS.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that feasibility of this option
may be explored.   If not found possible, steps may be taken for setting up a centre in N-E region. (Para 19.4)
XX       INSPECTION
            The Committee notes that despite so many surprise visits, there is no indication of any increase in the overall efficiency in
these schools. It is equally disturbing that no details about the outcome of these inspections was provided to the Committee. The
Committee also notes the difference in pattern of such visits as, schools in Jammu & Kashmir have been visited only once,
whereas Manipur has been inspected eight times. (Para 20.4)
 
            The Committee recommends that there should be periodic inspection depending on the number of schools in these areas
and staff available for inspection. The guidelines for inspection should be circulated to all regional offices. Action taken on these
reports should also be checked periodically and as far as possible the local M.Ps may also be invited during the inspections to
have the benefit of their experiences. (Para 20.5)
 
            The Committee is of the view that in because of JNVs being residential schools spread over different parts of the country,
monitoring mechanism through regular and surprise inspections followed by corrective action is essential for their smooth and
effective functioning. The Committee, however, feels that with the present set up in the Regional Offices, inspections are not

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
being carried out in the real sense.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department/NVS should take steps for
augmenting the required staff at all the Regional Offices.   The Committee would like to be apprised about the details of follow-up
action taken on the 95 surprise inspections carried out during 2003-2004.  (Para 20.6)
 
XXI     REGIONAL OFFICES
 
            The Committee notes with concern that the Regional Offices are functioning in rented buildings.  The Committee
recommends that concerted efforts with the concerned State Governments should be made to get suitable land so that Regional
Offices could be shifted to their own permanent buildings.  The Committee would like the Department to accord due importance
to the Regional Offices, which are instrumental in managing the affairs of the JNVs in that particular region more effectively and
efficiently.  The Ministry of HRD should take the lead and pursue the State Government, if possible at the Minister’s level.  (Para
21.2)
 
            The Committee notes that in spite of expansion of JNVs from 2 Vidyalayas started in 1985-86 to 509 at present, the staff
strength at Regional Offices has not increased proportionately.  These eight Regional Offices with the meagre sanctioned staff
strength, functional strength may be even less, are supposed to supervise the functioning of 509 sanctioned NVs (485 NVs being
functional), many of them located in remote and inaccessible areas.   The Committee can well imagine the state of affairs.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends to have an O&M study done urgently for the evaluation of the work & staff in ROs, so that the
requisite number of posts could be created for smooth functioning of NVs. (Para 21.4)
 
XXII    GRIEVANCES REDRESSAL
 
            The Committee is not satisfied with the functioning of the grievance redressal mechanism in NVs and feels that if teachers
grievances were not attended to in time, they will not be able to concentrate on teaching.  The Committee recommends that all the
Regional Offices should have a Grievance Cell so that the cases are attended to and disposed off quickly.  The principals should
also endeavour to get the matter sorted out early in consultation with the Regional Offices. The aggrieved person should also have
easy access to the officers. For this, a day in a week may be fixed enabling them to meet the officials.  The Teacher's Association
should also be encouraged to participate in the decision making process of the Samiti.  (Para 22.2)
 
XXIII    NON ACCEPTANCE OF THE SCHEME OF NAVODAYA VIDYALAYAS
 
 
23.3     The Committee is not convinced by the arguments of the State Government mainly because the JNVs are catering to the
educational needs of meritorious students from the poor and deprived sections of the society, with special emphasis on the girl
students.  The three language formula adopted by the JNVs needs to be encouraged by all the State Government as an element of
national integration.  The Government should, therefore convince and persuade the State Government on these broad objectives to
adopt the schemes of JNVs.  (Para 23.2)
           
XXIV  PROBLEMS BEING FACED IN RUNNING THE JNVS
24.2     The Committee feels that most of these problems can be solved with proper coordination and support from the State
Governments.  Since the Navodaya Vidyalayas do not have financial provision for laying connecting roads, electrical lines, and
levelling the lines, etc., the State Govt. should be requested to periodically monitor the support given to the Vidyalayas and ensure
that the minimum infrastructural facilities are extended uninterruptedly.  District Magistrate being actually associated in all such
issues  can take lead in  getting these problems redressed quickly. (Para 24.2)
 
XXV    SURVEY OF JNVs

required infrastructure, condition of school/hostel buildings, availability/non-availability of proper hostel facilities in all respects.  
Such a survey should also cover the student intake capacity and present student strength alongwith the required and present
strength of teachers/non-teachers (Vidyalaya-wise), need for relocating some Vidyalayas in view of optimum utilisation not being

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
II BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
2.2       The Committee notes that increment in the allocations of the Department for the year 2004-05 is nominal with which
Department would hardly be able to carry out two of its main schemes (SSA & MDM) let alone other schemes.  These two
schemes would require Rs.10,919.00 crores for the year 2004-05, according to the Department.  The Committee notes that
the Government recognizing this need of the Department has provided for 2% education cess from this year. 
Department should put forth this aspect before the Ministry of Finance at appropriate stage.
 
2.3       Even if the entire Rs. 5000.00 crores expected to be generated from Education Cess is fully utilized to meet the
additional requirements, there will still be a shortfall of Rs.187.00 crores.  The Department should put forth this aspect
before the Ministry of Finance at appropriate stage.
 
Action Taken
 
2.2 & 2.3 Requirements for SSA and MDM for 2004-05 mentioned in para 2.2 was based on information furnished by the

155th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/155threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
Department to the Committee on 22.7.2004.
 
At that time, extension of MDM programme to Upper Primary stage was envisaged from this year itself.  Subsequently,
Government decided not to extend MDM programme to the Upper Primary stage for the present, resulting in reduction of
requirement for this programme from Rs.4499 crore to Rs.3261 crore, and of total requirement for SSA and MDM from
Rs.10,919 crore to Rs.9681 crore. As against this, additional provision of Rs.2000 crore and 1232 crore (total Rs.3232 crore)
have been made for SSA and MDM schemes respectively in 1
st    Supplementary Budget for 2004-05. With this, total
allocation for SSA and MDM has risen from Rs. 4732 crores to Rs. 7964 crores.
 
As suggested by the Committee, Department will continue to forcefully project its financial requirements before Planning
Commission and Ministry of Finance at every opportunity.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
2.4       The Committee also notes considerable gap between the demand projected by the Working Group Report of the
Department before the Planning Commission both for the Elementary Education as well as Adult Education for the 10
th
Plan Period.  It feels that primary education has suffered from deprivation and degradation mainly due to inadequate
allocation of resources over several decades.  The Committee is happy that the education of children has received some
attention but is still not treated as priority area as far as resource allocation is concerned.  Some very good schemes have
been started with valuable components, which need to be strengthened and expanded.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that need for adequate funds for elementary education should be projected effectively by the Department
before the Ministry of Finance and the Planning Commission at the RE stage.  At the same time, the Committee has a word
of caution for the Department.  Although allocation of Rs.1951.25 crores for Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan in 2003-04 was
enhanced to Rs.2732.32 crores at the RE stage, the Department could utilize only Rs.2582.29 crores.  In the event of their
projected demand of Rs.6420.00 crores being met, the Department will have to take effective steps for optimum and
judicious utilization of enhanced allocation.
 
Action Taken
 
2.4       The issue of future requirements for the Department’s programmes will be projected to the Planning Commission as
part of its Mid-Term Appraisal exercise for the Tenth Five Year Plan.  
                                                        
BE for SSA in 2003-04 was Rs.1951.25 crore, which was raised to Rs.2732.32 crore at RE stage.  As against this, total
expenditure during 2003-04 was Rs.2710.64 crore (Rs.2582.29 crore under non-EAP and Rs.150 crore under EAP
components) which works out to be 99.2% of RE.   It appears that while quoting the expenditure figure of Rs.2582.29 crore
in para 2.4, the Committee omitted to include the expenditure of Rs.150 crore shown under EAP. 
 
However, Department has taken note of the Committee’s concern regarding effective steps for optimum and judicious
utilization of enhanced allocation, and will make all possible efforts in that behalf.
 
III SARVA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN
 
 Recommendations/Observations
 
3.7       The Committee notes that there had been some underutilization of funds during the Ninth Plan.  Underutilization, in
Committee’s view, is a cause for serious concern.  It points out more towards the laxity on the part of the implementing
authorities than anything else.  Such a performance does not inspire confidence as to the success of this programme, hence it
should be avoided at every cost.
 
Action Taken
 
3.7       The concern of the Committee is noted for guidance and compliance.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.8       The Committee notes that assistance under the programme is on a 75:25 sharing arrangement between the Central
Govt. and State Governments.  The Committee is not aware about the acceptance level of this distribution by the States

155th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/155threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
already burdened by financial constraints.  The Committee apprehends that proposed 50:50 sharing between Central and
State Governments after Tenth Plan may not find favour with majority of the States.  The Department may need to have a
re-assessment of this funding pattern by having a Mid-Term appraisal of Tenth Plan during the current year, 2004-05.
 
Action Taken
 
3.8       A proposal for change in the sharing arrangement between the Centre and the States has been sent to the Planning

th Plan.

educationally backward also, Mid-Day Meal Scheme still remains to be implemented in the true sense and as per the
Supreme Court directive.

5.3       The Committee would like to know the reasons as to why five states are still not serving cooked meal under MDM

III.              INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS)
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.13   The Committee notes that ICDS takes the major share of the budgetary allocation of the Department.  Success
of the scheme largely depends on the functioning of Anganwadi workers (AWWs).  The Committee is, however, not
satisfied with the plight of these workers.  The meagre pecuniary benefits and poor facilities do not attract people to
work as AWWs.  The Committee is surprised to see that their role still remains undefined; they are asked to do all
kind of odd works such as census operation, distribution of drugs etc.  This puts extra pressure on them and their
main role is diluted. 
 
Action Taken
 
            The role and responsibilities of the AWWs and AWHs are well defined in the ICDS Scheme.  However, over the
years, AWWs and AWHs have been increasingly called upon to discharge duties in relation to various other
schemes/programmes of Government of India, State Governments and local bodies, in addition to the task assigned to them
under ICDS Programme.  In view of this, a Core Committee comprising  of Secretary, D/WCD as Chairperson and
representatives from concerned Departments and State Governments has been set up to review the role and responsibilities
of AWWs and AWHs.  Three meetings of the Committee have already been held so far.
 
V.      CRÈCHES  & DAY CARE CENTRES
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
5.6.   The Committee is happy to note that the Department proposes to merge the National Crèche Fund Scheme  with the
Scheme of Creches/Day Care Centres to take care of the problem  of reduced cash flow due to fall in interest rates from the

schemes are identical and implementation of two parallel schemes was only resulting in confusion and uneconomical use of
funds.  The Committee emphasizes that a final decision in the matter should be taken at the earliest so that implementation of
the scheme does not suffer.

XII. SWADHAR
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
12.3    The Committee is not happy to note that the scheme was limited to only ten States/UTs and the Central Social
Welfare Board.    It appears that the scheme was not getting good response despite the three tier monitoring
mechanism.  The Committee recommends that all out efforts should be made to popularize such useful scheme in all
States/UTs.  A wide publicity campaign should be launched across the country to highlight the activities and benefits
under the scheme.
 
Action Taken
           
During the current financial year, detailed advertisements, inviting applications for projects under the scheme of
Swadhar, have been brought out in the national newspapers all over the country to popularize the scheme.  Besides, senior
officers of the Department have been organizing workshops all over the country.  So far workshops had been held in
Hyderabad, Patna, Chandigarh and Bangalore to encourage and guide the organizations to submit proposals under the
scheme.  The Department is fully confident that budget earmarked for the scheme will be fully utilized.

VI.   INFORMATION, MASS MEDIA & PUBLICATION
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
6.3       Information, Mass Media and Publication, the Committee believes, are very important components of any
activity/scheme to help fulfill its objective.  In the absence of publicity, even a very good scheme would be rendered
ineffective, if beneficiaries were not aware of it.  Apart from this, it has educative role as well, clearing many a
myths/misconception that people may be having about implication etc. of a scheme.  The Committee finds implementation of
this scheme tardy.  The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends to take up its implementation with full vigour.  Services
of Akashwani having access to 35 crores audiences should also be considered

During the current financial year 2004-05 budget of Rs.12.00 Crores have been allocated for Media activities for
Awareness Generation of policies & programmes of the Deptt. & the expenditure has been planned. Out of this Rs.5.01
Crores has been committed to Doordarshan for telecast of video spots on Child Trafficking, Women’s Empowerment and
Sex Ratio on National Channel and these spots are being telecast.

X.   NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR WOMEN
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
10.5     The Committee notes that some very important laws need immediate attention viz., Domestic Violence Bill, Dowry
Prohibition Act, Indecent Representation of Women, Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act 1956 etc.  The   Committee  
believes that    these amendments were long over due.  It, therefore, recommends that immediate steps be taken to complete
consultations and other formalities for bringing drafts of these laws before Parliament with no loss of further time.
 
Action taken
 
Protection from Domestic Violence Bill 2002
 
            
After re-examining the provisions of the Protection from Domestic Violence Bill 2002 (which was pending before the
13th Lok Sabha and subsequently lapsed on dissolution of the House) and taking into consideration the recommendations made
by the Parliamentary Standing Committee in its 124th Report on the said Bill, the views expressed by the Prime Minister’s Office
(Vide PMO’s U.O. Note dated 19.8.2004) and women voluntary organizations, the Department has drafted a Bill on the subject. 
The various provisions to be included in the Bill have been approved by the Minister of Human Resource Development.  The
draft cabinet Note was circulated to the concerned Ministries such as Ministry of Home Affairs, Department of Justice,
Department of Legal Affairs etc. for their comments.  The comments of Ministries/Departments  have been received.  The draft
Bill has been referred to Ministry of Law and Justice for examination and vetting.  Their views are awaited.
         
The status of review of the 4 women-specific Acts administered by the Department is as under:
 
The Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act, 1987
 
The recommendations made by NCW and the Task Force on amendments in the Act were circulated to the State
Governments and Union Territory Administrations and the concerned Ministries/Departments  have been compiled.  HRM
has approved the recommendation of the Task Force on Women and Children.   A Note for the Cabinet  has been  circulated
to other  relevant Ministries/Departments for comments.
 
The Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986
 
The Task Force on Women and Children suggesting for amendment of the definition  of Indecent  Representation of
Women has been  referred to the Ministry of Law and Justice.  Their views are awaited.

The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 Amendment Bill
 
This Amendment Bill has been approved by Hon’ble HRM on 25.8.2004 and has been circulated to all concerned
Ministries in Government of India. We have received comments from all of the concerned Ministries.  The Bill will now be
drafted by the Law Ministry and, thereafter, a note will be placed before the Cabinet for approval.
 
Provision in Indian Penal Code relating to Rape
 
NCW had recommended certain amendments in the provision of the Indian Penal Code, 1860; the code of Criminal
Procedure 1973; the Indian Evidence  Act, 1872, relating to the offences of Rape.  Ministry of Home Affairs has circulated a
draft note for Cabinet containing proposed amendments to these provisions based on Law Commission’s review and
recommendation of the legal provisions relating to rape. Most of the recommendations of NCW have been covered therein.  
Department of Women and Child Development has concurred with the  draft note for Cabinet circulated by the Ministry of
Home Affairs, at the level of HRM, as well as reiterating the remaining recommendations of NCW.
 
The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961
 
National Commission for Women’s recommendations on the amendments need examination of this Department. 
Further  clarifications have been sought from the NCW.
 
In so far as the laws to give equal rights to women in ownership of assets is concerned, the laws relating to intestate
succession among Hindus are codified under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The NCW has reviewed the said Act and one
of its major recommendations was to amend Section 6 of the Act with a view to make recommendations for amending the
Act so that women get an equal share in the ancestral property. The recommendation of NCW was forwarded to the
Legislative Department, which is concerned with the legislative aspects of the said Act. Legislative Department informed
that the Law Commission of India, in its 174th Report on `Property Rights of Women : Proposed reforms under the Hindu
Law’ recommended amendments to section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. That Department has circulated a draft
Cabinet Note for amending the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 to implement the recommendations made by the Law
Commission of India. The Department has examined the draft Cabinet Note and with the approval of the Minister of Human
Resource Development conveyed the concurrence to the proposals in it and also requested the Legislative Department to
consider the recommendations made by the NCW regarding amendments in the Act.

XV.  INSURANCE FOR WOMEN WORKERS
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
15.2   The Committee observes that Insurance is an essential economic support to women during crises and recommends
that efforts should be made to link insurance with health programmes. The Committee would like the Department to explore
feasibility of linking insurance to other financial services - savings and credit – which  promotes long-term insurance
coverage and work out the modalities in consultation with some renowned NGOs who have already started this exercise.
 
Action Taken
 
Life Insurance Corporation of India offers Group Insurance Scheme called Janashree Bima Yojana for those working
in the informal sector and are below poverty line or slightly above poverty line.  The scheme provides for an insurance cover
of Rs.20,000 on natural death.  On death/total permanent disability due to accident, the benefit is Rs.50,000.  On partial
permanent disability due to accident, the benefit is Rs.25,000.  The premium for the scheme is Rs.200 per member, 5o per
cent  premium under the scheme will be met out of  Social Security Fund.  The balance premium is to be paid by the

          The Ministry of Labour  had already moved a draft Cabinet Note for enactment of the ‘Unorganised Sector Workers
Bill 2004’ for comments of the concerned Departments.  Under this legislation, it is proposed to cover initially only those
workers in the unorganized sector who are most vulnerable and whose monthly income/wages are below Rs.5000 per month
and are engaged in the scheduled  employments. The Act provides for schemes to be formulated by the appropriate
Government for ensuring  safety, social security and welfare of workers including  health and medical care, employment

The Universal Health Insurance Scheme has been redesigned targeting only the BPL families.  The premium has

Reasons for shortfall and remedial measures
 
            The scheme of Condensed Course stipulates that the objectives of the scheme is to provide educational opportunities
to the girls and women who are school  drop-outs or who could not join mainstream education system due to their adverse
circumstances.  The CSWB, during the initial years of 9th Five Year Plan i.e. the year 1997-98, 98-99 & 2000-01 took a
decision.
 
i)
                     Not to consider proposals of such voluntary organizations for above Primary level courses who did not have
educational experience.  Even proposals from the institutions with experience of literacy or non-formal education were not
considered for sanction, though the scheme makes it clear that the proposals of the institutions who were engaged in women
welfare activities can be considered.  By imposing such restrictions many institutions could not avail the grant under the
programme which led to non-utlization of funds.
 
ii)
                   The CSWB also took a decision not to sanction residential courses whereas there was persistent demand from the
voluntary organizations functioning in rural, tribal and backward areas for residential course.
 
iii)            Though, there is no provision in the scheme to stipulate the condition of 50% result in examination, the CSWB took
a decision that continuation courses (IInd & IIIrd batches) should not be considered for the institutions whose result of earlier
batch was less than 50% in spite of the fact that in many States results of even candidates from regular schools in
CBSE/Higher Secondary Examination was even less than 50%.
 
The above conditions restricted the scope of implementation of the scheme as per objective of the programme. 
However, the CSWB took remedial measures and the Executive Committee of the CSWB in its 136th Meeting held on
20.7.2000 had decided that 50% passed percentage for continuation courses shall not be insisted upon.  The average State
result of girl candidates shall be taken as a criterion for giving continuation grant.  The Executive Committee has also taken a
decision that educational experience for middle and matric/equivalent level courses should not be insisted upon as voluntary
institutions having experience in conducting women’s programme are also eligible for assistance as per the scheme.  It was
also decided that the applications of residential courses should also be considered particularly for the courses which are to be
conducted in tribal, rural and backward area.

             INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS)
 
Recommendations/Observation
 
3.7       The fact that nearly 95 out of 1000 children under five die is nothing less than shocking.  The latest position of IMR
is not known as this figure is   for the year 1998.  Such a high IMR is certainly a very sad reflection on our efforts for child
development.  ICDS's main aim, in fact, is to lower the infant mortality because it focuses not only on child care but on
pregnant and lactating mothers as well.  If the IMR is taken as indicator, the performance/effectively of the ICDS tells a sad
story. The inability to operationalise ICDS projects, the Committee feels, is the main reason for this situation.  The
requirement must be much more as the sanctioned projects are as per the 1991 census. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department should take up this issue with the States/implementing agencies at higher level to chalk out
an action plan to be taken up at emergency level and in time bound manner.  The Committee also emphasizes the need for
constant and effective monitoring of implementation of this scheme.  Having independent channel of getting feedback is
also of prime importance which needs to be put in place immediately.
 
Action Taken
 
There are various factors like low birth rate, pneumonia, birth asphyxia etc. which are attributable to death of
children.  One of the major findings of the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER), which  conducted an
independent survey of ICDS projects in 1998, was that the infant mortality rate (IMR) was lower in ICDS areas than in non-
ICDS areas.
 
Regarding operationalisation of ICDS projects/AWCs, there has been continuous emphasis upon States to

letter from Secretary (WCD) to Chief Secretaries of the States.   In response to a Public Interest Litigation (PIL), the

The Committee notes with concern that even after the directions of Supreme Court, the Department has shortfall of

The population of the country has increased over the years. The Supreme Court vide its order dated 28.11.2001 and
29.4.2004, has directed the Government of India, inter-alia, to increase the number of Anganwadi Centres so as to cover 14
lakh habitations.  The CMP states that attempts will be made to universalize the ICDS Scheme to provide a functional
Anganwadi in every settlement and ensure full coverage of all children. It may be noted that as on 31.3.2004, out of 7.5 lakh
sanctioned AWCs there are about 6.59 lakh functional Aganwadis in the country. These have been set up since the inception

Court, an Inter-ministerial Task Force has been setup to review the existing population norms for sanction of a Project and
Anganwadi Centre under the ICDS Scheme and suggest the revised population norms.  This will necessitate further
additional Projects and Centers and consequential increase in the Department’s Plan Outlay.
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee finds the reply of the Department to be too technical and hence evasive.   The Committee's intention
was to evolve a more rationale approach in the norm of setting up Anganwadi Centres in case of Manipur and other States
having similar geographic location so that more Anganwadi Centres could be set up in these areas.  The Committee,

Recommendations/Observations
 
3.12    The Committee is surprised to know about so many schemes of child nutrition being implemented simultaneously by
different Department/Ministries.  Incidence of large scale malnutrition in children indicates that there is serious lacuna in the
existing system.  It is incomprehensible to the Committee as to why there is malnutrition in the children despite the number
of schemes operated through different Department as also by the State Governments.  The Committee feels that multiplicity
of schemes as well as Departments is also creating confusion leading to wastage and duplication of resources and efforts. 
The Committee recommends that a coordinated approach amongst all the concerned Department/Ministries is the need of
the hour.  The Department of Women and Child Development should be a nodal agency for all such scheme to achieve
optimum results.  Inter-departmental meetings should be held regularly to review the progress on nutritional level of the
children. 
 
Action Taken
 
Different programmes of the Government in the area of health and welfare are indirect nutrition interventions for
promoting nutrition of the people, including vulnerable groups like children and pregnant and lactating women. The existing
nutrition interventions namely the ICDS, anaemia control and vitamin A prophylaxis programmes, iodisation of salt,
targeted public distribution system touch only the outer edge of the complex problem of malnutrition which requires a multi-
pronged action at different levels with substantial resources.  The problem of malnutrition is so huge and complex that inter-
sectoral efforts in the area of food security, health and education are necessary.
 
The Department of Women and Child Development is the nodal agency for institutionalizing the multi-sectoral
strategy of National Nutrition Policy.  Interdepartmental meetings are held from time to time to set the nutrition goals and to

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee is aware that the problem of malnutrition is so huge and complex that inter-sectoral efforts in the

Recommendations/Observations
 
18. 1     The Committee was informed that some of the schemes of the Department were being implemented through NGOs. 
Idea of NGOs involvement, no doubt, is a noble one, functioning of some of the NGOs, however, leaves much to be

There are allegations that in some cases different organization were being run by one person and same NGO was receiving
grants under different names.  The Committee is aware that not all NGOs were defaulters and many of them were rendering
yeoman service.  Department gave a list of NGOs blacklisted by it.  The Committee feels that simply blacklisting such
NGOs would not deter the delinquent ones and they might come back with change names/address.  Government needs to
streamline the procedure of their selection as well as regular monitoring of their work.  We should have penal provisions for
recovering the grants given to defaulting NGOs.  The NGOs doing good job needs to be suitably rewarded so as to motivate
others.   
 
Action Taken
 
            A State Level Empowered Committee (SLEC), under the Chairpersonship of Secretary, WCD/Social Welfare of the
concerned State, comprising  representatives of Finance/Planning/Technical Department etc. has been set up in all the States
for scrutiny of proposals  under various schemes of the Departments.    The proposals received from NGOs/
Corporations/Undertakings are scrutinized by the SLEC before these are passed on to GOI for consideration.  The idea is
that the SLEC would be in a better position to know about the credibility, reputation, genuineness and past performance of
the Organisations/ NGOs.
 
            As regards monitoring of implementation of projects, the same is being undertaken by the State WDCs/Central
Social Welfare Board(CSWB).  Besides, the University Women Development Centres are also engaged by the Department
for monitoring the implementation.  A performance report (i.e.Mid-Term Evaluation Report) from the State Government is
insisted upon at the time of release of second instalment to the NGOs/organisations.

NGOs/organisations.  The  NGOs/ organisations found wanting in certain respects or defaulting in the implementation of the
projects are black-listed/penalised accordingly.

            The Committee feels that there must be at least one representative from the Centre also in the SLECs in the States.

wonders.  Despite existing penal provisions for erring NGOs, not many of them are being penalized, the Committee feels.

training which could be initiated immediately after the completion of ICDS III project on 30.6.05.  (Para 4.4)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE

The Committee notes that the recommendations of the national level Conference on Crèche Programme held in July,

Department in implementing these recommendations.  Department’s reply clearly indicates that no final decision is likely to
be taken in the near future.   The Department did not say anything about the reasons for non-functioning of 28 crèches. The
Committee recommends that a time-bound action-plan should be made and implemented with regular supervision at various
levels to achieve the desired objectives. (Para 5.5)
 
VII. BALIKA SAMRIDDHI YOJANA
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
The Committee observes that after a prolonged phase of indecision about the fate of Balika Samriddhi Yojana, a
decision has been taken not to transfer the scheme to the States and it shall be operated by the Central Govt as being done
earlier.  The Committee would like to emphasize that the scheme was not running well under the administrative control of
Centre.  There were huge unspent balances lying with the State Govts.  The Committee apprehends that pendency level
continues to remain the same.  The Committee is not satisfied with the stand taken by the Department that only States
submitting satisfactory utilization will be sanctioned funds.  The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for
evolving an effective monitoring mechanism to ensure that financial assistance as envisaged under the scheme reaches all
the targeted beneficiaries. (Para 7.2 & 7.3)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
           
If the Committee was to accept the explanation given by the Department of Women and Child Development, then
there must be some problem with target fixing.  Does it mean that lower targets are fixed deliberately to avoid large gaps in
achievements at the end of the year?  The Committee feels that a more realistic approach needs to be taken by the
Department of Women and Child Development. (Para 9.5 & 9.6)

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
The Committee is not aware whether there exists any mechanism to get the feedback on the complaint sent to the
Department of Women and Child Development of State Governments/State Women Commission.  The Committee
recommends that the feedback should be obtained on quarterly basis.  The Committee also recommends that those
complaints which do not come under the mandate of the Commission may be treated as disposed off and should not be
shown as pending complaints. (Para 10.2)

The Committee is of the view that, Department of Women and Child Development has to play a proactive role for
this purpose by working as facilitator for setting up the State Women Commission in the remaining States. Mere writing
letters or taking meetings has not worked so far. (Para 10.3)

2.2       The Committee notes that initially, Rs. 9.32 crores was earmarked for the Afro-Asian Games in BE 2003-04 on the
plan side and subsequently Rs. 55.00 crore was obtained as supplementary grant for this purpose, but on non-plan side.  The
Committee also notes that Rs. 8.00 crore was re-appropriated from plan side to non-plan side for a newly created head.  In
view of this, the Committee feels that assessment about Afro-Asian Games requirements was highly unrealistic, because
ultimately, a total Rs. 64.32 crores had to be given (Rs. 9.32 crores + Rs. 55.00 crore) for this purpose, instead of Rs. 9.32
crore originally provided for.  Secondly, the re-appropriation of funds from plan to non-plan, according to the Committee, is
not a healthy practice, which leaves less money for the schemes, which are already cash-starved.
 
Action Taken
 
The Games were earlier scheduled to be held at New Delhi from 3
rd to 11 th November, 2001.  The details of
expenditure and financial arrangements for the Games were to be settled between Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Youth
Affairs.  However, on 14th September 2001 Government after reviewing the overall security scenario that emerged as a result
of the terrorist attacks in USA decided to postpone the Games.  Subsequently on the proposal of Indian Olympic Association,
on 1st September, 2003 Government had approved the holding of the Games from 24 th October to 1 st November, 2003 at
Hyderabad instead of New Delhi.
 
As such at BE 2003-04 a nominal provision of Rs.9.32 crores was kept at the time of preparing the estimates. 
However, as per the financial arrangements settled between Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports,
this Ministry was to provide Rs.8.00 crores and Ministry of Finance was to provide Rs.55.00 crores as additionality for
First Afro Asian Games.
 
Since the funds were to be transferred to State Government, a new budget head under Non-Plan was opened.  In
view of this, the plan allocation of Rs.8.00 crores (as a Central Government Share) was re-appropriated from Plan to Non-
Plan.  The additionality of Rs.55.00 crores (Non-Plan) provided by Ministry of Finance was also kept under this head.
 
In view of the above there has been no financial impact on any plan scheme of this Ministry.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
2.3
              The Committee notes that the allocation of the Ministry for the year 2004-05, has been marginally increased and
believes that it would hardly suffice to implement the ongoing projects, leave alone new initiatives proposed by the
Ministry.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should place its requirements for this year, before the
Ministry of Finance/Planning Commission justifying its need for higher allocation at the RE Stage.
 
Action Taken
 
Ministry has already projected its requirement of additional funds for expansion of National Service Scheme (NSS)

3.3       The Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry to take interest in the development of sports among the

Schemes to identify talented sportspersons in the age groups ranging from 8-25 years (Boys & Girls) and admit them in

b. Special Area Games

            The talented sportspersons (Male & Female) are identified through talent scouting as per the scheme selection

scientific training.  The efforts are always made to attract greater number of women trainees so that female participation in
the sports could be improved.  During 2003-04 the percentage of female participation, in the above four SAI Schemes was
29.47%.  The percentage of female participation during 2004-05 (as on 31.12.2004) has slightly improved in comparison
to last year.  It is hopefully presumed that the gender participation in respect of female trainees shall improve to some
extent by the end of this academic year.  It is pointed out that under each scheme the selection is done as per the scheme
criteria and also that talented sports persons who have potential to perform at National & International competitions are
admitted for regular training in SAI Schemes.

16.6     Last few years have seen a number of sportspersons specially the weightlifters and athletes testing positive for
banned drugs.  These instances have brought shame instead of fame to the Nation.  Our Scheme for Dope test was
launched only three years ago.  The SAI has anti-doping lab set up a decade ago in New Delhi, it has still not acquired the
requisite international certification to gain legal sanctity. So, even if anybody fails a test, he or she can successfully
challenge it in a Court.  Such a situation allows the over-ambitious ones to take the easy route.
 
Action Taken
 
As submitted above, after acquiring the essential requisites viz ISO/IEC 17025:1999 in September 2003, DCC SAI
got temporary accreditation by IOC for testing of 1 st Afro Asian Games. The application for permanent accreditation
submitted to WADA on Feb. 6, 2004.  Even though a special scheme was launched recently, the funding for Dope test
laboratory was being covered under the Ministry’s overall budgetary allocations.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
16.12   The Committee recommends that the Ministry should make efforts to streamline the procedure for Dope testing,
upgrading the test facilities, employing experts in the area for making the test results foolproof.  Involving many agencies
in this, Committee feels, would only complicate the matter.  Only SAI and IOA, therefore, should be made responsible for
this work.  And they should put necessary guidelines in tune with World Anti-Doping Code.
 
Action Taken
 
The quality of test results given by DCC, SAI is satisfactory. The technology being used in terms of analytical
methods and equipment facilities are the latest. This has been reviewed by the following: -
 
§           Team of Japanese scientists
§           Assessment team for ISO/IEC 17025:1999 accreditation which included Technical Assessor Dr. John H. Vine from
Australia. (Who is an International Technical Assessor for Doping Labs.)
§           Participation in International proficiency testing programmes.
 
All the methods have been developed as per WADA International Standard for Laboratories. The same methods are
being used by all WADA accreditated Labs.  In case of all new drugs introduced, methods are developed and then testing
is conducted as per approved method.  For example THG was detected in the month of October, 2003 and the methods for
testing the same was given by WADA to all accreditated labs.  DCC SAI was able to detect THG and is one of the few
labs in the world, which could detect the THG.  Moreover DCC SAI is also participating in the proficiency testing which is
one of the mandatory requirements for getting the permanent accreditation from WADA.  The samples were received in
DCC from WADA. It is pointed out here that DCC was able to detect all the drugs, which were in their scope and was able
to obtain Z score within the prescribed limits.  There were 24 accreditated labs, who had participated in the above said
proficiency testing.  However, New Delhi, DCC was the only non-accreditated lab. Who have achieved the Z score within
the prescribed limits?  The overall performance of DCC Lab. was within first five labs.  This also shows that this Lab. is
following all the methods, which are being followed by the accredited lab. of WADA.  All the guidelines issued by
WADA are followed from time to time.

3.2       The Committee notes that percentage of funds spent on women component is not upto the mark under various
schemes of the Ministry except the NSS, NSVS and sports scholarship.  In some schemes, especially those run by SAI, it
is very low.  It is matter of great concern to the Committee that only 33.60% of the total allocation of the Ministry was
spent on women component during the year 2003-04.  The very fact, that data have been assumed for some schemes,
shows thatgender analysis of its scheme is being done neither systematically nor regularly.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the gender-based analysis of the allocations of the Ministry should be done regularly, as it would provide
an idea about the percentage of funds being spent on the women who constitute about half of our population.
 
Action Taken
 
All the schemes of the Ministry are designed to benefit sports persons belonging to both the sexes. However, under
a specific scheme of National Championship for Women, Govt. gives grants to States/ UTs for holding women sports
competitions at block, district and State levels.
 
Under the scheme of Sports Scholarships, there is a provision for giving special scholarships for women. Fifty (50)
scholarships @ Rs.1500/- per month are given to senior women champions per annum, 20 scholarships @ Rs.7, 500/- per
course are given to women doing diploma in sports coaching at SAI center; and 10 scholarships @ Rs.10,000/- per annum 
are given to women doing M.Phil / Ph. D. in physical education.   Instructions have been issued to various implementing
agencies to maintain gender-disaggregated data for effective monitoring of the gender analysis of various schemes.
 
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
The Committee appreciates the Ministry’s move of issuing instructions to various implementing agencies to
maintain gender disaggregated data for effective monitoring of the gender based analysis of various youth as well as sports
schemes of the Ministry.  However, the Committee feels that Ministry's gesture in this direction should move further. An
exclusive Cell in the Ministry may act as a watchdog to oversee the progress made by the implementing agencies with
regard to funds being spent on the women component under various schemes. The Committee hopes that the budgetary
documents of the Ministry would reflect the gender component of allocations under different schemes.

NEHRU YUVA KENDRA SANGATHAN
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
6.3       The Committee notes that out of 500 posts of district youth coordinators, 134 posts are lying vacant.  The Ministry
has to expand activities to all the districts in the country.  The Committee finds the Ministry in the catch-22 situation. 
Funds have been reduced and there is ban on filling up the posts, let alone creating new posts.  Then, there is the target to
cover the remaining districts also.  The Committee is dismayed at the casual manner the scheme is being run with such a
less number of District Coordinators and how the targets were going to be achieved.  The NYKS having all India network,
the Committee feels, its volunteers can play vital role in areas like literacy, family welfare, health awareness, national
integration, gender equality etc. in rural areas.  The Committee feels very much concerned at the way this scheme is sought
to be implemented.  The Committee, therefore, recommends to initiate effective measures for improving the situation and
taking this scheme out of the morass it is presently in.
Action Taken
 
It is a fact that District Youth Coordinator (DYC) offices exist in 500 districts.   Out of these, a large number of
posts of Youth Coordinators are lying vacant.  Against these 134 vacancies, 47 Regional Coordinators have been posted as
a result of recommendations of the Committee of Secretaries in connection with the report of Expenditure Finance
Commission.  As on date, there are 97 vacancies of DYCs in these 500 districts.  There are vacancies but no sanctioned
posts available at present.
The additional charges of vacant offices have been given to the Regional Coordinators or Youth Coordinators of
the adjacent District Kendras.  With a view to expeditiously fill these posts with regularly recruited officers, the Ministry
has approved a proposal to create 97 posts and the proposal stands referred to Ministry of Finance, Department of
Expenditure.  There is also a proposal to universatize the scheme in all districts of the country.  The proposal also seeks
approval of the Department of Expenditure in this regard.
 
Recommendation/Observations

6.3-6.4             The Committee expresses its unhappiness that a large number of posts of District Youth Coordinators are
lying vacant continuously for more than 8 years. Some posts were advertised in December 1996, interviews were also held

the posts created by the Governing Body of Nehru Yuva Kendras (NYKs) did not have the mandatory approval of the

SCHEME FOR DOPE TEST
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
16.7     In view of cases in Athens Olympics and earlier experience, the Committee notes that our weightlifters are most hit
by the scourge of doping.  Every time an Indian contingent prepares to leave the country for a mega event, doping tests are
hastily conducted and surprisingly they do not test positive here but fail the test in International events.
 
Action Taken
 
As per the WADA code of ethics, pre-departure testing is not permitted. Hence, it is mandatory for the Federations
to have a testing plan for the year. It is also required to send the samples at least fifteen days prior to the participation. The
details of the procedure have been sent to all the federations for compliance.
 
            As regards two recent cases of weightlifters are concerned, the role and responsibility of DCC starts from receiving
of sample.  DCC SAI is responsible for testing the sample.  There is a possibility that an athlete takes the drug after giving
the sample for dope testing.  For example Ms. Sanamachu, was tested positive for Furosemide, a short acting drug.  This
drug could have been taken either a day before or on the day of competition.  Again, Ms Pratima Kumari was tested
positive for testosterone.  This could be applied as gel, nasal spray, and cream just before the event.  It may also be
mentioned here that the testing of Ms. Pratima Kumari was also done by WADA in the month of July and was found
negative.  Due care is being taken that the sample which are received are tested as per the methods adopted by all
accredited Labs.  Process of sample collection is also being streamlined.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
16.8     The Committee was surprised to know that nobody seems to take the responsibility for the same.  Even the Sports
Ministry and SAI claim that it is not their duty to conduct dope tests on athletes who are under control of IOA and various
federations.  Federations have a ready-excuse about the high cost of conducting dope test.  Thus, at the end of the day
nobody is ready to own the responsibility for the bad name that a few athletes bring to the nation.
Action Taken (16.7-16.8)

All Federations are required to undertake testing of sports person as they are affiliated to international Federation,

‘out of competition’.  They are expected to have a plan for testing for the whole year.
 
It may be mentioned that Federations do not incur any cost of conducting dope test. Dope test for the disciplines
covered under the priority and general category under the Govt. guidelines are conducted free of cost under the Scheme
relating to Dope Test.  Most of Olympic disciplines are covered under the priority and general category.  Thus, NSF
cannot escape from their responsibility on the plea of ‘heavy costs’.  SAI has taken up various measures to spread
awareness and stop dope the menace among the Indian sports persons.
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
16.7-16.8         The Committee takes a serious note of the explanation given by the Ministry regarding instances of our
sportspersons being tested positive for banned drugs. The Committee is distressed that while cases of doping are
increasing, the Ministry and its concerned agencies instead of owning the responsibilities, still continue to disown their
responsibility.  The Committee terms the situation very deplorable as ultimately the individual sports-person is held
responsible for having been tested positive in doping at international events. The Committee feels that if the Ministry is
really serious to combat the malaise of doping it should not even hesitate to de-recognise those Sports Federations who are
not getting the dope-testing of the athletes conducted as and when required.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
16.9     The Committee feels extremely unhappy about the continuing indifference shown by all sports bodies – the
Ministry, IOA, Federations and the SAI about the serious malaise. They appear to be passing the buck to each other and no
serious attempt has been made so far by them to clean the mess that has plagued our sports persons.
 
16.10     The very fact that sportsperson after having been cleared by our test, get caught during the events shows how
rudimentary or outdated procedure we adopt about this testing.  It means lab at SAI does not have the necessary facility for
this test.  The Committee was informed that the procedure allows for tempering of the samples also.
 
16.11   The Committee, therefore, recommends that more sports scientists should be deputed by SAI to efficiently put all
sportspersons to dope testing.  It should evolve some mechanism so that the samples could not be tempered.  The entire
procedure should be transparent and the punishment has to be as per international norms.  Though there is a provision for
withdrawal of grants and facilities to the offender, but that of course, is rarely resorted to.  The Coaches and doctors of
Sportspersons testing positive should be made liable because during the training they are in-charge of their trainees. 
Blaming the sportsperson alone will not be fair.
 
Action Taken (16.9 – 16.11)
 
Dope Control Centre has got the necessary equipments for testing the samples. This can be collaborated with the
fact that in the last two years DCC has obtained ISO/IS 9001:2000 (December, 2002) and was able to achieve a mandatory
requirement of ISO/IEC 17025:1999 for permanent accreditation.  It is further pointed out that there all the methods to test
the various banned drugs as mentioned in the prohibited list issued by WADA have been developed and adopted.  These
methods have been developed with the help of Accredited Lab of WADA.  The testing is being conducted with due care
and is well documented.  The Surveillance Audit is being conducted by National Accredited Board for Laboratory

157th Report of HRD

(NABL) for testing.  The Department of Science and Technology, Govt. of India and their Lead Assessor had assessed the
functioning of the Laboratory.   The last surveillance audit was conducted by NABL in the month of June, 2004 and it was
a great pride for DCC that not even a single non-conformity was observed by the Technical Assessor of NABL. Thus, the
DCC has been following all the methods approved by WADA and is in tune with the WADA International Standard of
Laboratory Version 4 (Aug 2004).     As regards the procedure for tempering with the sample is concerned, the same is
well documented.  Due care is taken that the sample is not tampered and is not known to anyone except the person who is
authorized to handle the custody of the sample.  The samples are received in a sealed condition and are stored in deep
freezer in a controlled temperature.   These codes are further decoded and are given to the analyst for sample preparation.
There are only three persons in the Lab. who have the knowledge of the assigned Lab. Codes.  Further, all the staff of
DCC, has given an undertaking that they would maintain the secrecy and confidentiality regarding drug testing of samples
and other issues. The procedure being adopted by this Lab. is same as being followed by all other accredited Lab.

Over the years, the performance of Indian sportspersons in Olympics has been improving.  In 1996 and 2000 India
won only a bronze medal.  No medal could be won in 1984 and 1988 Olympics.  Moreover, during the Athens Olympic

in the disciplines of Athletics they created new national records.  During Athens Olympic Games, Indian sportsperson

since India’s independence.

would, therefore, reiterate that the coaches as well as doctors of sports persons who are incharge of their training, need to
be made equally accountable. The Committee would also impress upon the Government to depute more sport scientists at
DCC, SAI.
            The Committee finds it quite disturbing that no concrete efforts have been made to streamline selection criteria of
sports persons at the international level. The fact that we could win only one Bronze medal in 1996, one Bronze medal in
2000 and a silver medal in recent Olympic games indicates the level of sports and the selection of sports persons in our
country. In a country of more than 1000 million people, the performance of our sportsmen continues to be very
discouraging at the international level. The Committee, therefore, emphasises upon streamlining the entire selection
criteria of our sports persons to get better results in future. For that matter, the participant sportspersons for the next Asian
Games, Olympics and even Commonwealth games in 2010 should be selected without further delay. (Para 16.16)
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee appreciates the initiative for adoption of 27 schools for promotion of indigenous games/martial art
and Navodaya Vidayalas for providing opportunity to the aspiring rural children to undergo sports training. The
Committee, however, fails to understand the linkages of the new initiatives taken through Sports Authority of India with
the scientific training modules. Even crucial issues like sports medicine and sports psychology have also been not
addressed in the reply. The Committee would like to be apprised about the training modules framed to achieve best results
at international level. There should not be any difficulty in exploring the training modules being implemented in other
neighbouring countries like China, Japan, Korea etc.  (Para 16.17)
 
GRANTS FOR PROMOTION SPORTS IN UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES
 
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee welcomes the initiative taken by the Ministry to bring to the notice of the VCs of various
recognized Central Universities the existence of the scheme of grant to colleges/Universities.  However, the Committee
would like the Ministry to pursue the matter constantly with the State Governments to take benefit from the scheme.  (Para
18.3)
GRANTS FOR INSTALLATION OF SYNTHETIC SURFACE
 
Comments of the Committee
            It is surprising to note that 31 out of 44 projects approved since 1998-1999 have not been completed as some of the
State Governments/Grantees could not submit the UCs, progress reports etc.  The Committee hopes that the revised rates

157th Report of HRD

of central assistance would lessen the financial burden of State Govts and ease the problem to some extent.  The
Committee while reiterating its earlier recommendation would like the Ministry to expedite finalisation of projects which
otherwise may keep on piling ultimately affecting the performance of our sportspersons. The Committee appreciates the
proposed upward revision of funds under the revised Sports Infrastructure Scheme.  (Para 19.3)
 
PROMOTION OF SPORTS AND GRANTS IN SCHOOLS
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            The Committee feels that non-utilization of funds by States is not a recent development. Instead the Committee has
been pointing out problems time and again but no concrete efforts seems to be done by the Ministry as the situation has not
improved.  The Committee would like to be  apprised about the outcome of the Conference of State Sports Ministers and
the follow up action taken by the Ministry with regard thereto.  (Para 20.3)
 
ASSISTANCE TO NATIONAL SPORTS FEDERATIONS
 
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee is not satisfied with the state of affairs prevailing in the sports federations.  The Committee feels
that the efforts made by the Ministry with regard to ensure the financial accountability has not yielded any results.  The
Committee emphasises that these sports federations, registered under the Societies Act, are duty bound to file their
accounts.  The money they spend is the public money, and therefore, it is obligatory on their part to publish these
accounts.  They should therefore, not only file their annual accounts but also reflect the funds released to them by Central
Government as well as money received from other sources.  Errant federations should be de-recognised. (Para 22.8)
