committee observes that stoppage of some scheme without finalizing the schemes to substitute it would adversely affect the
Research and Development and HR Development in Information Technology.   The Committee therefore, recommends that
in future the existing programmes can be discontinued only after the alternative programmes have been formulated.
XVII.   VOCATIONAL EDUCATION
17.1     Under the scheme, job-oriented courses at +2 level are being provided in the areas of Agriculture, Business and
Commerce, Engineering and Technology, Home Science, Health and Paramedical, Social Sciences, Humanities etc. The
Scheme has created an infrastructure in 20600 Sections in7300 Schools with an enrolment capacity of 10 lakhs with the total
expenditure of approximately Rs. 727 crores since the inception of this scheme.
 
17.2     The Committee was informed that vocational education is facing a number of problems.  The first one is that the
Department of Secondary and Higher Education is doing it in isolation.  Secondly, the machines given to the vocational
education students have become totally obsolete. Lack of coordination among various agencies, which are implementing
various vocational schemes, is the third problem area.  The Ministry of Industry, Ministry of Rural Development, Ministry of
Urban Development, SGRY, PMGRY, with a plethora of schemes are all doing their bit in their own way.  There is no
vision.
 
17.3     The budget allocation for the 10th Plan is Rs. 350 crores and the budget allocation of the Annual Plan 2004-05 is Rs.
50 crores.  However, the Department could utilize only Rs. 10.80 crores in 2004-05.  The Committee was informed that the
scheme was under revision and it was expected that the revised scheme can be implemented from 2005-06 onwards. An
outlay of Rs. 20 crores has been proposed in the BE 2005-06 since at this stage it is not known what will be components of
the revised scheme.
 
17.4     The Committee is surprised to note that though the proposal for revised Scheme of vocational education was mooted
in the year 2002, the revised plan is yet to be finalized.   As a result, it could not be implemented last year also. 
Vocationalisation of education is our priority area and need of the hour, specially in view of  the shrinking employment
opportunities.  The Committee recommends that the revised Vocational Education and Training Programme must be
implemented during this financial year itself and adequate fund allocation may be made to the scheme to achieve  its
objectives.

of the Government of India with the aim of harnessing the scientific/technical knowledge available with Polytechnics to
secure Community/Rural Development.         The region-wise distribution of Community Polytechnics is given below:-

could be made  against an allocation of Rs. 297.26 crores.   During the  first three years of Tenth Plan also, funds remained
underutilized.  The committee notes that in 2002-03, allocation of Rs. 65.00 crore had to be reduced to Rs. 37 crores and

and determination of standards of universities.

                  General development of universities and colleges.
(ii)                Enhancing access and equity.

Higher Education. However, the Committee feels that UGC needs to be strengthened to cope with the emerging trends of
liberalization, privatization and globalization.  The uncomfortable proliferation of private universities with the off- campus
centers are one of areas where the UGC has not been effective.  The Committee therefore, recommends that the UGC Act
may be reviewed and amended to enable the UGC to cope up with the emerging challenges of Higher Education.

University (IGNOU) decreased during the last three years on account of the reasons that the IGNOU is expected to meet the
remaining share of the plan size and the entire Non-Plan (Maintenance) outlay from its own internal resources.

Rs. 56.00 crores, Rs. 35.30 crores (including unspent balance of Rs. 3.31 Crores) and Rs. 20.00 crores (including Rs. 3.44

XXII.   NATIONAL MERIT SCHOLARSHIP SCHEME
22.1     The National Merit Scholarship Scheme provides support to talented students and encourages them to excel
academically in studies by giving recognition and financial assistance from post-matric level to post graduation level on
state-wise merit basis and also separately to talented and meritorious students in rural areas from IX to X classes.
 
22.2    The 'National Scholarship Scheme' and the 'Scholarship Scheme for Talented Children from Rural Areas' have been
merged into a new scheme viz. 'National Merit Scholarship Scheme'. Under the existing schemes, the total BE for 2004-05
was kept at Rs. 7.00 crores. As the requisite approvals for merger of the existing schemes were received late, the new
scheme could not be implemented during the financial year 2004-05.    The Committee was informed that the total outlay of

announced.   However, under the new National Merit Scholarship Scheme the total number of Scholarships awarded will be

students in rural areas and 9750 scholarships from class XI to Post Graduate level at state level.   The reduction in

22.4    The Committee notes with concern that the total number of scholarships has been reduced to approximately 28,000 in

XXIII. SCHEME OF THE NATIONAL RESEARCH PROFESSORSHIP
 
The Scheme of National Research Professorship was instituted in 1949, to honour distinguished academics and
scholars who have attained the age of 65 years and who have made outstanding contribution in their respective fields and are
still capable of productive research are considered for appointment as National Professors, at any time, excluding those who
have retire on life pension, should not exceed 12. The Committee was informed that at present there is no National Research
Professor in position. The Committee does not know the reasons for not having any national Professors currently. The
Committee feels that the process of selection of National Professor should be finalized at the earliest and more funds be
provided for this Scheme. 
 
XXIV.  INDIAN INSTITUTE OF SCIENCE
The Committee opines that granting Rs. 100 crores to Indian Institute of Science is a welcome step to make it a world-class
institution.  The Committee recommends that at least seven more reputed Institutions may be selected for grant of Rs. 100
crore each for conducting research and development in basic science.

XXVI.PRIVATE UNIVERSITIES
26.1     The issue of private universities has been receiving the attention of the Committee all through. The Committee was
informed that recently, the Supreme Court of India, vide
 its order dated 11 February, 2005, has declared the provisions of
Sections 5 and 6, of the Chhattisgarh Niji Kshetra Vishwavidyalaya (Sthapana Aur Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 2002 to be ultra
vires of the Constitution.  The Supreme Court has further directed the State Government that, in order to protect the interests
of the students who may be actually studying in the institutions established by such private Universities, it should take
appropriate measures to have such institutions affiliation provided if it fulfills the requisite norms and standards laid down
for such purpose.
26.2     The Ministry of Human Resource Development informed the Committee that as per the information furnished by the
Chhattisgarh Government and the UGC, out of the 37 notified universities, 19 universities were providing class room
teachings and, approximately 23 thousand students were enrolled with these erstwhile private universities.  A majority of the
students were enrolled with the off-campus centers outside the State of Chhattisgarh  and a majority of them numbering
around 35000 in the National Capital Region.
 
26.3     The Ministry of Human Resource Development informed that they are extremely concerned about the future of the
thousands of students, who were studying in these now defunct private ‘universities’, particularly those outside Chhattisgarh.
 
26.4     The Ministry of Human Resource Development also promised expeditious action on whatever procedural obligations
are expected under the relevant laws governing these bodies, so that the standards of higher education are maintained.  The
UGC and the other statutory bodies would willingly provide any technical or academic assistance for determining the
standards of education or equivalence of degrees or other awards.  Since a majority of the affected students enrolled in the
off-campus centers are reported to be from the National Capital Region (NCR) of Delhi, the Delhi Government is also taking
appropriate steps. The Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University has, in principle agreed that requests received from
affected universities before the 31
st March, 2005 would be considered for affiliation as ‘special cases’, provided such
institutions met the required standards of higher and professional education. 
 
26.5     The Committee was further informed that a Committee of the CABE, under Prof. B.L. Mungekar, Member of the
Planning Commission, is specifically looking into all issues relevant to the financing of higher and technical education.  The
terms of reference of the Committee are: to examine the adequacy of investments and to find ways of augmenting the
resource flow in Higher Education; to examine the question of fair share of 6 percent of the GDP to Higher Education; and to
suggest the ways of encouraging and regulating private participation and investments in Higher/Technical Education.
 
26.6     Central bodies such as the UGC, the AICTE, the NCTE would, without compromising with the quality and standards
of higher education and technical education, collapse the processing time required, in the best interests of the affected
students.  Also in the short run, the Ministry have to see that those who obstruct a practical and just solution to the problem,
only because their commercial interest are uppermost in their minds, are dealt with sternly and appropriately.
 
26.7     The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Department of Secondary & Higher Education to deal with the
various aspects of the proliferation of the private universities and the fall out of the Supreme Court judgment in Chattisgarh
University Act. The Committee would however, like to add that the recent problem being faced by a very large number of
students of private universities should have been foreseen by both  UGC and the Department.  At the initial stage only, some
corrective action could have been taken. Future of enrolled students in these Universities should not be allowed to suffer. The

XXVII.            GENERAL
27.1    The Committee enquired from the MHRD about the programmes and schemes available to the States which are
advanced in elementary education for continuing their performance in Higher Education sector also.   The Committee was
informed that at present, no such distinction is drawn between the States, which have done better in the Elementary
Education and the others, which have not, while allocating resources for the higher education sectors.
 
27.2    Due to the universalisation of primary education under SSA, it is expected that the demand for secondary education
and higher education will go up in the coming years. A committee of the Central Advisory Board on Education has been set
up to examine the various aspects of this matter. The schemes to be formulated will depend on the Committee's
recommendations.
 
27.3    The Committee opines that the States which have done better in elementary education obviously would need more
facilities of Higher Education to accommodate all those coming from the elementary stage.   If the State Government is not
in a position to manage the demand on Higher Education, they are likely to face unrest and strain in the society. It may dilute
the achievements in the elementary education. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Government of India should
ensure that those States, which have performed well in elementary education, should get higher fund allocation to sustain the
achievements in elementary education as well as furthering the Higher Education.
 
27.4    National Policy on Education, 1986 as well as the NCMP aim at achieving the target of investing six per cent of the
GDP in education but upto 2005-06, slightly more than three per cent only could be achieved.  With this rate, the Committee
feels that, this goal shall remain unfulfilled.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the target of investing six per cent
of GDP in education should be tried to be achieved by the end of the Eleventh Plan.
 
27.5    The Committee opines that the ground for growth of Higher Education will be made only when there is advancement
in elementary education in the region.   If not, it may again lead to imbalance in the higher education system.  The
Committee therefore, recommends that more and more higher education institutions may be established in States where
there are advancements in elementary education.

OBSERVATONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
II         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
The Committee appreciates the enhancement in total allocation of the Department but is not satisfied with the trend of
utilization of allocations. It is intriguing that Rs. 267 crores were spent in just 25 days i.e. from 4 to 29 March 2005. Going
by the Department's claim of 95 per cent expenditure, the figure would actually cross Rs. 2100 crores, which means more
than Rs. 400 crores were spent in the month of March 2005 itself. This is certainly a disturbing trend of expenditure.  (Para
2.4)
            The Committee was informed that whereas some of the schemes had been approved as late as early 2005, there are
others for which funds were released in the last quarter.  The Committee is aware that 100% utilization was difficult in view
of some structural problems.  For example State Governments were not able to furnish the Utilization Certificates in time,
which causes delay in the further release of funds.  However, this should not be taken as a plea for less/under utilization of
funds.  The Committee feels that the first installment to the States, must begin in April itself and the further installment may
be released in the next quarter, if they are able to show that they have spent 50% of the first installment.  For the remaining
50%, sufficient time can be given to them for submitting Utilization Certificates and completing other formalities. (Para 2.5)
It is therefore, evident that non receipt the Utilization Certificate is not the only reason for under-utilization of the
allocations. The Committee feels that lack of  preparedness, foresight  and commitment of the part of Department are also
equally responsible in this regard. (Para 2.6)
            The Committee notes that there are some schemes, which have become difficult to implement/monitor from the
Centre, resulting in their poor implementation.  The Committee is of the view that the Department may identify such schemes
and take up with the States as well as the Planning Commission to find out on effective strategy for their smooth
functioning.  The Committee would also like to review its past financial commitment in regard to those schemes, which it
wants to close or revise before starting new schemes. (Para 2.7)
The Committee expresses its displeasure at the non-utilisation of funds and the way in which these programmes are
being managed. The Committee would like to be apprised of the reasons for the non-utilization of funds and recommends
that steps be taken  to see that the hurdles were removed and the Schemes were implemented in the year 2005-2006. (Para
2.8)
 
The Committee is concerned to see that the money being allocated could not be utilized for the last three years,
despite allocations being made every year for the college.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that urgent measures
should be taken for removing the hurdles so that money could be utilized. (Para 2.9)

is not a good practice.  The Committee may be apprised about the details about utilization of the re-appropriated fund meant

of students participating in this programme is declining from 92.12 per cent in 1997-98 to 78.70% in 2003-2004.  The
Committee feels that there must be some valid reasons for this sudden decline. The Committee desires that the Department
may look into the reasons for this decline and take necessary steps to improve the percentage. (Para 6.8)
 
VII.  NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF OPEN SCHOOLING
            The Committee observes that the mission of National Open Schooling is to provide continuing education to those
who have missed opportunities to complete their school education.  To achieve this noble aim, the Committee feels that,
paucity of funds should not be an obstacle. (Para 7.3)
 
            The Committee noted that the number of study centers of NIOS have come down from 2500 in 2003-2004 to 2400 in
2004-2005.  The Committee fails to understand why there is a reduction of hundred study centers in a single year.  The

159threport of committee on HRD

Committee may be apprised about the reasons for the reduction in the number of Study Centres.  The Committee
recommends that Government should take every possible step to ensure that more and more study centers are opened for
reaching the unreached. (Para 7.4)
 
VIII     INFORMATION COMMUNICATION TECHNOLOGIES IN  SCHOOLS
 
The Committee feels that the delay in approval of such a good scheme is not acceptable.  The Committee holds the
Department and the related agencies responsible for this, who failed to get the revised scheme approved in time.   The
Committee recommends that all out efforts should be made for the full utilization of Rs. 45 crores allocated in the budget
2005-06.  The Committee feels this allocation would hardly be adequate for implementing the scheme with required pace.
(Para 8.3)
 
IX.       INTEGRATED EDUCATION FOR DISABLED CHILDREN (IEDC)
             The Committee appreciates the targets achieved in the IEDC scheme despite the fact that some of the major States
are not implementing the scheme.  The Committee is of the view that the Department should effectively intervene to remove
the difficulties/constraints being faced in the implementation of the scheme by these States.   The Department may take the
initiative for special focusing on these States by arranging exclusive training programmes for teachers and also required
specialized educational aids and assistive devices.  If need be, the matter may also be taken up with respective Chief
Ministers of those States, which are not implementing the schemes meant for disabled children.  (Para 9.4)
The committee would like to be apprised about Statewise funds released to States and NGOs separately during 2002-
03, 2003-04 and 2004-05. (Para 9.5)
            The Committee also recommends that all out efforts may be made to ensure that allocation of 3% of education sector
outlay for disabled children's education is adhered to.  The Planning commission may be approached for any support to
ensure that the nation should not undermine the aspirations and needs of the disabled children.  (Para 9.6)
            The Committee welcomes this ambitious Action Plan for Children with special needs and hopes that action to
implement the same will be initiated at the earliest.  The Committee is of the opinion that the Department ensure that all the
schools be made disabled friendly by the end of the Eleventh Plan i.e. 2012. (Para 9.8)
X.        QUALITY IMPROVEMENT IN SCHOOLS
10.2     The Committee is surprised to note that revision of this scheme is hanging fire for a long time.  Even after a lapse of
almost 9 months the Department could not finalise the draft Cabinet Note for the CCEA.  Allocation of only Rs. 9.00 crores
for 2005-06 as compared to much higher allocations being made in the first three years of Tenth Plan indicates that the
chances of the Scheme being finalized and becoming operational during 2005-06 are not there.    The Committee is
constrained to say that an important scheme for improving quality in schools has not been handled in an effective manner.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that all out efforts be made to ensure that the scheme gets approval from all the
concerned authorities and implemented without any further delay. (Para 10.2)
 
            The Committee in the past also has been emphasizing the need for converging schemes with overlapping mandates
with a view to avoiding duplication of efforts and resources.  But in the instant case, the Committee notes that schemes with
different mandates are being converged under one Scheme for Quality Improvement in Schools. (Para 10.3)
 
10.5    Apparently, there is no co-relation between the name of the Scheme and the nature of the components that are
proposed to be put under it.  The Committee does not know the rationale behind this convergence, unless it is being done for
administrative convenience.  The Committee would like to know the reasons behind it.
(Para 10.5)
 
XI.      ACCESS AND EQUITY
 
11.4     The Committee is not convinced by the criteria for grant of funds to NGOs under the existing scheme.    There has to
be an even distribution of grants as this scheme is meant for the entire country.  Presently, it is seemingly being confined to
only a few States. It reflects the lop-sided  manner in which this scheme is being handled. The Committee recommends that a
clear policy for providing grants to NGOs from all areas may be put in place at the earliest. (Para 11.4)
 
The Committee observes that there is lack of seriousness on the part of the Government to finalise the programme at
the earliest and implement in right earnest. (Para 11.6)
 
The Committee recommends that the State Governments may be directed to depute a senior officer of Education
Department, if the District Magistrate is not available for carrying out the required inspections. (Para 11.7)

            The Committee feels that in the case of 'Access and Equity' also there is hardly any co-relation between the name of
the scheme and the components of it.  It creates confusion, which should be avoided. (Para 11.8)
 
XII.     RELEASE OF FUNDS
           The Committee is not at all happy with this tendency of last minute spending.  The Committee notes that this is
happening in many other schemes year after year.   The Committee further notes that all the required formalities are
completed only in the last quarter and funds are released in bulk.    Utilization of funds has to be even in all the quarters.  It
is not a healthy practice in fiscal area.  The Committee therefore, recommends that the release of funds may be made
uniform throughout the year. (Para 12.3)
XIII.     CENTRAL BOARD OF SECONDARY EDUCATION (CBSE)
            The Committee notices that students are under tremendous pressure, which leads sometimes to suicides by them
particularly during Board examinations.  The Committee is alarmed on this aspect.  The Committee has been informed that
CBSE has taken a number of steps to reduce stress among students as indicated below –
-
                     Launching of ‘helpline’ one month before the commencement of examination also before the declaration of
results.
-                     Publication of sample question papers and marking schemes to familirise students and teachers about the
nature of questions and question papers.
-                     Elimination of overall aggregation of marks to reduce unhealthy competition among students.
-                     Introduction of comprehensive and continuous school-based evaluation.  (Para 13.2)
 
            The Committee is of the view that besides examination stress, there are various other contributory factors such as
parental pressure, increasing competition, fast changing social and economic conditions, etc. which cause depression in
students.  The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the CBSE and hopes that these measures would result in giving
a better environment to students.  The Committee feels that the current practice of holding Board exams for Secondary and
Senior Secondary students at schools other than their own, also generates a kind of fear psychosis amongst them.  The
Committee is of the view that in order to avoid this, holding board examinations in their own schools, with
supervisors/invigilators from different schools, may also be considered. (Para 13.3)
 
            The Committee notes that there is a malpractice cell set up by CBSE whose main objective is to keep a vigilant watch
on educational activities of private organizations and institutions.   The committee has been informed that so far the
following have been identified as fake boards:   
-           Central Board of Higher Education, Vachaspati Bhavan, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi.
-
                     All India Board of Secondary Education, Gazipur,
-                     Central Board of Higher Education, East Patel Nagar, New Delhi.
-                     Board of Adult Education and Training, Brahmpuri, Nangalrai, New Delhi.     (Para 13.4)
            These institutions, the Committee is sure must be fleecing the unsuspecting students for providing degrees/diplomas
having no recognition.  It must stop. The Committee would like to be apprised about action if any taken against these boards.
(Para 13.5)
 
XIV.    ALL INDIA COUNCIL OF TECHNICAL EDUCATION
            The Committee is amazed to see that funds have been allocated for the purpose of restructuring the AICTE Technical
Bureau and its Committees but the Department says that there was no such proposal.  The Committee would like to have a
clarification in this regard. (Para 14.2)
 
            The Committee has learnt that a lot of delay is caused in clearing the proposals for avoiding new approvals by the
AICTE.  In the current scenario, we could ill afford to do that.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that process of
according approval by the AICTE needs to be streamlined and made more transparent. (Para 14.3)
 
XV.      NATIONAL COUNCIL OF RURAL INSTITUTES
 
            The Committee is at a loss to see that the Government has not been able to ensure that Institute starts functioning,
which was set up in 1995.  It is not convinced by the purely technical explanation given for the delay by the Department.  It
is baffling that it took almost ten years to create a post of Director of an Institute, which was set up in 1995.  And now, it is
claimed that everything would be in place by 2005-06.  The Committee does not have any reason to believe this.  The
Committee, however, recommends that Department must ensure that the Director is appointed and remaining posts are filled
up during 2005-06.  It also calls upon the Ministry of Finance to provide necessary clearances, etc. on priority basis in the
year 2005-06 itself. (Para 15.3)

XVI.    RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT AND HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT IN IT
 
            The Committee therefore, recommends that in future the existing programmes can be discontinued only after the
alternative programmes have been formulated. (Para 16)
 
XVII.   VOCATIONAL EDUCATION
 
            The Committee is surprised to note that though the proposal for revised Scheme of vocational education was mooted
in the year 2002, the revised plan is yet to be finalized.   As a result, it could not be implemented last year also. 
Vocationalisation of education is our priority area and need of the hour, specially in view of  the shrinking employment
opportunities.  The Committee recommends that the revised Vocational Education and Training Programme must be
implemented during this financial year itself and adequate fund allocation may be made to the scheme to achieve  its
objectives. (Para 17.4)
 
XVIII.    SCHEME OF COMMUNITY POLYTECHNICS
 
However, the Committee is dismayed to note that the utilization of this enhanced allocation has been only Rs. 11.05
crores as on 4.3.2005 which is a mere 34.84 per cent of the allocation.  The Committee would like the Department to see that
the funds for 2005-06 are utilized properly and judiciously for such an important scheme. (Para 18.2)
 
            The Committee feels that the regional distribution of Community Polytechnics is uneven.  Particularly, eastern region
has only 97 Community Polytechnics.  The Committee is of the opinion that the Department should try to open more
Community Polytechnics in eastern region which is a backward area having the highest concentration of rural population. 
The imparting of technical skills will help ameliorate the pitiable conditions prevailing there.  The Committee feels that the
underutilization of funds must have affected the training programmes, thereby defeating the very objective of the Scheme. 
(Para 18.4)
 
XIX.    UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION
The Committee was given to understand that UGC is actively pursuing its mandate of promotion and coordination in
Higher Education. However, the Committee feels that UGC needs to be strengthened to cope with the emerging trends of
liberalization, privatization and globalization.  The uncomfortable proliferation of private universities with the off- campus
centers are one of areas where the UGC has not been effective.  The Committee therefore, recommends that the UGC Act
may be reviewed and amended to enable the UGC to cope up with the emerging challenges of Higher Education. (Para 19.3)
 
XX.      INDIRA GANDHI NATIONAL OPEN UNIVERSITY (IGNOU)
The Committee appreciates that IGNOU gradually is becoming self-supporting.  It also has taken certain innovative
steps recently and started modern professional courses in a big way.  The Committee feels that such an institution should not
suffer on account of paucity of funds.  It, therefore, should continue getting funds at least to develop infrastructure and
maintenance of the university to ensure that IGNOU is not forced to overcharge its students. (Para 20.2)
 
           The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Distance Education Council (DEC) to ensure the quality of the
degrees awarded in the Open University system. (Para 20.4)
 
XXI.    OPEN UNIVERSITY SYSTEM IN THE NORTH EAST
           The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken in the North Eastern Region for development of Open University
system.   The Committee recommends that more centres may be opened in the North Eastern to augment the already existing
system. (Para 21.2)
 
XXII.   NATIONAL MERIT SCHOLARSHIP SCHEME
 
           The Committee notes with concern that the total number of scholarships has been reduced to approximately 28,000 in
a year, which by any standard is very low.  The Committee therefore, recommends that the number of Scholarships and the
total outlay of the scheme may be substantially increased progressively, so that more and more intelligent and needy
students are benefitted.  (Para 22.4)
 
XXIII. SCHEME OF THE NATIONAL RESEARCH PROFESSORSHIP
 
The Committee does not know the reasons for not having any national Professors currently. The Committee feels that

the process of selection of National Professor should be finalized at the earliest and more funds be provided for this Scheme. 
(Para 23)
 
XXIV.
                 INDIAN INSTITUTE OF SCIENCE
The Committee recommends that at least seven more reputed Institutions may be selected for grant of Rs. 100 crore
each for conducting research and development in basic science. (Para 24)
           
XXV.   MAHATMA GANDHI ANTARRASHTRIYA HINDI VISHWAVIDYALAYA
 
The Committee notes that no response came from the Department to its specific and pointed queries regarding
reasons for its previous VC functioning from Delhi and also for not starting academic activities of the university even after
more than 8 years of its existence.  Main civil works are yet to commence and the university is housed in some temporary
structure at Wardha.  (Para 25.4)
 
            On a specific query, the Department informed that a fact-finding committee was being set up to go into the affairs of
the university.  The Committee expresses its displeasure on the way this Vishwavidyalaya named after Mahatma Gandhi has
been treated so far.  The Committee appreciates that fact-finding Committee has been appointed and its efforts are on to help
improve its functioning.  The Committee would like to be apprised of the finding of the proposed fact-finding Committee.  It
feels that those found guilty should not be allowed to go unpunished. (Para 25.5)
 
XXVI.PRIVATE UNIVERSITIES
 
The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Department of Secondary & Higher Education to deal with the
various aspects of the proliferation of the private universities and the fall out of the Supreme Court judgment in Chattisgarh
University Act. The Committee would however, like to add that the recent problem being faced by a very large number of
students of private universities should have been foreseen by both  UGC and the Department.  At the initial stage only, some
corrective action could have been taken. Future of enrolled students in these Universities should not be allowed to suffer. The
Committee recommends that the Department should vigorously further purse the initiatives they have taken to streamline the
private university system. (Para 26.7)
The Committee recommends that private investment in higher education is welcome provided it is really helpful to
meet the need and aspirations of the young generations and it fits into the overall policy of the Government at the Central
level and at the State level.  There should be no compromise in relations to standards and quality. While encouraging the
private participation, blatant commercialization of higher education needs to be discouraged. (Para 26.8)
 
            Obviously any structured private investment in higher education would have to be made through a legislative
framework.  That may take some time.  Investment in this sector has already been put on the automatic route.  In this light,
till a suitable legislation is in place, at least a Policy Framework be made at the earliest. (Para 26.9)
 
XXVII.            GENERAL
 
           The Committee opines that the States which have done better in elementary education obviously would need more
facilities of Higher Education to accommodate all those coming from the elementary stage.   If the State Government is not
in a position to manage the demand on Higher Education, they are likely to face unrest and strain in the society. It may dilute
the achievements in the elementary education. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Government of India should
ensure that those States, which have performed well in elementary education, should get higher fund allocation to sustain the
achievements in elementary education as well as furthering the Higher Education. (Para 27.3)
 
           National Policy on Education, 1986 as well as the NCMP aim at achieving the target of investing six per cent of the
GDP in education but upto 2005-06, slightly more than three per cent only could be achieved.  With this rate, the Committee
feels that, this goal shall remain unfulfilled.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the target of investing six per cent
of GDP in education should be tried to be achieved by the end of the Eleventh Plan. (Para 27.4)
 
           The Committee opines that the ground for growth of Higher Education will be made only when there is advancement
in elementary education in the region.   If not, it may again lead to imbalance in the higher education system.  The
Committee therefore, recommends that more and more higher education institutions may be established in States where
there are advancements in elementary education. (Para 27.5)

REPORT

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Human Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present its
sixteenth report on its behalf, present the Report of the Committee on the Assam University
(Amendment) Bill, 1994.

2. The Bill, which was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 20th December, 1994,
seeks to amend the Assam University Act, 1989. In pursuance of the rules relating to
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha,
referred* the Bill to the Committee for examination and report.

3. A Press Communique, inviting memoranda containing opinions and suggestions from
individuals, organisations and institutions interested in the subject matter of the Bill, was
issued on 9th January, 1995 (Appendix-I).

4. The Committee considered the Bill in three sittings (Appendix-II) and heard the oral
evidence of the Secretaries of the Ministries of Human Resource Development (Department
of Education) and Law, Justice and Company Affairs (Department of Legal Affairs), the
Secretary, University Grants Commission the Commissioner and Secretary, Department of
Education, State Government of Assam, and the Registrar, Assam University, Silchar.

5. In its meeting, held on the 16th February, 1995, the Committee considered the Draft
Report and adopted it for presentation/aying in both the Houses.

6. The Department of Education, in the background note on the subject submitted to
the Committee, explained the need to introduce the Assam University (Amendment) Bill,
1994, (Appendix-III)

7. Elaborating on the circumstances which led to the introduction of the Bill, the
Secretary, Department of Education, State Government of Assam, informed the Committee
that objections had been raised by various sections of the people regarding the affiliating
status of the Assam University, Silchar. A feeling had grown that the jurisdication of the
Assam University at Silchar overlapped the jurisdiction of the Guwahati and the Dibrugarh
Universities.

8. As a result of this, the issue was taken up by the Human Resource Development
Minister with the Chief Minister of Assam. The Chief Minister, after having discussions with
the academicians, the Vice-Chancellors of the concerned universities, as well as the
representatives of the Teacher’s association, etc. wrote back to the Minister of Human
Resource Development about the need to restrict the jurisdiction of the Assam University by
amending Section 6 of the Assam University Act, 1989.

9. The Minister of Human Resource Development, thereafter, convened a meeting of
Union Ministers and Members of Parliament from Assam, the Chief Minister of Assam,
representatives of Assam Gana Parishad and Vice-Chancellors of both the Central
University in Assam to discuss the affiliating status of the Assam University. There was
unanimous agreement that the Assam Government’s proposal to restrict the jurisdiction of
the new university be accepted. Hence, the Assam University (Amendment) Bill, 1994 was
introduced.

10. The Department, in its note, has stated that the Bill seeks to amend Section 6 of the

parent Act, with a view to ensure an equitable distribution of territorial jurisdiction of
different universities in the State; and to see that the older universities of the State, set up
by the State Government, also remained viable.

11. Section 6(i) of the Assam University Act, 1989, which provides that the jurisdiction
of the Assam University shall extend to the whole of the State of Assam, was, therefore,
sought to be amended in order to restrict the jurisdiction of the University to only five
districts: Cachar, Karimganj, North Cachar Hills, Karbi Anglong and Hailakandi. It will be
deemed to have been effective from the 15th January, 1994, i.e. the day on which the Assam
University Act came into effect.

12. The amendment seeks to add one more district Hailakandi to the names of districts
already mentioned in Section 6(2) of the parent Act. This district, the Committee was
informed, had been carved out of the district of Cachar after the enactment of Assam
University Act 1989.

13. The amendment also seeks to omit altogether sub-section 3 of the Section 6 which
empowered the University to grant affiliation to any other college existing in any part of the
State of Assam provided the University concerned in whose jurisdiction the college was
located, had no objection.

14. During the evidence, Members expressed apprehension about the admission policy
of the University. In the absence of a definite stipulation in this regard, some Members felt
that students from other parts of the State or the country might not be admitted in the
University. The Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs, informed the Committee that no
such expressed stipulation had been provided in the case of other Central Universities as
well. The Secretary, UGC, clarified to the Committee that even in the absence of such a
provision, complaints regarding discrimination in admission on the basis of region had never
come up. In practice, however, the University shall be open to the students from all parts of
the country.

14.1 The Committee, however, feels that in order to remove the doubts about the
admission policy of the University, government should bring forward an amendment into
clause 7 of the Act so as to make it clear that admission is open to all students, irrespective
of race or class or place of domicile, on the pattern of the amendment suggested by this
Committee to Clause 7 of the Dr. B.R. Ambedkar University Bill, 1994.

15. The Committee also sought to know the reason as to why the Assam University Bill,
which was passed in 1989, was notified only in January, 1994. The Secretary, Department of
Education, informed the Committee that the delay was mainly due to lack of infrastructure
and inadequate funds. It was also delayed, he said, due to demand for seting up another
university at Tejpur. Both the Universities were set up more or less at the same time.

16. To a query regarding lack of adequate facilities, including roads, buildings, etc. in
the University, the Registrar, Assam University, apprised the Committee of the works
completed and the projects undertaken in this regard. The main reason for the slow pace of
works, according to him, was the non-availability of requisite funds. The Committee,
however, was informed that efforts were on to provide sufficient funds to the University.
Department of Education, in fact, had proposed to release three crore rupees for this
University from its savings in the Revised Estimates for 1994-95. The Committee desires that
this should be ensured so that the university might starts functioning soon.


17. The Committee approves the Assam University (Amendment) Bill, 1994, alongwith
the recommendation made in para 14.1.

 REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION
1.1       The Department of Women and Child Development was set up in 1985, for providing a focused and coordinated
impetus to the holistic development of women and children who together constitute 70% of the total population of the
country.
1.2       The Department formulates plans, policies and programmes, moots proposals to enact and amend legislation
affecting women and children and guides and coordinates the efforts of both governmental and non-governmental
organizations working in the field of women and child development.   Apart from this, the Department implements
certain innovative programmes for women and children which are in the areas of training and capacity building,
employment and income generation, welfare and support services, awareness generation and gender sensitization.
 
II.        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       Plan allocation of Rs. 3875.29 crores has been made for the Department of Women and Child Development for
2005-2006 against Rs. 2400.00 crores allocated in 2004-2005, thereby increasing the allocation by Rs. 1475.29 crores. 
The Department has informed that the Plan Allocation has been enhanced in 2005-2006 for the schemes such as
Creches/ Day Care Centres for Children of Working/ Ailing Mother; Swadhar; General Grant to CSWB; GIA to
Research, Publication and Monitoring; Nutrition Education (FNB) and ICDS-General.
 
2.2       The Committee notes that against a Ninth Plan allocation of Rs. 7810.42 crores, expenditure figures stood at Rs.
6248.53 crores.    An enhanced provision of Rs. 13780.00 crores has been made for the Tenth Plan.   The Committee
observes  that during the first three years of the Tenth Plan, allocated funds remained underutilized. Major funding is
there for child welfare related schemes and there has been optimum  utilization of the funds with expenditure exceeding
the allocated funds during 2004-05.   However, status of women related schemes are entirely different.   Allocated
funds for Women related Schemes, in spite of being very less when compared with Child Welfare Schemes remained
underutilized in all the first three years of the Tenth Plan.
2.3       The Committee's attention has also been drawn by another disturbing trend in the manner of utilisation of
allocated funds during the year. Against a total plan allocation of Rs. 2400.00 crores in 2004-2005, expenditure
reported upto December, 2004 is Rs. 1944.48 crores.   However, in the last quarter of the year, expenditure figures

reached Rs. 2161.67 crores upto 28  February.   This is more evident in the case of child related schemes.  In spite of
expenditure in respect of women welfare schemes although showing considerable increase in the last quarter remained
allocated funds underutilized.
 
2.4       The Committee expresses its serious concern over major part of the expenditure being rushed through in the last
quarter of the year.  Such a trend, in fact, points towards some inherent drawbacks both in the system of flow of funds as
well as in the delivery mechanism adopted by the Department.  The Committee fails to understand the purpose of
formulating Annual Action Plan for each and every scheme, clearly identifying both the physical and financial targets to
be achieved in every quarter.  The Committee calls upon the Department to discuss with the States the structural and
functional problems that are responsible not only for poor utilization of resources but also manpower and planning.
Resources both human and fiscal meant for the welfare of women and children - bedrock of our future society and
economy can not be allowed to go waste.  
 
III.       INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS)
3.1       The ICDS Scheme aims at holistic development of children (0-6 yrs) and pregnant and lactating mothers from
disadvantaged sections, by providing a package of  integrated services comprising of supplementary nutrition,
immunization, health check-up, referral services, pre-school, non-formal education and nutrition and health education.
 
3.2       Introduced in 1975 in 33 blocks, on an experimental basis, the scheme has been gradually expanded to cover
5652 projects till the end of the Ninth Plan.
 
3.3       The Committee observes that Tenth Plan allocation of Rs. 10,391.75 crores for ICDS is more than double of the
provision of Rs. 4980.00 crores in Ninth Plan.   There has been optimum utilisation of allocated funds during the first
three years of the Tenth Plan.   The Committee  notes that against an enhanced  allocation of Rs. 1837.44 in 2004-2005,
expenditure reported upto 18
th March, 2005 is Rs. 1653.97 crores   The Committee, however, observes that during 
2003-2004 and 2004-2005 funds allocated to NE  states remained under utilized .BE provision of Rs. 214.00 crore
during 2003-2004 for NE states had to be reduced to Rs. 196.68 crores at the RE stage and actual expenditure reported
at the end of the year was only Rs. 125.21 crore.   During 2004-2005 against BE provision of Rs. 214.00 crore, only Rs.
144.69 crore could be utilized upto 28th  February, 2005.   In view of considerable  enhancement in the provision for
ICDS during 2005-2006, the Committee recommends that  operationlisation of ICDS projects/AW centres 
should be closely monitored in NE States.
 
3.4       The BE for 2005-06 for this scheme is Rs. 3142.25 crores.  Explaining the reasons for this significant increase in
the allocation for the year 2005-06, the Department informed that since many States were not providing adequately for
supplementary nutrition in view of resource constraints, it has been proposed to support States by providing 50% of
expenditure incurred by them on supplementary nutrition.  A sum of Rs. 1500.00 crore has been earmarked for this
purpose.  The Scheme is also proposed to be expanded to cover 467 additional Projects and 1,88,168 AWCs, in the first
phase.  Kishori Shakti Yojana, which is currently sanctioned for 2000 ICDS Projects, is also proposed to be extended to
all ICDS Projects.  This would involve estimated additional expenditure of about Rs. 300.00 crore in 2005-2006. 
 
3.5       The Committee was informed that the Supreme Court in its order dated 29.4.2004 directed the states to

desired that micro planning by the State would be necessary for laying down the revised population norms.  States
were, accordingly, requested, to suggest revision in norms and submit their requirement of more AWCs/Mini AWCs.

3.12     The Committee would also like to reiterate its earlier recommendation that the norm of one Anganwadi Centre
for 700 populations in tribal projects needs to be re-looked for revision in the case of inaccessible areas.  Instead of one
AWC for 700 population, one centre per hillock/ cluster should be the criteria for hilly or desert areas like Manipur and

3.13     To run the ICDS programme effectively, Anganwadi workers are the key persons.  The Committee is  happy to

Workers and Helpers, as envisaged under the ICDS Scheme, and additional responsibilities being assigned to them in

VI.       DAY CARE CENTRES
6.1       The scheme aims to provide day care services for the children (0-5 yrs) of mainly casual, migrant, agricultural
and construction labourers.    The scheme is being implemented by the Central Social Welfare Board and by two
national level voluntary organizations, namely Indian Council for Child Welfare, New Delhi and Bharatiya Adimjati
Sevak Sangh, New Delhi.   The scheme covers 12,470 creches covering 3.11 lakh children.
 
6.2       The allocation for the Tenth Plan for the scheme is Rs. 60 crores.  The Committee notes that although increased
funds are being allocated from the first year of Tenth Plan, utilization thereof has failed to show the same pace.  In
2003-2004, Plan allocation of Rs. 18.00 crore had to be reduced to Rs. 7.00 crore at the RE stage and final expenditure
figures at the end of the year were only Rs. 6.03 crores.  During 2004-2005, there was yet another increase at the
beginning of the year (Rs. 27.00 crore) which had to be drastically reduced to Rs. 15.92 crore and the figures upto 28
th
February, 2005 showed an expenditure of only Rs. 10.49 crore.  An enhanced allocation of Rs. 28.50 crores has been
made for 2005-06.
 
6.3       The Committee observes that delay in the revision of the Scheme is being cited as the main reason for
underutilization of funds.  This position has continued since the beginning of the Tenth Plan.  The Committee however,
finds that only progress  made since then is that this proposal  has received the approval of the Minister and an EFC
memo is under circulation.  Keeping in view the number of procedural formalities to be completed before revision of a
scheme gets final approval, the Committee apprehends that the scheme would continue to be at the revision stage in the
last two years of the Tenth Plan also.
6.4       The Committee finds that enhancement in allocated funds for the scheme of Day Care Centres was also meant
for expansion of the scheme by starting more crèches.  However, the number of crèches continues to remain the same. 
Another striking feature of this scheme is that out of 12,470 creches in the country, largest number (1,340) are
concentrated in Andhra Pradesh, followed by 1,327 in Madhya Pradesh and 1,171 in Maharashtra.   The Committee  is
not happy with the  coverage of children as well as number of crèches in the country.
 
6.5       This scheme is meant to provide day care services for the children (0-5 years) of mainly casual, migrant,
agricultural and construction laborers. The Committee wonders about the constraints being faced by the Central Social
Welfare Board and two national level voluntary organizations, Indian Council for Child Welfare and Bharatiya
Adimjati Sevak Sangh in establishing these crèches in underserved areas.  The Committee recommends that necessary
steps should be taken to increase the number of crèches and make then operational.
 
6.6       The Committee observes that a total amount of Rs. 18,480 per year per crèche is being extended to NGOs every
year.  With the number of creches remaining the same, variation in the level of expenditure every year does not seem to

VIII.    BALIKA SAMRIDDHI YOJANA (BSY)
8.1       Balika Samriddhi Yojana is a comprehensive girl child specific scheme launched in 1997 with the objective of
raising the overall status of the girl child and bringing about a positive change in family and community attitude towards
her.  During 1997-98 and 1998-99, the scheme was implemented as a Central Sector Plan Scheme under which the

160threport of Committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/160threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:22:33]
funds were released to District Rural/Urban Development Agencies for giving a grant of Rs. 500/- to the mothers of new
born girl children.  The Scheme was reviewed in 1999 and recast as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme to extend 100%
central assistance to States/UTs  to provide the benefits through ICDS Scheme infrastructure.  Under the revised
Scheme, the post delivery grant of Rs. 500/- is deposited in a Bank/Post Office account in the name of the girl child.  In
addition, varying amount of money, as scholarship will be deposited in the account on successful completion of her
studies from class I to class X.  Accumulated value of the deposit is payable to the girl at the age of 18 years on the
condition that she remains unmarried till then.
 
8.2       Allocation of Rs. 100 crore has been made for the Scheme for Tenth Plan.  The Committee has been observing
the uncertain status of the Scheme since the beginning of the Tenth Plan.  This status is clearly reflected in the trend of
allocations being made for the Scheme – In the first year of the Tenth Plan, i.e. 2002-03, no provision was there
initially, Rs. 2.00 crores were provided at the RE stage, expenditure reported was nil.  In the next year, Rs. 1.50 crore
were provided at the BE stage to be drastically reduced to Rs. 1 lakh at the RE stage and an expenditure of Rs. 53
thousand being incurred during the year.  In 2004-2005, a token provision of Rs. 3 lakh was made to be substantially
enhanced to Rs. 50.00 crore at the RE stage.  As per the latest information made available to the Committee, Rs. 37.16
crores have been released to different States/UTs during 2004-2005.
 
8.3       The Department has admitted that the Scheme is under transfer to the States since 2002-03. The Department has
conveyed its no objection to the Planning Commission in this regard. The Planning Commission had stated that till the
transfer of Scheme to the states the implementation of the Scheme will be the responsibility of Department of Women
and Child Development. It was further clarified that as National Development Council has not approved the proposal of
transfer and States were pressing for funds, therefore, Rs 50.00 crore were demanded at RE stage during 2004-2005.
The funds under the scheme are being transferred from Department’s Head of accounts to State Consolidated Fund .The
scheme is being run by State Government machinery .The only difference after transfer will be that the funds will be
directly released to Consolidated Fund of States/UTs.
 
8.4       The Committee notes that the expenditure reported upto February,2005 is Rs. 30.84 crores.  Unspent balance of
Rs. 67.82 crores (including Rs. 39.75 crores released during the year 2004-2005) are lying with various State
Governments.  Maximum amount of unspent balance is with Bihar (Rs. 19.33 crores) and U.P. (Rs. 16.75 crores). 
 
8.5       The Committee expresses its serious concern about the way the Balika Samriddhi Yojana is being implemented. 
Scheme launched in the first year of Ninth Plan, i.e. 1997-98 had to be recast after two years of its implementation.  In
the third year, the scheme had to be reviewed again and recast.  The Committee is perturbed to note that Tenth Plan has
also completed three years but the air of indecisiveness still hangs around the Scheme meant for the welfare of the girl
child.  The Committee is left with no other alternative but to conclude that the scheme suffers from inherent drawbacks,
which continues to be there in spite of review of the scheme being done not once, but on two occasions.  The Committee
doubts whether the funds released so far have reached the targetted beneficiaries. 
 
8.6 The Committee is of the opinion that the final decision about its status should be taken without any further delay.  It
should not happen that the Tenth Plan period is also over and no decision has been  taken.  Level of allocation in 2005-
06 (Rs. 3 lakhs) hints at this possibility only.  The Committee would also like to mention that continuance of unspent
balances cannot be considered an ideal position.  Such a position confirms the inability of implementing agencies to

WOMEN WITH DAY CARE CENTRES FOR CHILDREN
 
9.1       The objective of the Scheme is to provide suitable, safe and inexpensive accommodation to women residing in
places away from their hometowns to be able to work.  Women being trained for employment and girl students
undergoing professional courses have also been made eligible for accommodation.  Financial assistance is provided
under the scheme to the extent of 75% of the cost of construction of the hostel building and 50% of the cost of land. 
Assistance can also be extended on the same pattern as above towards purchase of ready-built building for use as
Working Women’s Hostel.  Voluntary Organizations (Registered Societies, Public Trust etc.) Women’s Development
Corporations, Universities, Schools/Colleges of Social Work, Local Bodies, Cooperative Institutions, State
Governments and Union Territories Administrations are eligible to receive financial assistance under the scheme.
 
9.2       Against an allocation of Rs. 51.25 crores for the scheme during the Ninth Plan, an expenditure of Rs. 34.57
crores was made.  Physical target of setting up of 120 hostels also could not be achieved, number of hostels set up being
102 only.  The Committee notes that although an enhanced allocation of Rs. 85.00 crore for the scheme has been made
during the Tenth Plan, there is no noticeable improvement in its performance level.  Rather it is showing a downward
trend. In the first year of the Tenth Plan, an ambitious provision of Rs. 13.50 crore was made but allocation of  only Rs.
6.50 crore by the fourth year of the plan period  indicates that there is not much scope left for bringing out any
improvement.  The Committee is constrained to note that not only allocation, but the trend of utilisation also shows a
declining trend.  During 2004-2005, allocation of Rs. 9.00 crore had to be reduced to Rs. 6.20 crore at the RE stage and
by 28
th February, utilization  of only Rs. 2.29 crores has been reported to be made.  Thus, plan allocation for this
scheme which is very much required for the working women force of the country  remains grossly underutilized.  On a
specific query in this regard, non-receipt of good and viable proposals by the Department and inability of the
implementing agencies in utilizing their grant within the stipulated time were cited as the main reasons.  Last year the
Committee was given to understand that this scheme was also under revision.  However, this exercise seems to have
stopped as no mention about the same has been made.
9.3       The Committee notes that Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra seem to be the major beneficiaries of funds
amounting  to Rs. 2.84 crores released during 2005-2006.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the funding
pattern for these three States under the scheme during 2005-2006.
 
9.4       Committee’s attention has been drawn by the audit report No.2 of 2004 (for the period ended March 2003).  The
audit has pointed out failure of the Department to monitor the utilization of grants totaling Rs. 39.58 crore given to

10.1       Committee’s attention  has been drawn by two similar schemes for women welfare being implemented for
considerable time.  One is Swawlamban scheme whose objective is to promote women development through provision
of employment by training them in traditional and non traditional  trade such as computer, electronics, embroidery and
weaving etc. whereas the objective of the scheme of STEP is to provide training for skill  upgradation in traditional
sector like agriculture, animal husbandry , handloom, handicraft khadi and village industries etc. Implementing 
agencies for   both the schemes include women development corporation and public undertaking, cooperatives, women
development centres of universities, NGOs etc.  Targetted beneficiaries in both the schemes are also the same.
10.2     Last year also, the Committee had  raised  this issue.  It was clarified by the Department that both Swawlamban,
earlier known as NORAD, and Support toTraining and Employment Programme (STEP) Schemes aim at providing
training and skill upgradation to women to facilitate them obtain some kind of employment or self-employment.  The
two schemes, however, differ in the following aspects :
(a)    Unlike the Swawlamban Scheme which is a kind of stand alone scheme for training of women for a
fixed period ranging from 3 months to 12 months, STEP is a more comprehensive programme which is
usually undertaken on a project  basis for a period of 2-3 years
 (b) The number of beneficiaries in a training project under Swawlamban Scheme ranges from 30 to 100. 
Whereas the STEP Scheme, produces between 500 to 1000 beneficiaries in a single project.

15.1     Swadhar scheme was introduced in 2001-2002 with the objective of the scheme  to comprehensively rehabilitate
widows, victims of trafficking, victims of natural calamities, mentally disordered and destitute women.  The scheme
provides for support like food and shelter, counseling, medical facilities and vocational training to women.   The
implementing agencies are the Social Welfare/ Women and Child Welfare Department of State Government, Women’s
Development Corporations, Urban Local Bodies, reputed Public/ Private Trust or Voluntary Organizations who are
willing to take up the responsibility of rehabilitating such women. 
 
15.2     The Scheme for Rescue of Victims of Trafficking aims at supporting the efforts of the Non-Governmental
Organisations in rescue operation of victims of trafficking.  In order to encourage the participation of the Non-
Governmental Sector, it is proposed to provide assistance to NGOs to meet the cost of transporting the trafficked
victims to shelter homes and temporary stay of inmates in the shelter home etc. The Committee notes that the
Department proposes to examine in detail this new intervention scheme.   It is proposed to be launched during 2005-06
and accordingly a provision of Rs.30 lakh has been made for it.
 
15.3     Plan allocation under Swadhar Scheme in the year 2005-2006  has been increased from Rs.2.70 crore in 2004-05
to Rs.5.50 crore. The Department informed that allocation has been increased  since the Swadhar Scheme has been

applications for the projects and by holding workshops all over the country.  As a result, a large number of proposals
have been received.  In 2001-04, only 26 cases were sanctioned whereas in 2004-05 alone, 78 cases have already
beensanctioned. The Committee was given to understand that there is a delay in obtaining Utilisation Certificates  from
the NGOs/ States. The Committee also notes that the Department aims at funding atleast one Swadhar home and one
helpline for women in difficult circumstances in each district of the country to benefit mere and more women in difficult
circumstances.

16.1     The Direct and Indirect Instruments of National Nutrition Policy indicates that the ambitious goal of improving

background, the National Nutrition Mission was announced by the Hon’ble Prime Minister on 15
th August, 2001.
 
16.2.    The National Nutrition Mission constituted under the Chairmanship of Hon’ble Prime Minister in July 1993 with
a two tier supervisory structure aims at addressing the problem of malnutrition in a mission mode and enable policy
direction and effective intersectoral coordination for improving nutritional scenario in the country.
 
16.3     It was decided to constitute a Core Group to look into various issues like Nutrition Monitoring and Surveillance,
Intersectoral Coordination between concerned sectors, Infant and Young Child Nutrition, Prevention and Control of
Micronutrient Malnutrition including fortification, Vigorous Awareness Campaign on Nutrition and Administration and
Monitoring of activities under the National Nutrition Mission.
 
16.4     Intersectoral collaboration has been upscaled during the last six months.  Several issues of national importance
like reimposing ban on sale of non-iodized salt including iodized salt in the Mid Day Meal Programme and in the Public
Distribution System outlets, launching double fortification of salt with iron and iodine, integrating infant and young
child feeding issues in RCH training curricula, raising concern against the repeal of IMS Act in the light of the new
Integrated Food Law being formulated etc have been taken up with the concerned Ministries.

performed by the mission since some of the objectives are already covered under the scheme of ICDS.  The Department
should strive to define its target/objective and than implement the scheme.

1.         The University of Allahabad Bill, 2004 seeks to restore the status of the University of Allahabad as a Central
University with the objective of strengthening this prestigious university and improving the quality of teaching and
research.
 
2.         The University of Allahabad , established in 1887, is one of the oldest and prestigious Universities in the
country.   It enjoyed a national and international reputation as a premier institution of higher learning. It used to be
referred as the Oxford of the East for its attainments and contributions in teaching, research and the formidable
academic reputation of its faculty members.   The alumni of the University included many eminent and distinguished
personalities, several in almost every area of life.
 
3.         The Committee was informed that the University of Allahabad was established originally as a Central University
but after the Government of India Act, 1919 made education as a provincial subject, it became a provincial university in
1921, and was reorganized as a unitary, teaching and residential university under the Allahabad University Act, 1921.  
Presently, it is governed by the Uttar Pradesh State Universities Act, 1973 (UP Act No. 10 of 1973).
 
4.         According to the Department of Secondary and Higher Education the University was facing difficulties owing
mainly to its rigid governance and structure, financial inadequacy, inappropriate student-faculty ratio etc. Various kinds
of pressures and counter pressures were acting against its all India character and national outlook. Therefore, there had
been demands for restoration of its Central University status ever since Independence.  This move picked up momentum
in 1990s and had the support of different Governments from time to time as per the chronological background given
below:-
(i)
                  In February, 1991, the then Prime Minister publicly endorsed the claim of the University to be taken over
by the Central Government;
(ii)                in October 1993, the then Minister of Human Resource Development made an announcement in the Rajya
Sabha and a team of University Grant Commission was sent to Allahabad  for an exploratory visit.  
Subsequently, the Central Government agreed for restoration of central university status to the University in-
principle, on the condition that the Government of Uttar Pradesh would hand over all assets;
(iii)
               in 1998, the Governor of Uttar Pradesh and Chancellor of the University raised the issue of giving central
university status for the University;
(iv)              there was a special mention in the Lok Sabha in December 2000 on the need to declare the University a
Central University;
(v)                in September 2001, the Chairman, University Grants Commission conveyed the strong support of the
Commission to provide central university status to the university;
(vi)              in December 2001, the Principal Secretary to the Governor, Uttar Pradesh forwarded a proposal of the
University for its conversion into a Central University;
(vii)             in January 2002, the then Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh, in a letter to the Minister of Human Resource
Development, requested that the University be accorded the status of a Central University; and
(viii)           the Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh, in her letter dated the 23 rd May 2003 to the Prime Minister, made a
similar request.
 

161st report of Committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/161streport.htm[01-07-2016 15:22:34]
5.         The Department argued that in view of the persistent demands from various quarters for restoration of its Central
University status and the difficulties being faced by it,  the Government felt it expedient to provide the central status to
the University of Allahabad with a view to restore its glorious past and the excellence in academics and research in
different fields.  The University of Allahabad Bill, 2004 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 20 th December 2004
for the purpose.
 
6.         The salient features of the aforesaid Bill are as under:-
 
(i)
                  The Bill seeks to dissolve the existing University of Allahabad, a state university of Uttar Pradesh,
to declare the University of Allahabad to be an institution of national importance and to provide for
its incorporation and matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
(ii)                The University would be a unitary teaching and residential University with its Headquarters at
Allahabad having territorial jurisdiction extending to the area within a radius of sixteen kilometers
from the Convocation Hall of the University.
(iii)               It would function broadly on the pattern of the existing central universities.
(iv)              The existing Constituent College of the University, namely the Motilal  Nehru Medical College and
Swarup Rani Nehru Hospital, Allahabad, would continue to comprise the Faculty of Medicine of the
University as a University College.
(v)                The Kamala Nehru Post Graduate Medical Institute, Allahabad would be admitted to the privileges
of the University as a Constituent Institute of the University along with the other two existing
recognized Institutes, namely the Govind Ballabh Pant Social Science Institute, Allahabad and the
Harish-Chandra Research Institute of Mathematics and Mathematical Physics, Allahabad.
(vi)              All the eleven existing Associated Colleges of the University would be admitted to the privileges of
the University as Constituent Colleges of the University.
(vii)             The teachers of the University would be classified into those appointed by the University, and those
recognized by the University.  Both categories would have representation in the various decision-
making bodies of the University.
(viii)
           The annual accounts of the University shall be audited by the Comptroller and auditor-General of
India and shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament alongwith the audit report and the annual
report of the University.
(ix)              During the transitional period, the appointment of the first Officers like Chancellor and Vice
Chancellor and the constitution of the first bodies like the Court, Executive Council, and Academic
Council etc. would be made by the Central Government for specified terms.
 
7.         The Secretary, Department of Secondary and Higher Education during his presentation on the Bill before the
Committee informed inter-alia that the jurisdiction of the University of Allahabad, when it was established, was not
confined to the north only; it extended up to Nagpur in south also.   The University in fact, occupied a very important
place in the history of this nation.  The support being given by the U.P Government for the university including its own
income was highly inadequate. Therefore, need for central status was felt. During the process of consultation, the
Ministry had discussions with different interest groups including the officials, the students and the old distinguished
alumni as well, who by and large, supported making it a Central  University.  Apprehensions in the minds of the

161st report of Committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/161streport.htm[01-07-2016 15:22:34]
stakeholders in the university have been cleared during the process of consultation with them before the draft Bill was
finalised.  The Secretary assured the Committee that the prime position of the University would not be disturbed.
 
8.         The Committee heard the Vice-Chancellors of the two prestigious Central Universities - Jawaharlal  Nehru
University and Delhi University on various provisions of the Bill in the light of their experiences over the years.  They
pointed out that the present Bill was basically a replica of the Delhi University Bill, which was established as far back as
in the year 1922. They felt that the provisions of the Bill provided same type of structure, authorities etc. as provided
some 40 to 45 years ago when Delhi University was set up.  Their argument was that lot of changes have taken place in
the field of education and university and higher education was not same today as it used to be when Delhi University or
Jawaharlal Nehru University was established.  No two institutions can be similar; they have to have their own
specifications keeping in terms of time and place, they argued.  With these sentiments many  suggestions were made by
the two Vice-Chancellors for making Allahabad University more effective and meaningful.
 
9.         Thereafter the Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill in its sitting held on the 11
th March
2005 and suggested following amendments to various clauses of the Bill.
 
10.       The Committee recommends that in clause 7, line 45 of page 4, the number of sub clause is wrongly printed as
(xvi) which may be corrected as (xiv).
 
Clause 7(xii)
11.       Clause 7(xii) gives the power to the University to admit to its privileges colleges and institutions situated within
the territorial jurisdiction of the University, as University Colleges, Constituent Institutes and Constituent Colleges, and
to withdraw all or any of those privileges in accordance with such conditions as may be prescribed by the Statutes.
11.1     According to sub-clause xii of clause 7 the university can admit any number colleges, institutes etc to its
privileges.  The Committee feels that the ever-increasing size is something that affects both governance and standards
after a time.  This may dilute the quality of the University and for a Cental  University it is not advisable. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that sub-Clause (xii) of clause 7 may be deleted and the sub-clause xiii to xxii may
be renumbered as  Sub-clauses xii to xxi.
11.2
          The Committee recommends that the consequential changes necessitated due to the deletion may be made in
various clauses and Statutes of the Bill.
 
Clause 7 (xvii)
 
12.       Clause 7 (xvii), page 5, empowers the University to establish and recognize hostels and supervise residences of
the students of the University, make arrangements for promoting their health and general welfare and guide the
Constituent Colleges to like ends in respect of the students enrolled thereat.
 
12.1     Since the Bill contains provisions for the constituent institutes also, therefore, the Committee feels that
University should have similar powers with regard to hostels in constituent institutes also.  The Committee accordingly
recommends that in Clause 7(xvii) in line 7 after the words ‘Constituent Colleges’ the words “and Constituent

161st report of Committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/161streport.htm[01-07-2016 15:22:34]
Institutes” should be added.
 
Clause 10(3)
 
13.       Clause 10(3), page 5, provides that the Visitor shall have the right to cause an inspection to be made, by such
person or persons as he may direct, of the University, its buildings, laboratories and equipment, and of any college or
institution maintained by the University or admitted to its privileges; and also of the examinations, teaching and other
work conducted or done by the University and to cause an inquiry to be made in like manner in respect of any matter
connected with the administration or finances of the University, and the said colleges and institutions.
 
13.1     The Committee feels that libraries are an important and integral constituent of the University system and they
have not been included in the above provision for inspection.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in Clause
10(3) in line 48 after the word ‘buildings’, the word ‘libraries’ should also be added.
 
Clause 12
 
14.       Clause 12, page 7, provides that the following shall be the officers of the University: -
(1)
       the Chancellor;
(2)       the Vice-Chancellor;
(3)       the Pro-Vice Chancellor;
(4)       the Deans of Faculties;
(5)       the Registrar;
(6)       the Finance Officer; and

14.1     The Committee feels that the Controller of Examinations is an important functionary of any University and
therefore, he also should be included as one of the officers of the University, in the Act itself.
 
14.2     The Committee, accordingly, recommends that after ‘the Registrar’, the Controller of Examinations may be
added as the sixth Officer and the existing 6 and 7 items may be renumbered as 7 and 8.

15.       Clause 14(3), page7, provides that the Vice-Chancellor may, if he is of the opinion that immediate action is

report to such authority the action taken by him on such matter.
 
15.1     The Committee while accepting the rationale behind providing emergency powers to the Vice-Chancellor to deal
with urgent matters feels that the Vice Chancellor should be required to report such actions taken by him to the
appropriate authorities at the earliest available opportunity.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in Clause
14(3), in line 22, the words ‘at its next meeting’ should be added after the word ‘authority’.

Clause  21
16.       The Committee's attention was drawn towards the corresponding provision in the Delhi University Act, where

23.2     Consequently, in the proviso to this clause the word ‘nomination’ shall be replaced by words, ‘election to the
