NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF GOVERNMENTS’ REPLY
 
V         ISSUES FOR GENDER BUDGETING
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
4.1       The Committee is of the opinion that in view of integration of gender equality with sustainable development,
need and importance of gender budgeting can hardly be over emphasized.  The aim of gender budgeting is to
generate/capture the gender-based data/information, which will be relevant  input for assessing the gender specific
impact of budgetary allocations.  The Committee found that currently gender segregated macro-economic data were not
available in India.  In the absence of such data from different sectors of our economy, the Committee feels it will be
difficult to analyse the budgetary allocations on the basis of gender.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
process of gender budgeting should necessarily contain not only the segregation of gender based data but also aspects
like quantification of contribution of women in the economy; impact of Government budget on women; and policy
alternatives for evolving a gender sensitive social order.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
4.1       Recognizing the need to widen the ambit of gender budgeting, the Department held a consultation on 8
December 2004, with experts and representatives of various Government organizations and para-statal bodies to arrive
at a consensus on the framework of gender budgeting.  The meeting was chaired by Secretary (WCD) and was attended
by Advisor, Planning Commission, Joint Secretary (Budget), Member, NCW, representatives of UNIFEM and UNDP
and a few social experts.  The Department has adopted the following slogan as a mission statement for gender budgeting
–
 
            ‘Budgeting for Gender Equity’
 
The broad-framework recommended for gender budget analysis is as follows
 
Broad framework of activities
Quantification of allocation of resources for women in the Union, States and Local Administration budgets
and expenditure thereof.
q       Refining and standardizing methodology and development of tools.

q       Trend Analysis
q       Analysis of change in pattern, shift in priorities in allocation across clusters of services etc
q       Variations in allocation of resources and actual expenditure
q       Adherence to physical targets
 
Gender Audit of policies of the Government- monetary, fiscal, trade etc. at the Centre and State levels
q       Research and micro studies to guide macro policies like credit policy, taxes etc
q       Identification of gender impact of policies/interventions viewed as gender neutral
q       Micro studies to identify need for affirmative action in favour of women towards correcting gender imbalances
 
Impact assessment of various schemes in the Union and State budgets
q       Micro studies on incidence of benefits
q       Analysis of cost of delivery of services
 
Analyzing programmes, strategies, interventions and policy initiatives from the perspective of their impact
on status of women as reflected in important Macro Indicators like literacy, MMR, participation in work
force
q       E.g.- analysis of substance and content of various interventions directed at health of women and correlate the same
with indicator like MMR to establish need for corrective action in formulation of scheme/ approach.
 
Institutionalizing the generation and collection of gender dis-aggregated data
q       Developing MIS for feed back from implementing agencies
q       Inclusion of new parameters in data collection in Census and surveys by NSO, CSO etc
 
Consultations and Capacity building
q       Collation of research and exchange of best practices
q       Developing methodologies and tools for dissemination
q       Forums and Partnerships amongst experts and stakeholders.
 
Review of decision making processes to establish gender equity in participation-  review of extant
participation of women in decision making processes and to establish processes and models aimed at gender
equity in decision making and greater participation of women.
 
Formulation and reflection of satellite accountsto capture the contribution of women to the economy by
way of their activities in areas that go unreported like care economy, unpaid work in rearing domestic
animals etc.
 
It may be seen that various concerns expressed by the   Committee are part of the framework. As a coordinating
Department in Gender matters, we would be pursuing the gender budgeting mandate with all Departments.         This
framework has been communicated to all Ministries of Government of India to guide their further actions in terms of
allocation of resources and review of policy.
 
V         ROLE OF DEPARTMENT OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
5.3       After looking at these efforts made by the Department, the Committee notes that so far, this exercise had
remained confined mainly to holding Seminars/Workshops since November 1998.  The Committee is of the opinion that
the exercise of gender budgeting was not being carried out with the seriousness that it deserved.  The Committee feels
that the exercises undertaken by the Department so far, were hardly enough to sensitize the other Ministries and
Departments of the Government of India for undertaking this important activity.  Perhaps, the idea of making the
Department of Women & Child Development as a nodal agency for undertaking this exercise was to do the ground
exercise and evolve methodologies, etc. to be later on adopted by other Ministries/Departments for gender budgeting in
an organized and comprehensive manner.  The Committee is constrained to say that unfortunately this has not happened

and we have not been able to evolve till today the required tools, methodologies and institutional mechanisms for
segregating gender based data, leave alone the quantification of contribution of women in the economy and the impact
of budgetary allocations on the women in our society.  Unless it is done, the Committee firmly believes, the goal of the
gender budgeting shall remain elusive.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
5.3       The Department of Women and Child Development had commissioned the National Institute of Public Finance
and Policy to undertake a study on gender related economic policy issues to cover: Parameters to identify status of
women; Quantification of contribution of women; Assessing impact of Government Budget on women; Role women
can play in improving institutional framework for delivery of public services.
 
            Based on the interim report of the NIPFP, (January 2001), for the first time, the Economic Survey 2000-01
highlighted issues like, Gender Inequality and Status of Women.  Thus gender equality and empowerment of women
have been recognized as economic goals.  It is continued as regular feature every year.
 
            The second interim report of the NIPFP (August 2001), analysed the Union Budget 2001-02 from a gender
perspective.
 
            The model for analyzing the Union Budget developed by the NIPFP was carried forward by the Department to
analyse the Union Budget 2002-03 and 2003-04.  In 2002-03 a research study was also commissioned to undertake
gender analysis of all State budgets.  The report has since been received and results of preliminary analysis are reflected
in the annual report of 2004-05.
 
The Department of Women and Child Development is actively participating in the inter departmental committee
constituted by the Ministry of Finance for evolving the methodology for analysis of public expenditure from a gender
perspective.  Secretary (WCD) attended the first inter-Departmental Meeting chaired by Secretary, Expenditure on 7
December 2004. Action is thus on to develop a model for gender analysis of public expenditure
 
VI        GENDER BUDGETING IN OTHER MINISTRIES/DEPARTMENTS
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
6.4       The Committee is of the opinion that gender based analysis of allocations should be done for the entire Budget
of the Government.  This exercise, therefore, will have to be taken up by all the Ministries/Departments of the
Government of India, not only by those identified for this purpose so far.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the remaining ones should also be sensitized to infuse gender aspects into their allocations/expenditure without further
delay.  This is necessary to have holistic idea about gender-based allocations of the entire Budget of the Government of
India.  The Department of Women and Child Development being a nodal agency should assume greater responsibilities
for undertaking this exercise of the gender budgeting by all the Ministries/Departments without further delay.
 
6.5       The Committee notes that the objective of gender budgeting is there, the Ministries/Departments are identified,
but the results are not forthcoming in absence of any guidelines for this purpose.  The Committee fails to understand the
Department’s limitations in this regard.  The Committee recommends to have specific guidelines laid down regarding
gender budgeting to be followed by all the Ministries/Departments.  This would still be quite possible on the basis of
experiences/feedback received on the problems being faced in implementation of gender budgeting.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
6.4 & 6.5         The issue of gender based analysis of allocation being undertaken for the entire budget has been
addressed in the deliberations of the inter-departmental committee set up by the Ministry of Finance.  The Department
of Women and Child Development is an active integral part of this committee and   pressed for setting up of gender
budget cells in all Ministries and Departments so that there is a point of focus for coordinating gender friendly initiatives
for the Department of Women and Child Development.  Instructions have so far been issued for only 18 Ministries so

166th Report of Committee on Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/166threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:24:37]
that experiences gathered in this initiative can be suitably expanded to cover the entire Government Budget.
 
            The Ministry of Finance is a nodal Department for issuing all instructions on budgeting and therefore, the
Department of Women and Child Development hopes that instructions issued by them for reflecting gender
disaggregated data will result in reflection of allocation of resources for women in the budgetary documents.
 
Specific guidelines regarding gender sensitive budgeting have been prepared and issued by the Department to all
Ministries and Departments in GOI vide Secretary (WCD)’s letter dated 13.10.2004 (copy enclosed at Annexure I). 
These instructions were also enclosed with the letter sent by the Ministry of Finance for initiating gender budgeting in
select Departments.  With the setting up of Gender Budget Cells in all Departments it would be easier for coordinating
gender budgeting activities and obtaining feed back. It is expected that all this will facilitate gender mainstreaming.
 
VII      LACK OF INTER-MINISTERIAL COORDINATION
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
7.2       The Committee appreciates the idea of having a monitoring and coordination mechanism for the purpose of
gender budgeting exercise.  Such a machinery assumes greater relevance in view of the fact that gender budgeting has to
be ultimately taken up not only by all the Departments/Ministries but by the State Governments and local bodies as
well.  The Committee, however, fails to understand as to why no such inter-ministerial body could be created so far,
despite the specific suggestions made by the two important groups mentioned above.  The Committee is not aware
whether any initiative has been taken by the Department so far.  In view of the importance and urgency of such inter-
ministerial coordinating mechanism, the Committee urges upon the Government to take immediate steps to put such
machinery in place.
 
7.3       The Committee feels that apart from having an inter-ministerial body for coordinating and monitoring, it is
equally important to have intra-ministerial/Departmental cells for coordinating/facilitating this exercise within each
Ministry/Department.  Such cells would certainly provide required impetus for this exercise.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that such monitoring cell should be created in all the Ministries/Departments.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
7.2 & 7.3         The inter-Departmental committee on gender budgeting as recommended by the expert group on gender
budgeting has since been set up under the chairmanship of Secretary Expenditure, Ministry of Finance.   Secretary
(WCD) is member of the Committee.  As per instructions issued by the Ministry of Finance the various Ministries and
Departments are to open up Gender Budget Cells, which will facilitate coordinating the gender budgeting exercises.
 
X         NEED FOR IMPACT ASSESSMENT
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
10.1     The Committee notes that there are still a number of core issues like the increasing burden of poverty on women;
inaccessibility and unequal access to health, family welfare and educational services; inequality in access and control
over assets and resources, both within and outside the family; inequality and inaccessibility to work, employment and
decision-making; and violence against women including domestic and otherwise, which have apparently some direct or
indirect bearing on framing policy relating to gender budgeting.
 
10.2     In view of this, the need for impact assessment of gender allocation, the Committee feels assumes greater
importance.  This impact assessment should not only be restricted to women-specific and pro-women programmes but
also should extend to impact of mainstream expenditure on women.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
10.1 & 10.2     A Needs Assessment exercise was conducted by the Department in consultation with experts and

166th Report of Committee on Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/166threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:24:37]
representatives of various government departments and organizations in a meeting held on 8 December 2004. In view
of the plethora of core issues it was felt that priority areas should be identified every year for special attention and
concerted efforts. Four areas of priority were identified for immediate focus in the coming year for empowerment of
women.  These are:
 
a)
                              Food and Nutrition security (for the family with focus on women and girl child) and employment
guarantee
b)                             Water and sanitation
c)                              Adequate Health facilities
d)                             Asset base for women (land, home, livestock etc.)
 
This was followed up by detailed discussions with a few Departments to strategize concentrated action on the
above four areas.
            The first meeting was chaired by Secretary (WCD) on 13.1.2005. Representatives of certain select
Ministries/Departments that are perceived to have significant roles in the areas of food and nutrition security, water and
sanitation and   asset base for women were invited:
i.
                     Department of Rural Development
ii.                   Department of Agriculture and Cooperation
iii.                  Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying
iv.                 Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries
v.                   Department of Food and Public Distribution
vi.                 Department of Land Resources and
vii.                Department of Drinking Water Supply

social sector to achieve synergy in allocation of resources and implementation of schemes. Discussions encompassed
ð
     Identification of schemes which could be made more gender friendly and action thereof

impact of the interventions.
ð
     Steps to ensure allocation of adequate funds for women in Annual Plan outlays of the departments
ð     Convergence of initiatives
ð     Spread of best practices
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
10.3     The integration of gender in budgeting policies, Committee feels would not only ensure better transparency and
accountability in the allocations meant for women, it would, at the same time, help evaluate the effectiveness of
resources utilized in delivering the intended results.  Simply focusing on how much money has been allocated for
women-specific and pro-women schemes could be counter-productive, if the outcome and performance of schemes were
far from the desired level.  This would, in fact, help us monitor output as well as input.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
10.3
          Finance Minister in his Budget Speech had indicated that he had included in the Budget documents a separate
Statement highlighting the gender sensitivities of the budgetary allocations under 10 Demands for Grants.  The
total amount in BE 2005-06,is Rs.14, 379 crore.  Although this is another first in budget making in India it is
only a beginning and in course of time, all Departments will be required to present gender budgets as well as
make benefit incidence analyses
 
XI        GENDER BUDGETING IN STATES
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS

11.1     The exercise of gender budgeting, the Committee is of the view, would remain woefully incomplete without
extending it to State Budgets as well, because the States and Union Territories accounts for bulk of expenditure on
social sector which relate to welfare/empowerment of women.  The Committee is happy to note that the exercise of
State Budget from gender perspective was already on.  The Committee was informed that data from only ten States-
Assam, Bihar, Meghalaya, Gujarat, J&K, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, MP, Orissa and Manipur were received.  The
committee has learnt that due to wide variation in nomenclature of schemes/programmes across the States and
discrepancies in data, which require further validation, authentic collection of results and a comparative analysis is
difficult to be made.  The Committee, therefore, urges upon the government to formulate uniform procedures pertaining
to gender budgeting and analysis and disseminate these to the States.  The Committee also emphasizes the need for
standardizing nomenclature, terms etc. with a view to avoiding possible ambiguities and confusions across the States.
 
11.2     The committee is aware of the practical difficulties involved in having a meaningful analysis of State budgets,
but at the same time, it cannot ignore to emphasize about the necessity of undertaking and refining the exercise of State
budget analysis.
 
11.3     The Committee notes that of all the States and UTs, only ten have supplied data regarding their budgets, which is
not a very encouraging sign in this regard.  The committee does not know the reasons behind it.  The committee,
therefore, recommends that the States, which have not responded, should be approached and persuaded to under
take/start the exercises at the earliest.  The Department should act as a facilitator and provide necessary help, expertise,
etc for this purpose to the State.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
11.1 to 11.3     As a follow up to the study on ten states, the Department had commissioned a research proposal for
analyzing trend of allocation for women in all 35 State/UT s budgets. The Report has since been received and is under
review. The preliminary analysis of State budgets based on the trend for 1993-94 to 2002-03 is being included in the
Annual Report of 2004-05.  The Department’s findings of the research study on States and UTs will be sent to the
various State Governments for their comments.     The model being developed by the inter Departmental committee
chaired by Secretary (Expenditure), Ministry of Finance will be extended to State Governments.
 
XII      GENDER BUDGETING IN LOCAL BODIES
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
12.1     The committee emphasizes the need for taking up gender-based analysis not only for the States but also for local
bodies-nagarpalikas, panchayats etc., which also undertake social expenditure having gender specific benefits.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
12.1     Efforts will be made in this direction.
 
XIV     STRENGTHENING STATUTORY SUPPORT FOR WOMEN
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
14.1     The committee notes that the Task Force had reviewed the whole gamut of legislations concerning women and
had recommended amendment to 22 laws with a view to making them more effective.  The committee is also of the
view that existing states concerning women and girl child need to be reviewed minutely by the experts in the light of
latest developments and emerging scenario with a view to amending them to make them relevant and effective.  This
committee has emphasized this aspect in several of its earlier reports submitted to the Government.  But the committee
is of the opinion that the Department of Women & Child Development has not been able to act timely and sufficiently in
having the exercise of getting these laws amended expedited.  The committee, therefore, recommends that the
Department should submit a status report on those 22 laws identified along with latest position regarding the actions so
far taken for amending those laws.  The committee further feels that the Department should try and fix a time schedule

for amending every law and impress upon the concerned Ministries along with Ministry of Law & Justice to accomplish
the work within that time.

14.1     Details are given in the Annexure A.

III        GENDER BUDGETING IN INDIA
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
3.5       In the context of India, where the gender bias is inherent in a male-dominated society, Gender Budgeting
becomes all the more relevant.  The Committee observes that the trends in sex ratio and other socio-economic indicators
clearly show, how the bias is getting accentuated in many parts of the country.  Over the years, during the course of
examination of various women and girl child related programmes/schemes, one factor which has been constantly
drawing the attention of the Committee is that in spite of well-conceived programmes and the funds allocated, there has
been no noticeable improvement in the status of women/girls.   Recently released State specific sex ratio figures of
Census 2001, do not leave any doubt in this regard.  The Committee is of the view that it is high time that the Budget of
the Government provides a clear indication of how much is earmarked specifically for the benefit of women so as to
ensure effective implementation of women/girl related programmes.  Department of Women & Child Development is
not only the nodal agency for such programmes but also the nodal Department assigned with carrying out the task of
Gender Budgeting, the Committee accordingly decided to make a study on work done so far in this emerging area.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.5       The Department of Women and Child Development has been undertaking the role of a coordinating  
Department through monitoring of 27 beneficiary oriented schemes since 1985. The exercise of quantifying resources
earmarked for women was entrusted to the National institute  of Public Finance and Policy (NIPFP) and they developed
a model for gender analysis of the Union Budget, beginning with the Union Budget for 2001-2002. This model has  
been adopted by the Department to quantify allocation for women in the Union Budget for subsequent years.  
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
The Committee is of the opinion that the model for gender based analysis of the Union Budget developed by
NIPFP in 2001-2002, needs to be refined with a view to making it more precise and wider in scope. This model is not
able to provide adequate insight in the case of mainstream budgets. The Committee, therefore, recommends that steps be
taken to examine the same and a methodology evolved on this aspect at the earliest.
 
V         ROLE OF DEPARTMENT OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
5.5       It is not clear to the Committee, whether the decision to discontinue the chapter on Gender Budget Initiatives
was advertent or inadvertent.  If it was advertent, the Committee would like to know the reasons for this; and if it was
inadvertent, the Committee expresses its unhappiness in the matter.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the

chapter on Gender Budget Initiatives should be restarted in the Annual Report from the year 2004-05, which should also
list the development/steps taken in the year 2003-04.

5.5       The Chapter on Gender Budgeting initiatives has been restored in the Annual Report for 2004-05.
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee does not expect such a cryptic reply by the Department to a specific question. It is good that the
chapter on Gender Budgeting has since been reintroduced in its Annual Report after the Committee pointed it out. The
Department should have provided reasons for not doing so earlier, which has not been done.
 
VI        GENDER BUDGETING IN OTHER MINISTRIES/DEPARTMENTS
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
6.1.      The Committee however, observes that hardly any Ministry and Department had started this exercise so far.  The
Committee feels that the Department had not pursued this matter with other Ministries and Departments effectively. 
The Committee recommends that the Department should make all our efforts to persuade the other Ministries and
Departments to include a chapter on gender budgeting in this Annual Reports highlighting new initiatives/policies on
gender related issues, resources available and their utilization and gender disaggregated statistics for promoting gender
awareness within and outside Government.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
6.1       The Department of Women and Child Development had requested the Cabinet Secretary to issue instructions to
all Ministries and Departments to devote a chapter on gender issues in their annual reports.  While many Departments
have done so, it was seen that the reporting was limited in coverage. Very few Departments gave descriptive
sections/quantification of initiatives taken for enhancing allocation for women or stepping up gender friendly initiatives
or reviewing their respective facilities from a gender perspective.  As advised by the Committee, detailed check lists for
analyzing budgetary allocations and policies and schemes for all Departments in the Government were then drawn up by
the Department of Women and Child Development. (Annexure I).  These have been circulated to all Ministries and
Departments for appropriate action.  The guidelines have also been sent to the State Governments.
 
The Department has been making concerted efforts to mainstream gender and has also written to Ministry of
Finance and the Planning Commission highlighting various measures that required a gender friendly review.  For
instance in the letter addressed to Ministry of Finance (Secretary, Expenditure). Secretary (WCD) had pointed that a
decision like reducing the  debt burden of GOI should be seen from a gender perspective. While revising rate of return
on various debt instruments or retiring these instruments, the gender profile of beneficiaries should be reviewed so that
those instruments favoured by women are not adversely impacted.  The detailed guidelines prepared by the Department
under check list II, (Annexure I), are expected to help guide the mainstream sectors to undertake gender sensitive review
of policies and budgetary allocations. Thus the Department has been undertaking significant advocacy measures for
highlighting the importance of gender friendly and gender responsive action in policy and budget allocation.
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
6.3       The Committee appreciates the idea of identifying some Ministries/Departments for impressing upon them to
undertake the process of gender budgeting on a wider scale.  The Committee, however, feels that to the best of its
knowledge, the identified Ministries/Departments have apparently not been able to take up the exercise of gender
budgeting in their respective areas.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take up with

these Ministries/Departments to start the exercise of gender-based analysis of their allocations/expenditure from the next
year 2005-06 positively.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
6.3       After deliberations of the inter-Departmental Committee chaired by Secretary, Expenditure, the following
instructions have been issued by the Ministry of Finance on 24.12.2004.
 
i.
                     All Departments/ Ministries to establish a ‘Gender Budgeting Cell’ by 1st January, 2005.
ii.                   Eighteen selected Departments/Ministries to bring out scheme-wise provisions and physical
targets benefiting women in their Annual Reports/Performance Budgets for 2004-05 along
with their Detailed Demands for Grants for 2005-06. 
 
All Departments/ Ministries to prepare incidence analysis from the next financial year for inclusion in their
Annual Reports/Performance Budgets as per instructions/checklist prepared by the Department of Women and Child
Development.
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
The Committee expresses its satisfaction over reflection of Gender-budgeting in the Annual Budget since the
presentation of its 153
rd Report to the Parliament on 21st December, 2004. Only exception is the two instructions issued
by the Ministry of Finance on 24 th December, 2004. First being to all Departments/Ministries to establish a ‘Gender
Budgeting cell’. The Committee is happy to note that all Departments/Ministries have been instructed to establish a
Gender Budgeting Cell by 1st January 2005. The Committee only hopes that Gender Budgeting cells must have been set
up and made fully functional by now in all Departments/Ministries. Ideal position would have been if the Department
had ensured that this directive of the Ministry of Finance had been complied with by each and every Department.
The second directive was meant for eighteen selected Departments/Ministries to bring out scheme-wise
provisions and physical targets benefiting women in their Annual Reports/Performance Budgets for 2004-05 alongwith
their Detailed Demands for Grants 2005-06. The Committee is disturbed to note that virtually no progress has been
made in this regard inspite of Department pursuing the same since October, 2004. A test check made by the Committee
of some Ministries/Departments out of the selected 18 ones does not reveal a happy scenario. Annual Reports (2004-05)
of Ministries/Departments like Department of Elementary Education and Literacy, Department of Secondary and Higher
Education, Ministry of Labour and Employment, Ministry of Small Scale Industries, Department of Environment and
Forest and Ministry of Home Affairs do not have any chapter on Gender Budget Analysis. There is only a brief mention
in thisregard in the Annual Reports of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare & Ministry of Youth Affairs and
Sports.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department as a nodal agency must ensure that all the
instructions related to gender budgeting issued by the Ministry of Finance on 24
th December 2004 were carried out in a

time bound manner. There is need for an effective interdepartmental coordination to achieve the objectives of gender
budgeting in the true sense.
 
VIII     DEVELOPING SUITABLE METHODOLOGY
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
8.1       The Committee notes that we are yet to evolve suitable methodologies, tools etc. for doing an effective Gender
Budget Analysis.  The Department of Women & Child Development has, with the help of NIPFP, undertaken some
exercise in this regard, which is limited to only few Departments/Ministries
 
The Committee emphasizes the need for developing/refining methodologies and gender tools like gender audit,
gender impact assessment, gender analysis and gender budgeting to monitor implementation and impact of gender
policies.
 
8.2       The Committee also emphasizes the urgent need for undertaking research activities in different aspects of gender
budgeting including gender benefit incidence analysis.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
8.1 & 8.2         The Ministry of Finance through the inter-Departmental Committee is working on development of the
model for analyzing public expenditure. Instructions on conducting impact assessment studies have been issued vide
Ministry of Finance letter dated 24.12.2004 asking all Departments to prepare incidence analysis from the next financial
year for inclusion in their Annual Reports/Performance Budgets as per instructions/checklist prepared by the
Department of Women and Child Development.
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
The Committee notes the efforts made by the Department in association with the Ministry of Finance for
developing the model for analysing public expenditure. However, the aspects of developing methodologies, gender tools
and research activities in different areas of gender budgeting still leave much to be desired. The Committeerecommends
that theDepartment should frame guidelines for the purpose within a stipulated timeframe. The guidelines should be
uniform and the procedure followed should facilitate proper assessment of the impact of gender budgeting.
 
IX        NEED FOR TRAINING/CAPACITY BUILDING
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
9.1       The Committee notes that the exercise of Gender Budgeting, which is in the process of evolving suitable tools,
techniques and methodologies pre-supposes the need for orientation/training for the officials responsible for the job in
different Ministries/Departments.  They can undertake this exercise effectively and efficiently only if they are familiar
or have been adequately trained for the purpose.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the training and capacity
building efforts should be made for the officials working in the Government Department both at the Centre as well as in
States.  Possibility of arranging orientation/training for the people’s representatives in local bodies should also be
considered.
 
9.2       The Committee recommends that government functionaries and financial specialists should be sensitized since it
is with the help of these people that budget is made and auditing of expenditure is done at the end of financial year.  If

they would do their job effectively, it will help in further streamlining the gender budget analysis.  This should,
therefore, be specifically trained/sensitized to the importance of the task as their knowledge and motivation becomes
critical in determining the accuracy and validity of such an exercise.

9.1 & 9 .2
       The Department proposes to liaison   with training institutions like LBSNAA, Mussoorie to develop
focused resource modules on gender budgeting to impart training to public officials.

The Committee recommends that necessary measures should be undertaken to expedite the development of
focused resource module for training all the officials who are directly/indirectly connected with the work.
 
XIII     GENDER BUDGETING IN PRIVATE SECTOR
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
13.1     The committee emphasizes the need for undertaking the exercise of gender analysis of allocations/expenditure in
private sector also.  The committee would like to point out that of the total women workforce, their share in private
sector is far larger than those in the public sector.  In unorganized sector, there are not legitimate and other safeguards
even to claim minimum wages leave aside other benefits.  In view of this situation, the committee feels that no realistic
assessments and conclusions can be made about gender budgeting at the national level without involving private sector. 
The committee is aware of the practical limitations involved in taking up such exercise; it still emphasizes the greater
need for starting gender budgeting in private sector also.

REPORT
The National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions (Amendment) Bill, 2005 seeks to amend the National
Commission for Minority Educational Institutions Act, 2004, which provided to set up a Commission to advise the
Central Government or any State Government on any question relating to the education of minorities that may be
referred to it; to look into specific complaints regarding deprivation or violation of rights of minorities to establish and
administer educational institutions; to decide on any dispute relating to affiliation to a Scheduled University; and to
report its findings to the Central Government for its implementation. The said Act also provided right to a Minority
Educational Institution (MEI) to seek affiliation to any of six Universities listed in its schedule. The Commission was
also given power to determine disputes regarding affiliation between Minority Educational Institutions and the
Universities.
2.         The Committee was informed that based on the experience of the functioning of the Commission, it was felt that
by limiting the scope of affiliation only to six Universities given in the Schedule to the Act, the applicability of the Act
had been severely restricted. The Commission as well as the Government received several representations and
suggestions for making the Commission more effective in deciding on matters of deprivation or violation of the
educational rights of the minorities guaranteed under Article 30 of the Constitution. The majority of the representations
received by the Commission related to the problems faced by minority communities in obtaining ‘No Objection
Certificate’ (NOC) for establishing an Educational Institution and also in obtaining the status of a Minority Institution.
3.         The Amending Bill, accordingly, seeks to empower the Commission to be more effective and proactive in
protecting the educational rights of minorities in respect of seeking affiliation to universities; seeking NOC for setting
up MEIs; and in obtaining minority status without any harassment.
4.         The salient features of the Bill are as follows:-
It provides for the right to establish a Minority Educational Institution and also provides that wherever ‘No Objection
Certificate’ for establishing a Minority Educational Institution is either not granted within a period of sixty days or
where a decision in this regard is not communicated within such period, the Minority Educational Institution would
proceed with the establishment of the institution as if the No Objection Certificate has been granted to it.
It provides for the right of Minority Educational Institutions to seek affiliation to any University of their choice subject
to the Acts, Statutes, Ordinances, Rules and Regulations of the concerned University. It proposes to do away with the
Schedule.
It also proposes to give appellate jurisdiction to the Commission in the matters of refusal to grant ‘No Objection
Certificate’ for establishing a Minority Educational Institution.
It enables the National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions to enquire into and investigate complaints
regarding deprivation or violation of rights of minorities to establish and administer Educational Institutions of their
choice and, also to decide on disputes relating to affiliation of Minority Educational Institutions to a University.
It also enables the Commission to decide on all questions relating to the status of any institution as a Minority
Educational Institution.
It empowers the Commission to cancel recognition as a Minority Educational Institution, where it is found by the
Commission that the purpose or character on which a Minority Educational Institution status was granted and also in
admitting students belonging to the minority community as per rules and prescribed percentage, has failed.
It provides that every proceeding before the Commission shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding and, the orders
made by the Commission shall be executable by it as a decree of a civil court.
It empowers the Commission to utilize the services of any officer of the Central Government or any State Government,
with the concurrence of such Government, for the purpose of conducting investigation pertaining to complaints received
by the Commission.
It bars the jurisdiction of Courts (except the Supreme Court and the High Courts) to entertain any suit, application or
other proceedings in respect of orders made by the Commission.
5.         The Committee, heard the Secretary, Department of Secondary and Higher Education and took up `clause-by-
clause’ consideration of the Bill. It suggested the following amendments/additions to various clauses of the Bill.

Clause 1
6.1       The Committee notes that the present Bill does not contain the commencement clause.
6.2       The Committee, therefore, recommends that the date of commencement of the Amendment Bill may be
included in the corpus of the Bill.
Clause 3
7.1       The Committee notes that clause 3 of the Bill seeks to substitute section 10 in chapter III of the principal Act
with new clauses 10 and 10 A. Under the proposed clause 10, any person desiring to establish a Minority Educational
Institution may apply for a ‘No Objection Certificate’ from the competent authority, who shall decide every application
expeditiously.  In order to prevent delays on the part of the competent authority in granting the required NOC, a
provision in clause 10(3) is being made enabling the applicant to proceed with establishing an institution under the
relevant law, if the competent authority does not grant the certificate or fails to communicate the refusal, to the
applicant. It would then be deemed, as if the NOC has been granted.
7.2       The Committee feels that the deeming provision contained in clause 10(3) regarding the grant of NOC
after a period of 60 days, would allow enough scope for its frequent misuse. Chances of delaying the
communication from the office of the competent authority to the applicant either in his office or in transit cannot
be ruled out. The Committee is concerned about the possibility of a situation where communication about a
rejected application is so delayed and the applicant goes ahead with establishing an MEI after 60 days.
Therefore, adequate safeguards against possible abuses of this provision, need to be provided in the Bill itself.
One such measure, the Committee recommends, could be to extend the period of 60 days to 90 days.
7.3       The Committee also recommends that the person making an application for NOC may approach the competent
authority after a period of 60 days of submitting the application, to know about the status of his application.  A provision
for this should be made in the Bill.
7.4       The Committee notes that Section 10A of clause 3 provides that a Minority Educational Institution may seek
affiliation to any affiliating University of its choice, thereby removing the limitation for seeking affiliation to only a
Scheduled University. The applicant would be expected to seek affiliation in terms of the procedures prescribed by the
relevant Statutes, Ordinances or rules of the University.
7.5       The Committee has a strong apprehension about allowing MEIs to seek affiliation to a university of their choice,
irrespective of distance or geographical contiguity which is an important consideration for the convenience of both, the
universities as well as MEIs.  Secondly, the Committee feels that the good and reputed universities may face  problems
because all the MEIs would generally prefer to be affiliated to the best ones.  Although this choice of MEIs, the
Committee notes, would be limited by the provisions in the Acts, Statutes/rules of the universities, the Committee
neverthless emphasizes that some kind of restriction regarding geographical contiguity or State boundary must be
provided in the Bill itself.
Clause 4
8.1       Clause 4 proposes to amend Section 11 of the principal Act. Clause 4(c)  of the proposed amendment
empowers the Commission to intervene in any judicial proceedings, with the leave of the Court, in matters
involving deprivation of educational rights of minorities.
8.2       With regard to the question of the overall authority of the Commission to intervene in the Court, the Secretary,
Department of Secondary and Higher Education submitted before the Committee that it is an area in which a lot of
frivolous litigations come in and there are a lot of things which come in to hurt the interests of Minority Institutions. In
such a case, the Government, felt that the Commission should have some authority to intervene. It is therefore, an
enabling provision.
8.3       The Committee, as regards clause 4 (c ), feels that the power of the Commission to intervene in Court
cases involving deprivation of minority educational  rights  before a Court, may push the whole thing under
litigation.    If suo motu, the Court calls the Commission, there is no problem. Otherwise, the Committee, feels
that the Commission would become a frontrunner in a variety of considerations. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the intervention of the Commission in Court proceeding  might be restricted to those cases only
where the Courts demand it.
Clause 6
9.1       Under clause six new sections (12A to 12F) are proposed to be inserted in Section 12 of the Principal Act. In
order to prevent the misuse of minority status by institutions, it is being provided under section 12C that the
Commission shall cancel recognition as a Minority Educational Institution, in case the Commission finds that the
purpose or character for which an Educational Institution was granted a minority status has been amended or the
institution has failed in admitting students belonging to the minority community as per rules and prescribed percentage

governing admissions during any academic year.
9.2       The Committee recommends that on cancellation of the Minority Status of the institution, the provisions of this
Act shall cease to apply to such institution.
9.3 The Committee feels that the Bill must provide adequate safeguards for preventing the misuse of the `Minority
Status’ by an institution.
10.       The Committee adopts the remaining clauses of the Bill without any amendments.
11.       The enacting formula and the title are adopted with consequential changes.
12.       The Committee recommends that the Bill may be passed after incorporating the amendment /additions suggested
by it. 
13.       The Committee would like the Department to submit a note with reasons on the recommendations/suggestions

NOTE OF DISSENT
                                                                                                                                      RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD
                                                                                                                                                   Senior Advocate
                                                                                                                                             M.P., RAJYA SABHA
                                                                       
NOTE OF DISSENT
ON THE NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR MINORITY EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS (AMENDMENT)
BILL 2005
The above Bill seeks to comprehensively amend the “National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions Act
2005 (Act 2 of 2005)”. It is indeed surprising that the Act, which come into force only on 7
th of January 2005 is sought
to be amended by the Bill, which was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 23rd of August 2005. What were the compelling
circumstances, which required such a comprehensive amendment only after seven month, still remains unclear?
All of us agree with the proposition that minorities must be given opportunity to establish institution of their choice but
there is no empirical evidence available that the original Act, which only came into force on 7th of January 2005, was
posing so much difficulty in the fulfillment of the said objective that required such far reaching change. Obviously it can
not be because seven month is too short a period to examine the results of the working of any particular legislation.
Though, one acknowledges the right of the executive to bring the Bill but the hurried manner in which such far reaching
amendments are being introduced raises disturbing questions.
Of particular concern is the complete denial of any role of the State Government in the amendment Bill. Under the
original Act 2 of 2005 under Section 10 (ii) it was the obligatory on the part of the schedule University to consult the
Government of the State concerned and consider its view before granting affiliation. This provision has been given a
complete go by the amended Bill besides impinging upon the federal character of the Constitution. Besides the power of
the States it raises serious question of security. Only the State Government through its various organizations has the
capacity to discover the source of funding and the background of the people who have promoted the institutions in
question. The University granting affiliation does not have the infrastructure or the ability to inquire into these
circumstances.
It is again reiterated that minority should be encouraged to pursue their right to establish and administer their own
institutions. However, the troubled times in which we all live in India, issues of security concerned can not be brushed
aside altogether. Terrorist violence in most of the cases being sponsored by forces from across the border has become
the order of the day. Even the national capital is not spared. Terrorists are using different fronts as we see day after day.
Therefore, some suitable provision need be there to ensure that any particular institutions seeking protection and
affiliation under the Act may not become a front of some terrorist operations i.e. it’s sponsored and financers have links
with the terrorist network. Obviously, the State Government only has the ability and capacity to know these things.
Therefore, it is eminently desirable and in abiding public and national interest the view of the State Government must be
sought as originally enshrined in the main Act 2 of 2005. I have a very serious view on this issue, which I had
highlighted during the course of meeting of H.R.D. Standing Committee, hence this note of dissent.
It is equally important that geographical contiguity of the University with the affiliating minority institutions must be
duly kept in mind.
                                                                                                                                Sd/-(Ravi Shankar Prasad)

XIII     CENTRAL BOARD OF SECONDARY EDUCATION (CBSE)
 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS
 
Para No.13.3
The Committee is of the view that besides examination stress, there are various other contributory factors such as
parental pressure, increasing competition, fast changing social and economic  conditions, etc. which cause depression in
students.  The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the CBSE and hopes that these measures would result in
giving a better environment to students.  The Committee feels that the current practice of holding Board exams for
Secondary and Senior Secondary students at schools other than their own, also generates a kind of fear psychosis amongst
them.   The Committee is of the view that in order to avoid this, holding board examinations in their own schools, with
supervisors/invigilators from different schools, may also be considered.
 
ACTION TAKEN:    
            The CBSE has taken various measures to reduce the fear about examinations which includes restructuring of question
papers thus reducing the number of questions and also to provide options and internal choices.     It has considerably reduced
the panic situation because there is an alternative option to which students can respond.  The Board always promotes quality
education which also includes conducting examination in a very professional manner.  It also ensures that there is no unfair
practices and cheating in the examinations.
 
As per the norm for fixation of examination centre, an examination centre is created subject to the availability of the
bank/treasury facilities for the safe custody of question papers and also the availability of appropriate number of rooms with
ventilation, fan, light, furniture, access to school and overall safety to ensure fair and smooth conduct of examination.
 
In the case of CBSE, the schools are mostly  situated in urban areas and the students are not required to travel long
distances to reach the examination centre.  In order to reduce fear psychosis and feeling of being in an unknown school, the
CBSE has also made it mandatory to depute teachers at the examination centre from the school whose students are appearing
at the examination centre. 
 
In places having single CBSE school, a self-centre is created in that school itself and the students are allowed to take
up the examination in their own school.  In the case of a self-centre, the Centre Superintendent is appointed from outside the
Centre and Supervisory staff is appointed from among those who are not the employees of the same school. 

168th Report of Committee on Human Resourse Development

Thus, the situation in CBSE is very different from the State Boards where the schools are situated in rural and far
flung areas and where there are more than one school situated close by.  While pursuing the present policy of centre
fixation, the CBSE has been able to achieve twin objectives – (1) the students do not have to travel a long distance to
appear in the examinations and (2) the examinations are conducted in an environment which is free of any unfair practice.
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee does not agree with the explanations given by the Department for not allowing the students to
appear for board examination in their own schools with supervisors/invigilators from different schools.  The Committee
has learnt that this was being done in areas where single CBSE schools are existing and the students are allowed to take-up
examination in their own school.  The Committee feels that this proposal need further consideration.

Ministry of Expenditure. The Planning Commission has in July 2005 informed that committed liabilities of the

REPORT

The Department of Youth Affairs and Sports is one of the four constituent Departments
of the Ministry of Human Resource Development. The Department has taken a number of
new initiatives and programmes in the field of youth development and sports, as well as
physical education. The Programme undertaken by the Department can be broadly classified
under (I) Youth Programmes and (II) Sports and Games.

Youth Programmes

2. The Department finances various youth welfare programmes, which range from
personality development to vocational training. Most of these programmes are itnplemented
by reputed institutions. NGOs, as well as State Governments for which financial assistance is
provided by this Department as per stipulated norms. The major schemes for youth
development are: National Service Scheme, Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan, National
Integration Programmes, National Discipline Scheme, Youth Hostels and National Service
Volunteers Scheme, etc.

2.1 Many new initiatives have aiso been taken with a view to provide a new thrust to
the youth programmes. The Department has decided to set up Youth Development Centres
for a group of 10 villages each in order to give a fillip to participation of rural youth in
developmental activities. These centres will have facilities for information, sports, training
and youth programmes for rural youth. The land for the centre will be donated by the
Panchayats. This scheme will be implemented through Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan, an
autonomous Body under this Department.

2.2 The Department has also decided to add a few more important areas of national
priorities in the Action Plan of Nehru Yuva Kendras from the year 1994-95. These areas are:
Panchayati Raj Awareness, Health & Population Awareness, Vriksh Mitra Scheme for
environment promotion, SEWAK (Self Employed Workers Association Kendra), Youth
Festivals at block, district and national level, etc. Besides this, emphasis is being given this
year on making youth economically self-reliant.

Games & Sports

3. Sports is a State subject and as such development of sports is primarily the
responsibility of State Governments. The Department of Youth Affairs and Sports, however,
undertakes a number of programmes which aim at promoting sports activities, in the
country. It finances a number of such programmes including creation of sports infrastructure
various parts of the country, grants for laying of synthetic surfaces, spotting and nurturing of
excellence through various schemes of the Sports Authority of India (SAI), grants to
National Sports Federations for coaching camps, national championships, international
exposure and equipment purchase, grant of incentives in the shape of scholarships, cash
awards to eminent sportspersons, encouraging sports in the Universities by grants for
creation of infrastructure and holding of inter-University championships, organising
tournaments for rural youth, women and in the north eastern region. The Department has
launched a new scheme “Sports Fund for Pension to Meritorious Sportspersons” under

“ which Olympic Medalists and Gold Medalists of Asian Games are eligible for Life Pension
from the age of 30. The scheme is being operated through the Life Insurance Corporation of
India.

Youth Affairs
National Service Scheme (NSS)

4. The Committee is deeply concerned about the misutilisation and persistent failure of
the Department to appropriate resources allocated for the scheme during the last four years

and is constrained to observe that this is not a healthy phenomenon and should not be

4.1 The Secretary, Department of Youth Affairs & Sports, stated that the funds given
to the States were not being passed on to the Universities and also most of the Universities,
instead of giving money to Colleges, were utilising the money for purposes for which it was
not intended. It was further stated that the Department did not even get the required
feedback from the States about the money released to them.

4.2 The Committee is thus given to understand that, notwithstanding its earlier
recommendation to secure better cooperation from the States in operating this scheme, the
situation appears to have gone from bad to worse. The Committee is fully aware of the
practical problems involved in the entire process, yet it feels that the Department has failed
té make adequate efforts in this regard. Blaming the States and the Universities does not
solve the problem. It is also deplorable that the Department did not get any feed-back from

regard and recommends that it should make all-out efforts to prevail upon the States to
ensure not only proper utilisation of the grants but also to pass on sufficient feedback about
the progress of the scheme every year.

4.3 The Committee finds that the State Liaison Cells, which are basically meant for
maintaining coordination with various agencies involved in the scheme, in matters of timely
release of grants and proper implementation of the programme, were not doing their job at
all. The Committee emphasises the need to activate them.

4.4 The Committee is of the opinion that there is a need to recognise the NSS as a third
dimension of the academic activities and to provide incentives to NSS functionaries in
Universities and Colleges. The Committee feels that the recommendation of the expert
Committee, set up by the UGC on integration of NSS activities in Universities’ curriculum,
should be pursued effectively and vigorously.

4.5 The Committee also feels that the amount of Rs. 120 and Rs. 200, being provided
per volunteer per year for regular activities and special camps, needs to be substantially

Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan(NYKS)

5. Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan is one of the largest youth welfare schemes, run by
the Department which alone accounts for over one third of the total allocation for youth
welfare schemes. Several programmes of vital importance for non-student rural youth are
undertaken under this scheme.

5.1 The Committee finds, from the comparative statement on annual targets and
achievements during the last three years, that the targets of most of the programmes could
not be achieved during the years 1992-93, 1993-94 and 1994-95. The main reasons for the
shortfall ascribed by the Department were the uneven flow of funds to the NYKS and
vacancies of Youth Coordinators, particularly in the North Eastern States.

5.2 The Committee, after considering the matter, arrives at the conclusion that there
seems to be some slackness on the part of the Department and that it did not act as
responsibly as it ought to have been in this regard. The Committee desires that immediate
action should be taken to ensure an even and smooth flow of funds to the Kendras and
proper utilisation thereof.

5.3 In response to the Committee’s recommendation made last year for providing
adequate representation to the peoples’ representatives in the functioning of NYKs, the


Department informed the Committee that all the youth coordinators have been instructed to
involve peoples representatives in the programme. The Committee feels that simply
instructing the youth coordinators in such an important aspect, would not serve any purpose.
The Committee recommends that a proposal should be prepared with a view to associating
peoples’ representatives at different levels in the working of the NYKs. The Committee
reiterates its recommendation to make the functioning of NYKs more democratic and
transparent by introducing element of accountability in it.

5.4 The Committee feels that, in view of some new programmes (as mentioned in para
2.1) introduced under this scheme, the decrease in the allocation, both plan and non-plan,
this year would adversely affect the progress of the on-going as well as new programmes.
Therefore, the Committee recommends enhancement of the allocation for the scheme
adequately.

5.5 The Committee also recommends that the network of Programmes of Training in
Self Employment Project, Vocational Training and Youth Awareness drives should be
considerably expanded and strengthened so as to cover more and more youth of the country,
particularly in the rural and semi-urban areas, with the association of Panchayats and
Nagarpalikas.

5.6 The Committee is also of the view that the aims of the programmes of yocational
training and Training in Self-employment Projects overlap each other. Similar is the case
with schemes like Sports (Block level & District level) & Equipment Purchase and
Vocational Training and Sports Equipment Purchase. The Committee, therefore, suggests
that vocational Training and Training in Self-employment Project be merged, as well as
schemes like Sports (Block and District level) & Equipment Purhase and Sports Equipment
Purchase, with a view to avoiding duplication of activities in this regard.

5.7 The Committee is not aware if the Department is also assisting the youth trained
under the schemes of Vocational training and Training in Self-employment Project in setting
up income generating projects. If no such action is undertaken by the Department, the
Committee suggests that suitable action may be initiated to help them in this regard.

National Integration Programme

6. The Committee asked the Department to explain the reasons for reducing the
allocation for this programme, which aims at promoting national integration, from Rs. 525
lakhs in 1994-95 to Rs. 326 lakhs in 1995-96. The Department informed that the allocation
for this programme has been reduced this year because the provision for the NGOs has been
reduced from Rs. 265. Lakhs to Rs. 250 lakhs and that for the State Governments from Rs.
360 lakhs to Rs. 76 lakhs. This had to be done in view of the past experience where some
amount had to be surrendered due to lack of enough viable proposals from the States. Even
for a new component of Sadbhavana Shivirs, introduced in this programme, very few States
came up with viable proposals. As a result, the EFC, while approving the new component,
granted it for only one year on an experimental basis.

6.1 The Committee notes that while the reason attributed for bringing down the
allocation for the States was lack of enough viable proposals from them, no reason,
however, had been assigned for reducing the allocation in the case of NGOs. Whether it was
done due to resource crunch or their unsatisfactory performance is not clear.

6.2 The Committee feels that suitable programmes of interest to the youth be devised
with a view to promoting community living and sharing of common experiences.


Exhibitions for Youth

“7. When the Committee sought to know the reason for reducing the outlay for this
scheme from Rs. 30 lakhs last year to Rs. 15 lakhs in 1995-96, the Department gave the
usual reply that the allocation had to be reduced because not enough “viable proposals”
were received by the Department. It was further explained that many of the exhibitions,

Camps which were funded from the National Integration Scheme. In the Annual Action
Plan 1995-96 of the Department, the target had been brought down to 25 exhibitions only.

Besides, the term ‘viability’ does not appear to be appropriate.

separately when the National Integration Scheme is taking care of funds for organising such

7.2 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should examine the
matter with a view to merging this scheme with that of National Integration Scheme so as to
avoid unnecessary duplication which creates confusion and wastage of resources.

Scouting & Guiding

8. The Committee expresses its deep concern over the utilisation of only Rs. 60 lakhs
out of an amount of Rs. 92 lakhs allocated last year under this scheme. No plausible reason
was given for it except that the main beneficiaries of the scheme viz. Bharat Scouts &
Guides and All India Boys Scouts failed to utilize the full amount and expand their activities
despite all encouragement from the Department. The Committee feels that the scheme is not
functioning well and, therefore, recommends that the Department itself should make efforts
to pinpoint the factors responsible for the under-utilization and take corrective measures.
Evaluation of this scheme, undertaken by the Indian Institute of Management, be completed
early and followup action taken thereon.

Accountability

18. In its Sixth Report on Demand for Grants for 1994-95, the Committee had
mentioned about the lack of accountability and coordination among. the various sports
bodies. The Department in its reply, has stated that in a scenario where the performance
depended upon the joint effort of the National Sports Federations, Sports Authority of India
Coaches, Department of Youth Affairs and Sports, it has became difficult to bring about —
accountability for poor performance: ॥

18.1 The Secretary agreed with the Committee that somebody had to be made
accountable for the poor performance. Unfortunately, the way the system is working, it is
not really possible to do that. It is the National Federations, however, that are responsible
for bringing up the teams to a certain level. The Sports Authority of India, in fact, is mainly _
responsible for bringing out talents at the young age, and provide them the basic facilities
and inputs. Boys and girls having good potential are given exposure and training at th
centres of excellence. Thereafter, it is really for the Federations to select teams (one
nominee is there in the selection committee) and hold the caoching camps. The SAI gives a
necessary assistance and facilities for holding the national or international championsh
also. But when there is a failure, nobody could really be found accountable, as
there are many interconnecting factors. 7


18.2 The Committee inferms from the above that the Department also admits that there
is no accountability in the system. The Committee feels that any system without the element
of accountability is bound to prove disastrous and this is what is happening in the
Department. The Committee does not agree with the contention of the Department that due
to many agencies/bodies involved in promotion of sports it is not possible to identify and fix
responsibility on any one of them.

18.3 The Committee deplores the manner in which the entire system is being run where
not only there is no accountability but there is no coordination among the various agencies
responsible for promotion and development of sports in the country. There appears to be a
slinging match between various sports federations and the SAI. One generally blames the
other for encroaching upon each other’s spheres.

18.4 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the possibilities of having a
coordinating body at the national level be explored and suggests that an expert committee be
set up to look into the reports submitted by the coaches/managers and sports administrators
after each international tournament with a view to fix responsibility for poor performance
and to pin-point reasons therefor so that effective remedial measures could be taken.

18.5 The Committee is separately examining the issue of India’s poor performance in
international sports. Eminent sportsmen and administrators are being invited by the
Committee to give their views in this regard. The Committee proposes to deal, in that
report, with various aspects of sports organisation and management in the country, including
the role of SAI and sports federations, Ministers and Secretaries heading sports bodies,
talent search, training, infrastructure, excessive exposure to certain games to the detriment
of others, incentives to sportsmen to adopt sports as a career, introduction of sports as a
compulsory subject in school and college curricula, role of private sector in sports
promotion, etc. Hence the Committee is not spelling out is views on these aspects in the,
present report. :

6.3.        The Committee observes that delay in the revision of the Scheme is being cited as the main reason for

finds that only progress made since then is that this proposal has received the approval of the Minister and an EFC

ACTION TAKEN
In last few years, the implementing organizations were having unspent balances due to non-running of a few
crèches as per the scheme.  Due to availability of unspent balances with the organizations the amount of expenditure
differs to that extent.
 
RECOMMENDATIONS /OBSERVATIONS
 
6.9         The Committee is not satisfied with the monitoring mechanism of the Department. The very fact that unspent
balances are available with the implementing agencies indicates that crèches are not providing the services for which
they are meant. The Committee desires that steps should be taken for removal of constraints being faced in the
implementation of this scheme by regular monitoring and interaction between the State Boards and the CSWB. The
Committee also recommends that a special drive for settlement of accounts should be initiated to stop misutilization
/underutilization of funds.
 
ACTION TAKEN
The Department proposes to strengthen monitoring of crèches under the scheme by engaging independent
agencies. It has been proposed to include monitoring as part of the programme. The crèches would be monitored once in
two years by independent monitoring agencies to be identified in consultation with concerned State Govts.  Monitoring
will be a continuing process for which a separate budget provision is being made in the revised scheme. This will enable
the Department to ensure the minimum standards in the crèches.  The implementing agencies will be requested to settle
the account with their field units so that exact amount of utilization is known to the Department.

                       CONDENSED COURSES FOR WOMEN EDUCATION
 
RECOMMENDATIONS /OBSERVATIONS
 
7.6         The Committee is constrained to note that in a number of States, in spite of accounts being settled and
utilization certificates being received up to a particular year, unspent balances still remain with the State Boards.  The
Committee has been given to understand that funds for second year batch are released, subject to the condition of 50%
pass percentage, satisfactory performance and settlement of accounts.  The Committee is of the view that if this norm
had been strictly adhered to, unspent balances, would not have been there.  The Committee, recommends that special
drive should be initiated for settlement of accounts of the States under the Scheme.
 
ACTION TAKEN
The CSWB has already initiated action for settlement of pending accounts of State Boards.  State Boards have also been
directed to settle the pending accounts of voluntary institutions implementing the Condensed Course Programme on a priority
basis.

7.7       The Committee notes that during 2004-2005, Rs.2.63 crores have been released for 336 courses meant for 8400
beneficiaries.  Major beneficiaries are Assam (Rs.30.77 lakhs), Bihar/Jharkhand (30.37 lakhs) and UP (83.02 lakhs).  In
the case of Assam, neither the number of sanctioned courses is available, nor the number of beneficiaries.  In contrast,
there are a few States, where courses have been sanctioned but no funds have been released therefor.  The Committee
also observes that status of unspent balance does not seem to have any impact on the further release of funds.
 
ACTION TAKEN
During 2004-05, an amount of Rs. 581.25 lakhs has been released for 585 courses for 14625 beneficiaries.  The
sanctioned number of courses for Assam State is 23 courses (18 centralized 5 decentralized) and number of beneficiaries
is 575.  It is also informed that during 2004-05, courses were sanctioned to all State Boards and release was also made
except for one State Board i.e. Lakshadweep, from where no proposal was received during the year.  The unspent
balance lying with the State Boards was adjusted, where accounts were settled.  In some of the States more than
sanctioned amount was released to clear the past liabilities.

VIII.      BALIKA SAMRIDDHI YOJANA (BSY)
 
RECOMMENDATIONS /OBSERVATIONS
 
8.5         The Committee expresses its serious concern about the way the Balika Samridhi Yojana is being implemented. 
Scheme launched in the first year of Ninth Plan, i.e. 1997-98 had to be recast after two years of its implementation.  In
the third year, the scheme had to be reviewed again and recast.  The Committee is perturbed to note that Tenth Plan has
also completed three years but the air of indecisiveness still hangs around the Scheme meant for the welfare of the girl
child.  The Committee is left with no other alternative but to conclude that the scheme suffers from inherent drawbacks,
which continues to be there in spite of review of thescheme being done not once, but on two occasions.  The Committee
doubts whether the funds released so far have reached the targetted beneficiaries.
 
ACTION TAKEN
The scheme launched in 1997 was providing Rs. 500/- each, in cash, to the mother of girl child. The scheme was
recasted so that girl child must receive benefit. Rs. 500/- is now deposited in interest bearing accounts in Banks or Post
Offices which girl child receive at the age of 18 years and remain unmarried. In addition, scholarship ranging from Rs.
300/- from class I to Rs. 1000/- for class X is paid to the girl child.
 
              During 2004-05 an amount of Rs. 39.75 crore have been released to 16 states /UTs who submitted Utilization
Certificates for the grant released in past years. The states have submitted details of accounts opened in the Banks/ Post
Offices and details of cash certificates given to beneficiaries. However few states like Bihar and UP have not submitted
details of Utilization. These states are being reminded regularly.

WOMEN WITH DAY CARE CENTRES FOR CHILDREN 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS /OBSERVATIONS
 
9.3         The Committee notes that Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra seem to be the major beneficiaries of funds
amounting to Rs. 2.84 crores released during 2005-2006.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the funding
pattern for these three States under the scheme during 2005-2006.
 
ACTION TAKEN
              There is no separate funding pattern for Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra.  The funding pattern is the same
for all States.
 
RECOMMENDATIONS /OBSERVATIONS
 
9.4  Committee’s attention has been drawn by the audit report No.2 of 2004 (for the period ended March 2003).  The
audit has pointed out failure of the Department to monitor the utilization of grants totaling Rs. 39.58 crore given to
NGOs and local bodies for construction of hostels for working women that rendered the expenditure infructuous. This
clearly indicates that no effective monitoring mechanism exists under the Scheme .  The Committee would like to have
the feedback in this regard.
 
ACTION TAKEN
Realizing the difficulties in the monitoring of the Scheme throughout the country, from July, 2003, the
Department has made it mandatory that the proposals for construction of WWH (the initial proposal as well as those for
subsequent instalments) are to be routed through the State Government accompanied by an Inspection Report by a State
DWCD official.  Subsequent instalments are being released only on receipt of physical and financial progress reports
through the concerned State Governments.  The utilization of grants totalling Rs.39.58 crore released for Working
Women Hostels has been taken up with the concerned StateGovernments for reporting the status and initiating action to
ensure completion of incomplete hostel buildings and their proper utilisation.
 
X.                 SUPPORT TO TRAINING  AND EMPLOYMENT PROGRAMME FOR WOMEN   (STEP) AND

10.6       The Committee is constrained to note that instead of reviewing the feasibility of merger of both the schemes,
the Department simply took the decision to transfer both the schemes to States and even action on this Decision is yet to
be initiated.  The Committee apprehends that Tenth Plan would be over in another two years and fate of these two

12.1  NGOs are funded under this scheme to setup Short Stay Homes for those women who are victims of marital
conflict, family mal-adjustment etc.   The Scheme provides funds for suitable  rented accommodation for at least 30 in
one Home.   The Committee observes that achievement level both in physical and financial terms has been satisfactory
