3.19     The Committee was informed that in addition to emphasis on supplementary nutrition and convergence with health services, special focus is also being given to the pre-school education component of the ICDS scheme, so that the children are fully prepared for entering class I at the age of 6 years under the Sarva Siksha Abhiyan (SSA) & District Primary Education Programme (DPEP). For this, the States have been requested to ensure necessary convergence between ICDS Scheme and SSA & DPEP.
3.20     The Committee is happy to note the decision of convergence between ICDS scheme and SSA & DPEP. The success of ICDS programme depends purely on effective supervision, monitoring, co-ordination and convergence with other Departments and also with better and effective participation of local bodies and community. Convergence of various components is a good idea. The Committee recommends that the revised guidelines, if need be, may be issued without any delay and the State Governments and implementing agencies be pursued for smooth implementation of the converged scheme. Keeping in view the expansion
of the ICDS scheme and its proposed convergence with other programmes, the Committee strongly feels that an effective monitoring mechanism at all levels need to be put in place at the earliest. Only then, services envisaged under ICDS scheme can reach the intended beneficiaries. The Committee would like to be apprised about the steps taken in this direction.
3.21     The Committee notes the observations made in the Mid Term Appraisal of the Tenth  Five Year Plan regarding ICDS, which indicate the absence of the critical component of day-care in the package of services provided. Lack of day-care has its impact on the education of the girl child, since she is made to stay home to take care of younger siblings. The Appraisal also emphasizes that disabled children must be encouraged to attend the crèches and training be given to crèche workers for such children. The Mid Term Appraisal (MTA) further highlights other issues like District level strategies for pre-school education and training
of Anganwadi workers therefor.
3.22     The Committee would like the Ministry to take cognizance of the observations contained in the Mid Term Appraisal and take immediate remedial measures to streamline the scheme. The Committee desires that it may be apprised about the steps taken in this direction.
3.23     The Committee observes that in 17 States/UTs, Co-ordination Committees at state, district, block and village levels have been set up to ensure convergence between ICDS, Health, Drinking Water and Sanitation, Panchayati Raj, Primary Education, Rural Development etc. Welcoming the initiative taken by these 17 States, the Committee would like to point out that NE States, Sikkim, J&K, Orissa and Southern States have not come forward so far. The Committee hopes that with the matter being pursued by the Ministry, these States will be covered very soon.
3.24     The Committee understands that a study on ‘Three Decades of ICDS: An Appraisal’ has been conducted in all the States/UTs. Draft Report was likely to be completed by the end of March 2006. The Committee would like to be apprised about the findings of this study as and when finalised and reported.
 
IV.       TRAINING PROGRAMME UNDER ICDS (UDISHA)
 
4.1       Training is a crucial element in the ICDS scheme. The World Bank assisted ICDS Training Programme, Project UDISHA, was launched from April, 1999. It is a comprehensive training being undertaken through the National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child Development, selected training institutions and the State Governments. The project completed its normal period of 5 years on 30.9.2004 and was extended by the World Bank till 31.3.2006. The Ministry informed that training activities would continue under domestic funds in 2006-2007.
4.2       The plan allocation in BE 2005-2006 was Rs. 40.00 crore and raised to Rs. 82.50 crore due to extension of project from 1.7.2005 to 31.3.2006. The actual expenditure incurred upto 3.3.2006 was Rs. 62.77 crore (Statement VI-BE, RE and Actuals for 2005-06). The Committee would, however, like to point out that on a specific query, the Ministry, while giving the State wise allocation of funds under UDISHA during 2005-06, has informed that as on 16.3.06, there was an expenditure of Rs. 60.99 crores.   The Committee would like to know the acual expenditure incurred under the scheme.
4.3       The Ministry informed the Committee that funds were released to the States on the basis of their physical and financial quarterly progress reports (QPRs) and also keeping in view the trend of utilization and their capacity to utilize the funds by following strict schematic norms for Project Udisha. Therefore there was a slow pace of utilization of funds. Status of allocation of funds to NE States during 2003-04, 2004-05 and 2005-06 reveals that the States failed to take the benefit as these funds have remained underutilized. Not only this, from the details furnished to the Committee it is clear that during 2005-06, financial assistance
was released to NE States only in the last month of the financial year, which is not a healthy sign.
4.4       There is no denying the fact that judicious utilization of the allocation alone would yield desired results. The Ministry can better monitor the utilization by way of getting UCs and monthly progress reports from all the States/UTs and other agencies on quarterly basis. The Committee strongly feels that regular interaction with the States facing constraints will help in achieving the desired results.
4.5       The Committee opines that training is the most crucial element in ICDS as achievement of Programme goals depends upon the effectiveness of frontline workers in improved delivery of packages of services under ICDS. The Committee notes that the gap between trained and untrained functionaries is increasing every year. The following physical achievement of target and trained confirms this:-

            The training of various level of functionaries assumes added importance in view of the proposed increase of 467 additional projects and 1.88 lakh Anganwadi centres. The Ministry informed that due to the prevailing backlogs and operationalisation of new centres particularly for the ‘Job training’ of ICDS functionaries, the Ministry has taken the following measures in the recent past:
(i)         Duration of the training programmes has been reduced w.e.f. April 1, 2005 which would help in conducting more batches per training center in a year leading to reduction in backlog of trainees and imparting training to new recruits under Udisha.
 
(ii)        Some States like Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan have been permitted to use District Mobile Teams in addition to AWTCs.
 
(iii)       States have been asked to impart short duration induction training (pending the Job Training) to newly recruited AWWs to operationalise the AWCs at the earliest.

Since October 2004, there had been seven national level review meetings with the State Secretaries/Directors in New Delhi.
 
The Committee would however, like to point out that considering the huge backlog of untrained AWWs and AWHs, the steps initiated by the Ministry to train all the workers and Helpers have not yield the desired results so far.   The Committee observes that State Governments/UTs play the most important role in the implementation of the ICDS Training Programme.   The State Governments are responsible for setting up of Anganwadi  Training Centres and Middle Level Training Centres (MLTCs), Working of these centres are also monitored by them.   State Governments are also responsible for identifying NGOs/other organizations
for running the Training Centres.   The Committee feels that the status of these Training Centres both existing and required in different  states is an important aspect of  the Training Programme which perhaps has not been given due impetus so far.   The Committee is of the view that an on the spot assessment of all the existing Training Centres with priority being given to states lagging behind  needs to be made and remedial measures taken at the earliest.    Mere release of central funds would not serve the purpose. The Ministry has to play a more pro-active role in the implementation of training of ICDS functionaries, the most vital
aspect of the ICDS programme.
V.        RAJIV GANDHI NATIONAL CRECHE SCHEME FOR THE CHILDREN OF WORKING MOTHERS
 
5.1       Rajiv Gandhi National Creche Scheme for the Children of Working Mothers was launched with effect from 1
st January 2006 after merging the National Creche Fund and the Scheme of Assistance to Voluntary Organizations for Creche for Working and Ailing Women’s Children. The new scheme provides improved services and enhanced financial allotments besides increasing the number of crèches in the country. The financial norms have been revised from Rs. 18,480/- to Rs. 42,384/- per crèche per annum. It has been decided to set up 14,719 new crèches by the end of Tenth Plan. Eligibility criteria for those entitled to
availing services under the new Scheme have also been enhanced from Rs. 1800/- to Rs. 12,000/- per month.
5.2       The allocation for BE 2006-2007 has been enhanced to Rs. 81.00 crore for setting up of proposed crèches by the end of Tenth Plan across the country and for meeting expenditure required on enhanced norms.  Against an allocation of Rs. 31.50 crore in 2005-2006 Rs. 28.50 crore were utilized. The Committee would, however, like to point out that uptil 31
st December, 2005, utilization figures stood  at Rs. 10.03 crores.   However, thereafter, in the last quarter of the year, Rs. 18.47 crore were released.   The Committee is not happy with this uneven spread of fund allocation.   Besides, the Committee  is also constrained  to observe
that allocation meant for NE states has remained underutilized during the last few years, with nil expenditure been reported during 2004-05 and 2005-06. The Committee may be apprised of the reasons for non-utilisation of funds in NE region.
5.3       The Committee notes that the Ministry kept an ambitious target of 14719 creches by the end of Tenth Plan i.e. by 2006-2007; the new crèches will be allocated to the Central Social Welfare Board, Indian Council for Child Welfare and Bharatiya Adim Jati Sevak Sangh in the ratio of 80:11:9. The Committee would like to be apprised about the rationale of selecting only three agencies for operationalising the Crèche Schcme. The Committee further recommends that more and more reputed and established NGOs may be selected for implementing the Creche Scheme.
5.4       To strengthen monitoring of crèches, the scheme provides engaging of independent monitoring agencies. These agencies will be identified in consultation with the concerned State Governments and will conduct regular monitoring of crèches. In the course of inspection, these agencies are expected to assess the motivation and capacity of the implementing agencies also. It is expected that every crèche will be inspected at least once in a period of two years.
5.6       The Committee is satisfied with the steps taken to strengthen the monitoring of scheme, but has its reservations about the actual implementation aspect. It is surprising that the scheme has started functioning but consultations with State Governments are yet to take place. The Committee recommends that a time schedule may be prepared urgently in consultation with State Governments and implementing agencies for implementing its various aspects of the scheme. The aspect of utilization of funds also needs to be addressed properly.
5.7       The Committee understands that out of 4885 creches sanctioned under NCF (National Creche Fund), 2514 creches having completed five years were not receiving any grant from the NCF as they had submitted an undertaking that they would run the crèches on self-supporting basis after five years. The Ministry clarified that crèches sanctioned under National Crèche Fund have been merged with the revised crèche scheme namely Rajiv Gandhi National Creche Scheme for the children of working mothers, with effect from 1.1.2006.
5.8       The Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure that  2514 creches which were earlier provided grants are not given further grants under the New Scheme. The monitoring process need to be strengthened and responsibility fixed for any delay.
5.9       With a view to provide better services, to build up child friendly environment in the Creche Centre and to orient the crèche workers as well as the implementing agency, the component of a short term training has been added to the new Scheme. The training module will be prepared with the help of National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child Development and the training will be organized through the agencies identified in consultation with the concerned State Government.
5.10     The Committee recommends that the training module should be finalised in a time frame and a suitable plan of action devised so that the targets of the training are achieved.
           
VI.       CONDENSED COURSES FOR WOMEN EDUCATION
 
6.1       The Scheme of Condensed Courses for Women Education was initiated by CSWB in 1958 to cater to the needs of adult girls/women who could not join mainstream education system or who were dropouts from formal schools. The scheme aims to provide educational opportunities to girls/women above the age of 15 years alongwith additional inputs of skill-development/vocational training. The main focus of the scheme is to ensure that contents of the courses are need-based and modified according to local requirement and simultaneously targeting towards various stages of education levels of primary/middle/high school and
matric/secondary level courses.
6.2       Plan allocation of Rs. 5.40 crore was made for this programme in 2005-2006. The actual expenditure incurred upto 3
rd March 2006 is Rs. 2.70 crore. The Ministry has informed that sanctions were being issued and entire allocation was to be utilized by 31.3.2006.The Committee has, however, some reservations on the last minute spending by the Department. Rushing the expenditure in the last few days needs to be discouraged for effective utilization of resources.
6.3       The Ministry informed that in pursuance of the recommendations of National/State level workshops, a National Working Group has been constituted for revamping/evaluation of the scheme in the changing socio-economic and work environment. The report of the Working Group which was expected in August 2005 is yet to be submitted. The Committee is unhappy over the delay in submission of the Report and recommends that the matter be expedited without further delay. The Committee would also like to be apprised of its contents as and when the report is finalized.
6.4       The Committee has been given to understand that no residential course has been sanctioned to any State Board by CSWB in recent years due to paucity of funds as it involves more than double of the amount meant for Non-residential courses and the allocation under the programme is very limited and hardly sufficient to meet the demand of all the States.
6.5       The Committee is not happy with the present state of affairs. It feels that residential courses on selected basis should be sanctioned in those States where the response is encouraging. Obviously the girls/women are unable to pursue their studies further because of lack of hostels. The residential courses can help them fill the gap. The Committee further recommends that additional funds may be sought for the purpose.

VII.     BALIKA SAMRIDDHI YOJANA
7.1       The scheme was launched in 1997 with the aim of raising the status of girl children in Below Poverty Line families. The scheme was reviewed and recast in 1999.  Subsequently, as a  consequence of decision taken by the Planning Commission to relocate some of the Centrally Sponsored Schemes to the States, BSY was selected to be one such scheme and it was proposed to be transferred w.e.f. 2005-06
7.2       In 2004-05, funds were released to States, however no funds were kept in BE 2005-2006 and 2006-2007. The Ministry has informed that no monitoring/publicity was undertaken at central level.  The Committee observes that total funds released as on 1.3.06 is Rs. 216.15 crore whereas unspent balance as on 30.9.2005 is Rs. 74.97 crore lying with different States like Bihar, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Orissa and Uttaranchal.
7.3       Earlier the Committee in its 160
th Report had expressed serious concern about the implementation as well as the aspect of uncertainty in the transfer of BSY to the States. The Committee observes that situation instead of improving has worsened since no decision has been taken in this regard so far. The Secretary in her appearance before the Committee also conceded that this was a very unsatisfactory status.
7.4       The Committee is not happy with the uncertainty status of the BSY scheme, continuing for so long.  The Committee fails to understand as  why Planning Commission has taken such a long time to take a decision on transferring the Balika Samriddhi Yojana to states.  A decision taken by the Planning Commission at the beginning  of the Tenth Plan is yet to be finalized even though Tenth Plan period is in its  last year. The Committee is also not aware as to how the Committed Liability of Rs. 74.97 crore    lying with different states is going to be adjusted.   The Committee is of the view that this is a classic case of improper
formulation of a scheme launched in haste and inherent flaws being noticed during the course of its implementation.   The Committee does not have much hope about this scheme being effectively implemented by states, with  some States already facing severe financial constraints.   The Committee would once again reiterate that fate of BSY scheme needs to be decided at the earliest.   The Ministry being the nodal authority has to vigorously pursue this issue with the Planning Commission.

XI.       CENTRAL SOCIAL WELFARE BOARD (CSWB)
11.1     The CSWB was established as an interface between the Government and the voluntary sector to promote social development in the country. The Board is involved in the implementation of a number of programmes such as  Border Area Projects, Family Counselling Centres,  Working Women Hostels, Swawlamban and Swahadhar etc. CSWB implements the various programmes of the Ministry. These programmes are implemented through voluntary organizations in collaboration with State Social Welfare Advisory Boards. The Committee was informed that the Ministry has not made any effort to strengthen the network of
CSWB and its State counterparts for monitoring implementation of different schemes of the Ministry at different levels.
11.2     The allocation for the year 2005-2006 was Rs. 34.43 crore against which expenditure reported upto 31st December, 2005 is only Rs. 15.79 crore.  For the year 2006-2007 the allocation was reduced to Rs. 23.45 crore. The Ministry has informed that due to closure of Border Area Projects and Demonstration Projects w.e.f. 1.4.2005, provision has been reduced.
11.3     As per information available to the Committee, unspent Balance of Rs. 34.96 crore under various programmes are lying with the CSWB which includes Rs. 11.76 crore under the Rajiv Gandhi National Creche Scheme and Rs. 12.81 crore under  Short Stay Homes.
11.4     The Committee observes that CSWB is entrusted with the implementation of large number of schemes. The assignments have been spread to such an extent that CSWB has failed to devise proper monitoring mechanism for such schemes. CSWB is a central organisation directly under Ministry’s control and it is very surprising to the Committee that the Ministry has not made any effort to strengthen the network of CSWB.   It would be a better situation, according to the Committee, if CSWB is asked to focus its attention on onespecific assignment for a particular period of time. Declining Girl child ratio is a problem which is
assuming alarming proportion nation- wide. The Committee notes some initiative have been taken by a few States for improving the lot of girl child. But some sort of scheme totally dedicated for development of girl child needs to be initiated at national level. The Committee feels that CSWB can play a major role by focusing on this social problem. Nationwide campaign by CSWB in co-ordination with all States Boards and other concerned agencies will have a lasting impact on the thinking of public at large. The issue of huge unspent balances with the different agencies of CSWB would be addressed in case its mandate is specifically
defined. The Committee would, therefore, appreciate if the Ministry identifies some focused subjects for implementation by CSWB.

On a specific query about the status of Short Stay Homes,   the Committee has been informed that out of 342 SSHs, 331 are functional. rd March 2006 is ‘NIL’. SCHEME FOR RESCUE OF VICTIMS OF TRAFFICKING
 
15.1     This is a new scheme launched in 2005-2006 which aims at supporting the efforts of the NGOs in rescue operation of victims of trafficking. no expenditure was incurred since the formulation of scheme is still under consideration. Rs.0.45 crores has been kept in 2006-2007.
15.2     The Committee was informed that to deal with trafficking, the Ministry is in the process of amending the Immoral Traffic Prevention Act (ITPA). The Ministry also wants to set up a Central Nodal Authority as in the Department of Revenue so that they can mount very good, quick and effective rescue operations, as a result, of which women and children could be rescued from trafficking.
15.3     The Committee observes that allocation of Rs. 3.00 crore for this scheme was made in 2004-05 which was reduced to Rs. 30 lakhs in 2005-06.   Allocation in 2006-07 stands at Rs.45 lakhs. Since the scheme is to be implemented through NGOs, the Ministry has to be very careful while releasing funds. Monitoring of the scheme is to be strictly followed. The publicity should focus on protection and awareness-raising among parents and guardians.
 
RELIEF AND REHABILITATION OF VICTIMS OF RAPE
15.4     The Committee also notes that a scheme for the relief and rehabilitation of victims of rape is proposed to be introduced in compliance with a judgment of the Supreme Court delivered in the year 1994 which directed the Government to bring forward such a scheme specially considering that some of the victims of rape are too traumatized to continue in employment. The special feature of the scheme is an award of monetary compensation to the victim apart from rehabilitative action.
15.5     The Committee feels that the victims of rape undergo the conditions of psychological stress and trauma notwithstanding the physical assault. The rehabilitation process of such victim involves psychological support as well as economic assistance. The Committee would like the Ministry to create a separate rehabilitation fund for victims of rape to ensure that they get all sort of psychological and economic assistance in time.
XVI.    PREVENTION OF SEXUAL HARASSMENT AT WORKPLACE
 
16.1     The Government of India constituted a Central Committee under the Chairpersonship of the Secretary, Ministry of Women and Child Development to monitor the implementation of the Supreme Court’s Guidelines for prevention of Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace. The Committee in its Meeting held on 29.10.2002 recommended that Awareness needs to be given on this issue and this task had been assigned to National Commission for Women (NCW) and Central Social Welfare Board alongwith Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. The National Commission for Women has taken up sexual harassment of
women at work place as one of the focal issues in the realm of promotion of gender equality and women's empowerment.  The Commission had widely circulated the Visakha Judgement for compliance along with a code of conduct for workplace formulated by the NCW. The Committee is not aware of the activities/initiatives undertaken by the CSWB and Ministry of Information and Broadcasting to create awareness on the SC Guidelines. This has become all the more important in view of increasing incidents of sexual harassment in BPOs and other private institutions.
16.2     The Committee has been informed that in order to assess the extent to which guidelines and norms laid by the Apex Court have been implemented as well as to share the experiences/ difficulties faced by various organizations in dealing with complaints of sexual harassment, the Commission has been holding meetings with various Organisations/Government Departments since November, 2000.   The meetings proved to be an interactive forum for exchange of experiences with various organisations.  More than 30 Meetings, which have been attended by more than 799 organisations, were held in the past.  Details of Central/State

The private institutions may also be brought under the purview of the legislations related to prevention of sexual harassment.

XVIII.GENDER BUDGETING
18.1     Women face gender specific barriers to access of public services and expenditure. Gender Budgeting lends itself to strengthening of administrative processes and actions achieve the targets for improvement in the position of women. It not only entails a look at allocation of resources for women but goes beyond to cover tracking the utilization of allocated resources, impact analysis and beneficiary incidence analysis of public expenditure and policy from a gender perspective.
18.2     Gender budget has been conceived as one of the tools for achieving the goals and targets set in our plans and policies benefiting women. The basic intent is to achieve the objectives enshrined in the Constitution towards overall development of women. The Committee appreciates that the Ministry has undertaken a number of measures for achieving the targets of gender budgeting.
18.3     The Committee notes that during 2005-06, as a result of persistent efforts made by the Ministry Gender Budget Cells have been set up in 41 mainstream Departments  including Power, Petroleum, Culture, Heavy Industries, Science and Technology etc.
18.4     The Committee recommends that being the nodal Ministry, the Ministry of WCD should ensure that Gender Budget Cells which are set up in the Ministries have become operational and also pursue this issue with the remaining Ministries.
18.5     Committee’s attention has been drawn by a few gender concerns that the Ministry has raised with various Ministries in Government of India as indicated below:
-           Secretary, Sports and Youth Affairs has been addressed on the need for raising participation of women in sports and according due recognition to success stories.
 
-           The subject of Health Insurance Scheme for women in view of their vulnerabilities and barriers to access to medical services has been raised with Secretary (Health).
 
-           The Planning Commission has been requested to engender State Plans.
 
-           Secretary (Exp.) and Member-Secretary Planning Commission have both been requested to include a column on gender outcomes in the Outcome Budget of GOI
 
The Committee would like to be apprised about the implementation status of the aforesaid initiatives taken by the Ministry.
18.6     Committee’s attention has been drawn by the details regarding scheme-wise provisions and physical targets benefiting women in the Budget of Ministry of Women and Child Development as given in the Performance Budget (2006-07). The Committee finds that all the schemes whether targeting children or women have been shown to be providing 100% benefit to women alone. The Committee does not dispute the fact that welfare ofthe child is ultimately the welfare of its mother.However, in view of the emerging concept of child budgeting, it cannot be claimed that flagship schemes like ICDS are benefiting cent percent
women.The Committee recommends that the allocation on programmes and schemes benefiting women may be delineated specifically. The Committee also recommends that the components of gender budgeting may be made more clear and included in the guidelines for gender budgeting.

th Report had expressed serious concern about the implementation as well as the aspect of uncertainty in the transfer of BSY to the States. The Committee observes that situation instead of improving has worsened since no decision has been taken in this regard so far. The Secretary in her appearance before the Committee also conceded that this was a very unsatisfactory status. (Para 7.3)
 
                        The Committee is not happy with the uncertainty status of the BSY scheme, continuing for so long.  The Committee fails to understand as  why Planning Commission has taken such a long time to take a decision on transferring the Balika Samriddhi Yojana to states.  A decision taken by the Planning Commission at the beginning  of the Tenth Plan is yet to be finalized even though Tenth Plan period is in its  last year. The Committee is also not aware as to how the Committed Liability of Rs. 74.97 crore    lying with different states is going to be adjusted.   The Committee is of the view that this is a classic case of
improper formulation of a scheme launched in haste and inherent flaws being noticed during the course of its implementation.   The Committee does not have much hope about this scheme being effectively implemented by states, with  some States already facing severe financial constraints.   The Committee would once again reiterate that fate of BSY scheme needs to be decided at the earliest.   The Ministry being the nodal authority has to vigorously pursue this issue with the Planning Commission.                                                                                                 (Para 7.4)
 
VIII.    ASSISTANCE FOR CONSTRUCTION/EXPANSION OF HOSTEL BUILDINGS FOR WORKING WOMEN WITH DAY CARE CENTRES FOR CHILDREN
 
The Committee finds that both the financial and physical performance under the scheme have shown declining trend over the years. The utilization has been below the target.   It seems that there is no activity under this scheme in the NE region  as there was an expenditure of only Rs.9 lakhs against an allocation of Rs.1.00 crore in 2004-05 and nil expenditure  has been reported in 2005-06 as on 3.3.2006. The Committee is not aware whether any exercise has been initiated so far to make an assessment about the unsatisfactory performance of this scheme  and take remedial measures.   If not, done so far, the Committee feels that this is
the right time to initiate the same.     (Para 8.1)
 
                        The Committee was informed that there are 40 projects sanctioned from 2001-2002 to 2005-06 in the implementation stage under the Scheme of Working Women Hostel. Out of these projects, in respect of 17 projects, either the file is not traceable or no progress report has been received so far. In majority of these cases, implementing agencies are NGOs.  There are a few  cases where expenditure has already exceeded  the original estimate  and the building project is not yet complete.    The Committee has been informed that in most of the cases, organizations involve their own construction agency for the construction of
hostel building. Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) in its Report No. 2 of 2004 (Para 6.5) has also criticized  the Ministry for its failure to monitor the utilization of grants totalling Rs. 39.58 crores given to NGOs and local bodies for construction of hostels for working women.  The Committee is surprised to note that the requisite information is still awaited from most of the States.                                    (Para 8.2)
 
                        The Committee is of the considered view that the Ministry should not finance such projects or scheme, wherein it has no control over its implementation. In the present scheme, the Committee feels the accountability is lacking and control is missing. Implementation Agencies should not have the sole discretion to select construction agencies.   In any case, projects need to be handled by Government agencies. The Committee would also like to point out that there is an increasing need for setting up more Hostels. If need be, norms for opening of Hostels can be reviewed and revised. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the scheme needs to revamped and started afresh.                                       (Para 8.4)
 
IX.       SUPPORT TO TRAINING AND EMPLOYMENT PROGRAMME FOR WOMEN (STEP)
 
                        As is evident from above figures, the number of beneficiaries and the number of projects are coming down every year.    The Committee would also like to point out that although overall allocated funds have remained underutilized during the Tenth Plan, performance level has been somewhat different in respect of NE Region States.    Expenditure has been more than the allocated funds for these States.   The Committee would like to have an idea about the status of projects (State-wise) during the Tenth Plan.                                                                                    (Para 9.3)
 
                        The Ministry has cited the inadequate number of staff as one of the reasons for underutilization of funds. Lack of staff for a national level programmes aimed to benefit thousands of women in traditional sectors is hardly a convincing argument. The Committee also notes that the technical team is taking undue time in clearing the projects. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should initiate assessment of the scheme so that procedural bottlenecks can be removed and scheme can be implemented effectively.                                                                            (Para 9.4)
 
X.                    SWAWLAMBAN
 
                        The Committee finds that as many as 1988 utilization certificates are pending with the implementation agencies spread over in different States with the maximum number of UCs being in Andhra Pradesh (321), Uttar Pradesh (206), J & K (180) and M.P. (148).    The Committee is surprised to note that even Central Social Welfare Board has to account for 173 Utilization Certificates.                                     (Para 10.5)
 
                        The Committee in its 160
th Report had expressed its concern that transfer of the schemes not performing well to the States cannot be considered a wise decision.  The Committee is of the view that perhaps no efforts were made by the Ministry to sensitize the State/UTs before the transfer of the scheme.   As per the Performance Budget (2005-06) Rs. 2.00 crore have been provided under the scheme for 2006-07 also. The Committee fails to comprehend the reason for allocating fund for 2006-07 when the scheme stands transferred to the States from 1.4.2006.  The Committee would like the Department to clear the air of
confusion about its committed liabilities as well as the mechanism concerning flow of funds under the scheme.                                             (Para 10.7)
 
XI.       CENTRAL SOCIAL WELFARE BOARD (CSWB)
 
                        The Committee observes that CSWB is entrusted with the implementation of large number of schemes. The assignments have been spread to such an extent that CSWB has failed to devise proper monitoring mechanism for such schemes. CSWB is a central organisation directly under Ministry’s control and it is very surprising to the Committee that the Ministry has not made any effort to strengthen the network of CSWB.   It would be a better situation, according to the Committee, if CSWB is asked to focus its attention on onespecific assignment for a particular period of time. Declining Girl child ratio is a problem which
is assuming alarming proportion nation- wide. The Committee notes some initiative have been taken by a few States for improving the lot of girl child. But some sort of scheme totally dedicated for development of girl child needs to be initiated at national level. The Committee feels that CSWB can play a major role by focusing on this social problem. Nationwide campaign by CSWB in co-ordination with all States Boards and other concerned agencies will have a lasting impact on the thinking of public at large. The issue of huge unspent balances with the different agencies of CSWB would be addressed in case its mandate is
specifically defined. The Committee would, therefore, appreciate if the Ministry identifies some focused subjects for implementation by CSWB.       
(Para 11.4)
 
XII.                 SHORT STAY HOMES (SSHs)
 
                        The Committee observes that a number of Short Stay Homes had to be discontinued due to bad performance.  10 organizations spread over in different States have been issued show cause notices.  This confirms Committee’s apprehension about the shortcomings of a scheme which is meant for the welfare of the down-trodden.   The Committee strongly feels that the Government needs to play a more pro-active role in co-ordination with the State Governments so that the scheme is strengthened. Scheme may therefore be evaluated and revamped.                (Para 12.3)
 
XIII.                SWADHAR

                        Although the scheme is picking up, however keeping in view the needy women of such categories, this achievement is just a drop in the ocean. The existence of such Homes needs more publicity. The scheme may be allocated more fund to finance more number of projects. The Committee recommends that at least one shelter home may be constructed in each Districts in the country.                                            (Para 13.4)
 
XIV.                RASHTRIYA MAHILA KOSH (RMK)
 
                        Progress in microfinance activity is pre-dominantly measured in terms of numbers covered, amounts saved, amounts lent and repayment rates, and not by results achieved in genuine economic development. There is need to assess the impact on the upliftment of women. The RMK should evaluate the scheme on these parameters. The Committee recommends that RMK should develop a pool of projects/ schemes/activities which are locally viable and implementable and which can generate income. The RMK can advise the beneficiaries to opt for any of these schemes which will be beneficial for them. The Committee feels
that if such an option is available, the disbursement level will increase and the objectives of the scheme can be achieved.                                  (Para 14.5)
 
                        The Committee was given to understand that a Sub Committee has been setup to examine different aspects of micro credit programmes, economic viability and sustainability of Kosh under RMK.   In this connection, the Committee would like to recall its earlier recommendation with regard to lowering of interest rate on loans to be given by RMK.    The Committee is surprised to note that Governing Body of RMK in its meeting held on 21.12.2005 decided that constitution of a Sub Committee for examination of various operational issues including lowering of interest rate be left to the discretion of MOS, Ministry of
Women and Child Development and  Chairperson, RMK.    The Committee expresses its serious reservation on the handling of such a sensitive issue.    The Committee strongly feels that the existing system under which RMK charges interest@ 8 % on reducing balance from borrowing agency which in turn charges any rate on or above 8% on reducing balance from the ultimate beneficiaries subject to maximum upto 18% needs to be reviewed at the earliest.  One should not forget that the main objective of RMK is to provide micro credit support to poor women.          (Para 14.6)
 
XV.                  NEW  SCHEMES
 
SCHEME FOR RESCUE OF VICTIMS OF TRAFFICKING
 
                        The Committee observes that allocation of Rs. 3.00 crore for this scheme was made in 2004-05 which was reduced to Rs. 30 lakhs in 2005-06.   Allocation in 2006-07 stands at Rs.45 lakhs.  The Committee is not happy with the undue delay in launching of this scheme. The scheme needs more publicity and proper implementation. Since the scheme is to be implemented through NGOs, the Ministry has to be very careful while releasing funds. Monitoring of the scheme is to be strictly followed. The publicity should focus on protection and awareness-raising among parents and guardians.  (Para 15.3)
 
RELIEF AND REHABILITATION OF VICTIMS OF RAPE
 
                        The Committee feels that the victims of rape undergo the conditions of psychological stress and trauma notwithstanding the physical assault. The rehabilitation process of such victim involves psychological support as well as economic assistance. The Committee would like the Ministry to create a separate rehabilitation fund for victims of rape to ensure that they get all sort of psychological and economic assistance in time.                                                                                                   (Para 15.5)
 
XVI.                PREVENTION OF SEXUAL HARASSMENT AT WORKPLACE
 
                        The Government of India constituted a Central Committee under the Chairpersonship of the Secretary, Ministry of Women and Child Development to monitor the implementation of the Supreme Court’s Guidelines for prevention of Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace. The Committee in its Meeting held on 29.10.2002 recommended that Awareness needs to be given on this issue and this task had been assigned to National Commission for Women (NCW) and Central Social Welfare Board alongwith Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. The National Commission for Women has taken up sexual harassment
of women at work place as one of the focal issues in the realm of promotion of gender equality and women's empowerment.  The Commission had widely circulated the Visakha Judgement for compliance along with a code of conduct for workplace formulated by the NCW. The Committee is not aware of the activities/initiatives undertaken by the CSWB and Ministry of Information and Broadcasting to create awareness on the SC Guidelines. This has become all the more important in view of increasing incidents of sexual harassment in BPOs and other private institutions.(Para 16.1)
                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
                        The Committee is constrained to observe that that the Supreme Court Guidelines had not been properly followed both by the Government Departments.  In a number of cases, Complaint Committees had not been formed.  Where these committees existed, they did not have 50 per cent reservation for women.  Also in many cases the Committees were headed by men instead of women and without the involvement of a third party (NGO).  Lack of awareness among the Members of the complaint Committee was also noticed. The Committee is of the firm view that Supreme Court directive needs to be implemented in letter
and spirit.   The Committee would like to have full details about the 799 organisations covered so far by the NCW alongwith theorganizations where complaint Committees are yet to be set up.    The Committee would also like to have an idea about the additional organizations covered by NCW. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should come forward with a comprehensive legislation for prevention of sexual harassment in work places. The private institutions may also be brought under the purview of the legislations related to prevention of sexual harassment.   (Para 16.5)
 
XVII.               NUTRITION
 
                        The Committee notes that the FNB provides training to the Anganwadi functionaries. However the Committee notices huge gap between the target and achievement especially in case of training of grassroot level functionaries. The Committee wonders how the Ministry can take a casual approach to the gap reflected and let on increase in the number of malnourished children.                                                                        (Para 17.5)
 
                        The Committee’s attention is drawn by the media reports appearing on regular basis about large number of deaths of children due to malnourishment in the tribal belts of different parts of the country. Such incidents shows the non existence of Government machinery in those areas which can effectively cater to the nutrition requirement of the poor and deprived sections of the Society. The Committee recommends that it is the bounden duty of the Government to ensure that not a single child is dying due to malnourishment especially in view of the facilities being provided through AWCs  under ICDS. The Committee
strongly feels that the FNB needs to train maximum number of functionaries of AWCs so as to sensitize them about the preventive measures to be taken in malnutrition cases of children and mothers. The Committee would appreciate if FNB makes an effective beginning by targetting the functionaries of AWCs located in tribal belts.          (Para 17.6)
 
NATIONAL NUTRITION MISSION (NNM)
 
                        The Committee notes that not much progress has been achieved in the implementation of the scheme. The Committee notes that the objectives of the mission are realistic in nature and if implemented in its totality a healthy child population will be the result. The Committee emphasize that the Ministry should make the scheme functional so as to achieve the desired result of nutrition in a time bound manner.                                      (Para 17.10)
 
XVIII.             GENDER BUDGETING
 
                        The Committee recommends that being the nodal Ministry, the Ministry of WCD should ensure that Gender Budget Cells which are set up in the Ministries have become operational and also pursue this issue with the remaining Ministries.                                                                                                                                             (Para 18.4)
 
The Committee would like to be apprised about the implementation status of the aforesaid initiatives taken by the Ministry.                                      (Para 18.5)
 
                        Committee’s attention has been drawn by the details regarding scheme-wise provisions and physical targets benefiting women in the Budget of Ministry of Women and Child Development as given in the Performance Budget (2006-07). The Committee finds that all the schemes whether targeting children or women have been shown to be providing 100% benefit to women alone. The Committee does not dispute the fact that welfare ofthe child is ultimately the welfare of its mother.However, in view of the emerging concept of child budgeting, it cannot be claimed that flagship schemes like ICDS are benefiting cent
percent women.The Committee recommends that the allocation on programmes and schemes benefiting women may be delineated specifically. The Committee also recommends that the components of gender budgeting may be made more clear and included in the guidelines for gender budgeting.            (Para 18.6)

PREFACE
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development,
having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Hundred Seventy-
sixthReport of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No. 104) of the Ministry of Youth Affairs and
Sports for  the year 2006-2007.
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the Ministry of Youth
Affairs and Sports and also heard the Joint Secretary and other Officials of that Ministry on the said Demands for Grants
in its meeting held on 18th April, 2006.
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on 16th May, 2006.

REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION
1.1       The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports was set up as the Department of Sports in 1982 at the time of
organisation of the IX Asian Games in New Delhi.   Thereafter, during the celebration of the International Youth Year
in 1985, it was converted into the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports. It became a full-fledged Ministry on the 27 th
May, 2000.
1.2       The Youth i.e. those falling within the age group of 15-35 years constitutes nearly 40% of the total population of

176th Report of Committee on Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/176threport%20.htm[01-07-2016 15:28:47]
the country.   To optimally tap the constructive and creative energies of this most valuable human resource, the Ministry
of Youth affairs and Sports has taken a number of new initiatives since its inception.    The Ministry organises a large
number of programmes in the field of youth development, sports and physical education.
1.3       The Joint Secretary (Sports), while deposing before the Committee, highlighted the various activities undertaken
by the Ministry during the year 2005-2006. He informed the Committee that Nehru Yuva Kendra played a major role in
providing relief materials, organizations of camps, counselling and career guidance to Tsunami victims.  SAI hostel,
Port Blair acted as both the center for housing inmates and for giving relief to Tsunami victims.  Contribution made by
NYK in providing relief to the earthquake victims in Kashmir was also worth-mentioning. Another initiative taken by
the Ministry was identification of Sports Federations performing well for giving them additional Funds.
1.4       A mention was also made about the new initiatives planned for 2006-07. A new Scheme ‘Yuva Shakti Abhiyan’
was going to be launched in Panchayats in all the States. Similarly all the Youth organizations like NYKS, NSS, NCC,
Bharat Scouts and Guides are being involved in the campaign on HIV/AIDS. States are going to be involved more and
more in the monitoring of different schemes.  He also drew the attention of the Committee towards the commendable
performance of Indian players who won a total of 50 medals and retained 4
th position in Commonwealth Games held at
Melbourne, 2006. These achievements were made possible to a large extent by the financial assistance made available to
the Sports Federations by the Ministry and also providing the necessary facilities to the participating players.
II.         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The total outlay, both Plan and Non-Plan taken together provided to the Ministry for the year 2005-2006 was Rs.
506.99 crores which was reduced to Rs. 478.01 crores at RE stage.  The expenditure booked upto 20
th March 2006 was
approximately Rs. 413 crores which means the Ministry was supposed to spend  Rs. 93 crores in remaining 11 days of
last financial year. The allocation for 2006-2007 is Rs. 669.00 crores (Plan Rs. 600.00 crores and Non Plan Rs. 69.00
crores). The Ministry informed thatagainst a projected demand of Rs. 929.29 crores under Plan for the year 2006-2007 a
provision of only Rs 600.00 crores has been made.   The projections were made, taking into consideration, higher
requirements for a number of ongoing and proposed schemes to be implemented by the Ministry during 2006-2007.
2.2       The Ministry informed that the cut made in the actual allocation from the proposed allocation would definitely
hamper proper implementation and ultimately have a negative impact on performance of the following schemes:
(Rs. in crores)
 Proposed Actual Allocation
SAI 173 150
Creation of Sports infrastructure 90 27
Commonwealth Games 200 150
Training of Indian Athletes 75                      --
            Not only this, proposed expansion of NYKS to 123 uncovered districts and promotion of Rural Sports Club
movement in the Villages would also be adversely affected due to the cut in the proposed demand of the Ministry.
Activities proposed to be initiated under the Action Plan for Youth to combat HIV/AIDS epidemic in the country were
also going to be restricted. The Committee notes that no allocation has been made for Training of Indian Athletes
against its proposed allocation for Rs. 75 crores. Such sweeping cut may have some concrete reason. The Committee
presumes that the Ministry have some contingency plans to arrange the finance for the Training of Indian Athletes for
the forthcoming Asian, Commonwealth Games and other International events. The Committee would like to be apprised
of such plans/scheme.
2.3       The Committee is aware that under the Constitution, Sports being a State subject, State
Governments/autonomous organisations/NGOs have to play a very active role in the implementation of the different
Youth and Sports related schemes.  The Committee observes that Tenth Plan Outlay of Rs. 1825.00 crore is more than

VI.       NATIONAL DISCIPLINE SCHEME
6.1       The National Discipline Scheme was originally started in 1954 by the Ministry of Rehabilitation, which was
later transferred to Ministry of Education and Social Welfare in 1958. Consequent upon the recommendations of Dr.
Kunzru Committee in 1963, introducing discipline programme at school stage, the integrated scheme called “National
Fitness Corps” (NFC) was evolved.  The Scheme was transferred to the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports (Now
Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports) in eighties when a separate Department was formed.
6.2       On the basis of the recommendations of Dr. Kunzru Committee, the decision to transfer NDS Instructors to
various State Governments was taken in consultation with the State Education Secretaries.  In the year 1969, the Central
Cabinet took a decision that the employees under the NFC would be transferred to the services of the State Governments
on the condition that the Central Government would reimburse their pay and allowances so long as they remained on the
strength of the State Governments. The Committee was informed that 6145 NDS Instructors were transferred to various
State Governments after decentralization of NDS scheme.
6.3       Though physically the NDS Instructors were absorbed in the services of the State Governments, the Central
Government was committed to bear the liability of their pay and allowances and this system has been continuing since
seventies. Due to inadequate budgetary provisions, the Central Government has never been able to bear its liability to
the fullest extent and thereby the accumulated liability continued to grow to unmanageable level. The Committee was
informed that the total liability towards pays and allowances for States of M.P., Punjab, Haryana, H.P., Rajasthan,
Kerala and Maharashtra from which information has been received is to the tune of Rs. 184.21 crores. Information from
remaining ten States is yet to be received. The total projected liability in respect of all the States is to the tune of Rs. 300
crore. A budget support would be required on that account.          
6.4       The Committee regrets that repeated reminders from the Department to some States have not evinced any
response and the issue of committed liabilities remains un-resolved for years together. The Committee feels that this
situation of uncertainty should come to a halt. A time has come when the Ministry should fix a final deadline for such
States to avoid this never-ending chaotic scenario. The Ministry should settle the issue once for all after paying the
liabilities to those States who have furnished the information. The States who do not respond may have to forgo their
claims. The Committee hopes that the Ministry would plan the whole process to ensure settlement of committed
liabilities within this financial year itself. The Committee would also like the Ministry to appeal to the States to avail
this opportunity and expedite their claims without further loss of time.

11.5     Traditional/indigenous games have been the bane of Indian sports. Promotion of these sports particularly in our

through advertisement to such events.         (Para 11.9)
XII.     PROMOTION OF SPORTS AMONG DISABLED
                        Only a token provision was made for the scheme in 2003-04, 2004-05 and 2005-06 as the scheme had not
been formulated.   The Committee has been given to understand that the scheme is likely to be included in the umbrella
scheme related to events.   Accordingly, no provision has been made in 2006-07.  The Committee takes strong
exception to this kind of approach.   This clearly indicates that the Ministry is not serious about the necessity of
providing any kind of incentives to the disadvantaged segment of our
society.                                                                        (Para 12.1)
XIII.   SPORTS INFRASTRUCTURE SCHEME

176th Report of Committee on Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/176threport%20.htm[01-07-2016 15:28:47]
                        The Committee is not happy with this turn of events.   The Committee would like to draw the attention of
the Ministry towards its earlier recommendation about the non-advisability of transfer of such a vital scheme essential
for developing the sports potential of our youth.  The Committee reiterates that instead of transferring the scheme to the
State sector, Ministry should focus more on the monitoring and effective implementation thereof. The Committee would
like the Ministry to continue funding for rural sports infrastructure development to patronize the rural sports
under its direct supervision.
XIV.    SCHEME FOR  DOPE TEST
                        The Committee is constrained to note that at present, SAI has only 38 Sports Scientists including medical
doctors.  This strength of scientific personnel is not enough to provide optimum scientific support to the sports needs in
the country. Sports-related scientific research and development in India has not been able to keep pace with
international developments in various fields like Physiology, Psychology, Bio-mechanics etc. Greater attention is
required to be given to research and development of sports science, in case India has to excel in sports at international
level.      (Para 14.3)
                        The Committee is aware of the recent doping incidents during international sports events. It is understood
that out of 11 athletes 9 were found to be positive. This has become a recurring feature during the international
championships and during every international event the country’s prestige is thus put at stake. Perhaps our sports
administration have failed to make the players aware of the dire consequences if they are tested positive.  These
performance enhancing drugs have an adverse affect on their health and could even ruin them professionally. With the
advent of  technology dope testing methods have also faced new challenges. Undoubtedly it is a constant battle with
technology. Test methods have become more and more sophisticated. To generate awareness amongst the players
education is the best cure.  The Committee feels that though the Ministry claims that overall the doping instances
have decreased from 4% to 2-½% but the recent instances put a shadow on such claims. The Committee hopes
that the Ministry would endeavour to achieve all the international standards of dope testing towards fighting the
malice of doping which degrades the prestige of the nation.                                     (Para 14.5)
 
XV.      GRANTS TO NATIONAL SPORTS FEDERATIONS
                        Undoubtedly the existing guidelines/byelaws do not have provision to recover the dues from the
federations but this issue of prolonged non-payment needs to be addressed with some sort of authority. The Ministry
should, therefore, revise its guidelines by either adding a clause for derecognition  of defaulting NSF or authorising SAI
to recover the dues from the NSF. A beginning should be made by recovery of outstanding electricity and water charges
from such federations.                     (Para 15.3)
XVI.    SCHEME RELATING TO ‘HIV/AIDS’
                        The Committee is happy to note the introduction of the scheme aimed at achieving victory over AIDS in
India.  The Committee feels that proper strategy should be developed to achieve the objectives of the scheme. 
Adolescent/youth clubs and youth information centers  require proper back up of counseling and resource materials. 
The Committee underlines the need for establishment of linkages amongst all the field organizations with health
facilities and VCTCs for service access. The Committee would like the Ministry to pursue the Planning Commission
to seek in principle approval in respect of the scheme.                                                                                   (Para 16.3)
XVII.      COMMONWEALTH GAMES, 2010
                        The Committee recommends that the concerned agencies should be asked to expedite its planning and
projections so that the annual break-up of funds required during next four years could be worked out.  The special plan
of action prepared in respect of imparting training to athletes should be finalized at the earliest.  Committee would like
to be apprised about the evaluation of performance of Indian athletes in the Commonwealth Games, 2006.     (Para 17.4)

REPORT
 
1.         The Central Institute of English and Foreign Languages University Bill, 2006 was introduced on the 20th March,
2006, in the Rajya Sabha and was referred to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human
Resource Development on 27th March, 2006 for examination and report. 
 
2.         The Central Institute of English and Foreign Languages is currently functioning at Hyderabad offering courses
for the teaching/ study of English and major foreign languages.  It is a society registered under the Hyderabad Societies
Registration Act, 1950. In July 1973, it was conferred deemed university status under section 3 of the University Gants
Commission Act, 1956.
 
3.         This Bill seeks to accord the Central Institute of English and Foreign Languages at Hyderabad a Central
University status and dissolve the Institute as a society. 
 
4.         Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the Bill justifies the need for converting this institute into a
Central University in the following manner: “With the advent of globalization and opening of world economies, the
mobility of people of all walks of life, across international boundaries, had phenomenally increased during the recent
years, resulting into added pressure on the institutions offering foreign language courses world over.   The
responsibilities of the Central Institute of English and Foreign Languages, Hyderabad have also increased manifold on
this count and it would require greater autonomy for discharging its added responsibilities.   At the same time, it needs to
be made more accountable and transparent in its functioning.  Both these requirements, may be met by conferring on it
the status of a full-fledged Central University”.
 
5.         During the course of deliberations on the Bill, apprehensions were voiced by some members of the Committee
that there appeared to be unjustified haste in according the central university status to this Institute. It was pointed our
that there may be any number of more reputed and better performing educational institutions in the country, more
deserving to get central status than this Institute.  These members felt that the objective could be better achieved by
strengthening/empowering the Departments of Foreign Languages in the existing institutions/universities.   Doubts were
raised that the proposed university might also go the same way as the Mahatma Gandhi Hindi Vishvavidyalaya has gone,
where even after a decade of its creation, it remains virtually a non-starter.
 
6.         The Committee is surprised to note that instead of there being any demand from any quarter/stakeholder for
making the Institute a Central University, this idea was mooted by the Central Government.  Not only this, no formal
inspection of the Institute- its academic and other infrastructural facilities has been carried out so far.
 
7.         The Committee sought clarifications on a number of issues connected with the functioning of the Institute and its
present status from the Department of Secondary and Higher Education.  Representatives of the Department also
appeared before the Committee and replied to various queries raised by the members. With the advent of globalization,
manifold increase in the responsibilities of the Institute, resultant need for expansion and diversification of its activities
and greater autonomy emerged as the main factors on which Committee held extensive discussions.  
 
8.         As regards the increased responsibility, the facts made available to the Committee indicated otherwise.  The
Committee found that there were only 300 regular students pursuing M.A., M. Phil & Ph.d from five Schools of studies
and 700 students were enrolled for different courses through distance education mode.  Besides that, the Institute was

177th Report of Committee on Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/177threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:28:47]
also offering Part time 
Certificate/diploma/advanced diploma courses to about 650 students.  The Committee was given to understand that the
two regional Campuses of the Institute at Shillong and Lucknow were fully functional.  However, the Committee found
that although both the Campuses were set up in 1970s, they did not have their own buildings for academic,
administrative and hostel purposes.  The Committee also noted that large number of faculty positions were lying vacant-
44 at the main campus and 4 at the Lucknow campus. 
 
9.         The Committee was informed that over the years, the Institute had “grown in stature and had earned recognition
as a centre of excellence” in the study of English and major foreign languages.  The Department could, however, not
provide specific data/information, which could support this claim and provide an idea about the past performance of the
Institute.  Specific information indicating placement of the students passing out of the Institute also could not be made
available to the Committee by the Department, reason being that no formal study in this regard has been conducted so
far.   
10.       As regards the autonomy of the Institute, the Department argued that the CIEFL presently being a registered
society and an institution declared to be a deemed university under Section 3 of the UGC Act, was “susceptible to
erosion by the various authorities like Registrar of Societies, UGC and the Ministry of HRD.  Presently, the Institute had
to have prior approval of the UGC for starting any course, etc.  The Department contended that the Institute was
constrained tremendously by the procedures and guidelines laid down by the UGC.  The Bill, therefore, sought to
remove representation of the UGC from any authority of the proposed university and the VC will be appointed by the
President of India in his capacity as its Visitor.  The Department contended that the granting of central university status
would bring in systemic structural changes in the Institute with larger administrative and academic autonomy and
complete freedom from governmental control.
 
11.       The Committee then inquired about any specific case where the Institute could not take decision based on the
principles of autonomy.  The Committee further sought to know the structural bottlenecks that might have prevented
proper development of the Institute.  To this, the Department replied that any proceeding of the Institute may be annulled
by the Central Government, if it is not deemed to be in conformity with the rules and bye-laws of the Society.  It was,
however, argued that once the Institute was accorded the status of a central university, its autonomy would be
safeguarded in terms of the statutory provisions of the Act, where the Central Government or the UGC will not have any
say. 
 
12.       The Committee found these arguments/justifications given by the Department quite unconvincing. The
contention of the Department clearly implies that within UGC framework, there is no scope for autonomy and that UGC
works as road-block to development of educational institutions.  It further implies that the real autonomy and
development of an educational institution is possible only if it were a Central university.  The question arises: are the
State universities like Bombay University, Kolkata University and others are functioning without autonomy and
therefore, are not progressing?  The Committee finds this argument not only bizarre but also fraught with grave
implications.  It also raises question about the existing framework as well as functioning of the UGC.  It also underlines
the need for revisiting the whole concept/system of ‘deemed university’ because CIEFL is said to be ailing mainly due to
the UGC and the deemed university status and therefore, it needed no less than Central university status.          
 
13.       The Committee, despite all the questions and reservations on the aspects mentioned in preceding paragraphs,
would like to emphasize that it is not against empowering and strengthening an educational institution financially and
otherwise.  The Committee is aware of the importance of English and other foreign languages in the emerging scenario
at the global level.  India, today has become a force to reckon with in areas like science, information and communication
technology, medicine, space, nuclear energy, etc.  Apart from their/talent this can be upto a large extent attributed to the
compatibility of our young boys and girls with English and other languages.   In principle, therefore, the Committee
agrees with the strengthening of any institution promoting teaching and learning of English and foreign languages. 
Therefore, the Committee after expressing these sentiments suggests following amendments in the Bill:-
 
 Clause 1 (1)
14.       The Committee notes that the Act is named “The Central Institute of English and Foreign Languages University
Act, 2006”.  The Committee, however, feels that the use of words ‘institute’ and ‘university’ together should be
avoided.  Instead it would be more appropriate to call the proposed Act in Clause 1(1) as “The English and Foreign

177th Report of Committee on Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/177threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:28:47]
Languages University Act, 2006”.
 
Clause 3(1)
15.       In view of its recommendations for clause 1(1), the Committee proposes that the name of the proposed University
be named “English and Foreign Languages University”.
 
Clause 6(viii)
16.       Clause 6 relates to Powers of the University.  As per clause 6 (viii) the University shall have the power to appoint
persons working in any other University or organization as teachers of the University for a specified period.
 
17.       The Committee is of the considered opinion that the word “organization” in this clause leaves enough scope for
including extraneous agencies/bodies as well. The Department clarified that the word ‘organization’ generally meant “a
teaching or a research institution, other than a university”.  The Committee feels that it needs to specified.  It therefore,
recommends that the word ‘organisation’ may be substituted by the words ‘educational institution’ so as to remove any
ambiguity about the nature of the organization.
 
Clause 30(1)(i) 
18.       Clause 30 deals with power to make Ordinances. The Committee finds that this sub-clause provides for making
special arrangements “for residence, discipline and teaching of women students.”  The Committee is of the considered
opinion that while this is valid in terms of  residence and specific courses for women students, the word “discipline”  in
this clause appears to be unnecessary and discriminatory.  Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the words
‘discipline and’ be deleted from line 12 of clause 30 (1) (i) of the Bill.
 
Clause 30(1)(j)
19.       This Clause provides for cooperation and collaboration by the proposed University apart from other universities
with “other agencies”. The Committee feels that there is a possibility of considering agencies, which are private and
might be for profit.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the words ‘not for profit’ may be added before the word
‘agencies’ in page 10, line 15 of Clause 30 (1) (j).
 
 Clause 35(3)  
20.       Clause 35 pertains to conditions of service of employees. According to sub-clause (3) of this Clause, the decision
of the Tribunal of Arbitration shall be final and no suit shall lie in any civil court in respect of the matters decided by it. 
This sub-clause gives an impression that the employees were debarred from all other judicial remedies against the
decision of the Tribunal.  The Committee is aware that no Act can debar the remedies available under Articles 226 and
32 of the Constitution.  The Bill also doesn’t intend to do this.  The Committee, however, recommends that the following
Explanation may be added in the said sub-clause for removing the erroneous impression in this regard.
             “This does not preclude the employees from availing the remedies provided for under Articles 226 & 32 of the
Constitution.”
 
Clause 39
21.       This Clause provides for the final authority in respect of any question regarding election or appointment of a
member of any authority or other body of the University.  The Committee notes that the Bill nowhere mentions about an
elected membership of an authority of the University.  The Committee is of considered opinion that ideally the
composition/membership of these bodies should have been provided in the Statute itself as was done in the case of
Allahabad University. In view of the fact that the composition of authorities of the university would be subsequently
decided by the university bodies, the Committee wishes to emphasise the need for having elected elements in all the
bodies/authority of the university.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that suitable mention for the purpose be
made in the Bill at appropriate places.  The Committee further recommends that an enabling provision must be provided
in the Act itself to ensure democratization in true spirit.
Clause 46
22.       Clause 46 pertains to Transitional Provisions. The Committee is of the considered opinion that since the first
officers and authorities of the university is to be appointed or nominated by the Central Government, their term of offices
as provided in transitional provisions should not be long enough. The Committee notes that in some cases it is five years
and in others it is three years.  It, therefore, recommends that the term of office of the first Chancellor, the first Vice-

Chancellor as well as other officers and bodies provided in various sub-clauses of Clause 46 on page 13 should be
reduced from five and three years to three and two years respectively.     
 
THE SCHEDULE
 
Clause 6 and 7 (b), (c) and (d) of the Statutes
23.       The Committee notes that these provision of the Statute provided in the Schedule mention about College
Development Council but this body is not amongst the authorities of the university.  The Department clarified that it was
mentioned ‘erroneously’.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that name of this body be deleted from the above
clauses.
 
Clause 17 of the Statutes
24.       The Committee notes that in case of the ‘Finance Committee’, while its composition has been given, there is no
representation from the University Court.  The Committee opines that University Court being the largest body should
have representation in the Finance Committee. The Committee, therefore, recommends that  a new sub-clause “atleast
one person to be nominated by the Court” may be added immediately after line 11 of Clause 17 of the Statutes on page
22 of the Bill.
 
Clause 37 of Statutes
25.       The Committee is of considered opinion that the Act must provide for elected representation of students, teachers
and non-teaching staff in all authoritative bodies of the University and ensure their right to form associations.  However,
the Committee found no such provision for students.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the words ‘two
elected representatives of students” should find place in the constitution of the Student Council and Clause 37 be
redrafted accordingly.
 
26.       The Committee adopts the remaining clauses of the Bill without any amendments.
27.       The enacting formula and the title are adopted with consequential changes.
28.       The Committee recommends that the Bill may be passed after incorporating the amendment additions suggested
by it. 
29.       The Committee would like the Department to submit a note with reasons on the recommendations/suggestions,
which could not be incorporated in the Bill.
 
*****
OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
 
Clause 1 (1)
The Committee, however, feels that the use of words ‘institute’ and ‘university’ together should be avoided.  Instead it
would be more appropriate to call the proposed Act in Clause 1(1) as “The English and Foreign Languages University
Act, 2006”.                                          (para 14)
 
Clause 3(1)
            In view of its recommendations for clause 1(1), the Committee proposes that the name of the proposed University
