REPORT
 
I.          INTRODUCTION
 

183rd Report of Human Resourse Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/183rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:28:50]
1.1       The Report of the Committee focuses on certain vital issues linked directly or indirectly with the functioning of
Kendriya Vidyalayas (KVs).  Broadly speaking, these areas are: efficacy of existing norms for opening of Kendriya
Vidyalayas, problem of Project Vidyalayas, present status of KV buildings – both sanctioned and functional; existing
mechanism for construction/maintenance of KV buildings; problem relating to admissions; recruitment procedure for
KV Teachers; vacancy position; and grievances redressal mechanism and others.
 
II.        NORMS FOR OPENING OF KENDRIYA VIDYALAYAS
 
2.1       Opening of Kendriya Vidyalayas is based on specific norms prescribed for this purpose by the Government. 
One of those was the provision of 15 acres of land to be provided free of cost by the sponsoring agencies.  The
Committee was informed that this criterion had now been drastically reduced to 4.00 acres in a metropolitan city; a
contiguous plot fairly leveled measuring 6.00 acres in hilly terrain; 8.00 acres in urban area; and 10.00 acres in
rural/semi urban area.  The Committee appreciates that in view of the ever-increasing shortage of land in the present
scenario, lowering the land requirement is the need of the hour.  However, the Committee would like to emphasize that
there should be no deviation from the need to demarcate 40% as building area and 60% as play field of the 4.00 acres
provided in a metropolitan city.
 
2.2       The Committee came to know that out of 931 KVs in the country, there are 38 KVs where land had not been
provided by the sponsoring agencies even after several years, which in some cases is more than 20 to 25 years.    In the
case of as many as 27 KVs, sponsoring agencies were the Armed Forces.  The Committee notes that with the exception
of two KVs opened in the year, 2005-06, rest were opened between 1977-78 to 1997-98.  In the remaining 11 KVs also
the situation was, more or less, the same; the earliest KV was opened in 1973-74. Details of such KVs reveal a very
discouraging picture.  The Committee hopes that with the revision of land norms, situation would improve.  The
Committee would like the Department of Secondary and Higher Education and KVS to vigorously pursue the allotment
of land with the concerned agencies and report the progress made in this regard to the Committee within three months.
2.3       Besides the provision of land, the other basic criteria for opening a new KV is the availability of 200 children
(500 in big cities) and minimum concentration of 1000 Central Government employees.  In all the cases, proposal has to
emanate from State Government/ Departments/ Ministries/Defence authorities/PSUs.  Committee’s attention has been
drawn towards the opening of 98 KVs in a short span of two years, i.e. during 2003-2004 and 2004-2005.  On a specific
query in this regard, the Committee was informed that only three KVs-- two in the project sector and another one in
Tehran were opened on specific requests/proposals. As regards the remaining 95, the Committee noticed a very
disturbing aspect.  In the normal course, demands for opening of new KVs come from various sources, ranging from the
elected representatives to the State/project authorities.  However, the Committee was informed that these 95 KVs were
opened without there being a formal proposal from the KV Sangathan.  These KVs were opened on communications
received from the then Chairman, KV Sangathan at different points of time.  Opening of these KVs was apparently
justified by the availability of surplus teachers and need for utilizing their services. The Committee was given to
understand that ex-post-facto approval was proposed to be obtained from the Cabinet after the matter was discussed and
approved in EFC meeting.  That could, however, not be done.
2.4       The Committee takes a serious view of this development because the prescribed pre-sanction procedure for the
purpose was simply given a go by in these cases.  The Committee is perturbed to note that these 95 KVs were opened
without taking any prior approval/sanction.  Even the ex-post-facto approval could not be taken.  The Committee is not
happy with such an approach of short circuiting the established procedures.   In this case, in the absence of any formal
approval and there being no fund allocation specifically for these KVs., plan funds are utilized to fulfill the salary and
other requirement of staff members, of these KVs. This is not a healthy fiscal practice.
2.5       The Committee is of the view that the role of the Government should be to ensure that prescribed norms for
opening of new KVs were strictly adhered to.  Instead of giving priority to such districts where KVs are genuinely
required and where there are no KVs, setting up such schools arbitrarily is certainly deplorable. 
2.6       As per the information made available to the Committee, out of such 95 KVs, 13 KVs are yet to be functional. 
The Committee finds that the status of remaining 82 KVs cannot be considered as fully functional. The Committee fails
to understand the basis of there being surplus teachers and their adjustment in these 95 KVs.  Details given by the
Department indicate that out of 36 sanctioned posts of PGT, only 29 were in position; and there were 55 vacancies in
the sanctioned posts of TGT.  What is more disturbing is that, only 5 KVs had PGTs.  On a specific query in this regard,
the Committee was informed that rationale of surplus teachers was based on sanctioned posts.  However, in view of the
fact that number of posts filled up being less than the sanctioned posts, the Committee finds this justification untenable. 

183rd Report of Human Resourse Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/183rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:28:50]
The Committee views it with serious concern and deplores such adhocism.
2.7       Details about schools made available to the Committee clearly indicate that enrolment status in some of the
Vidyalayas was far from satisfactory.  The Committee would like to emphasize that the Department ought to have been
more concerned about the present status of these schools; availability of required teachers and infrastructure; and also
about the number of students enrolled. It recommends that the remedial steps be taken urgently to remove all the
shortcomings.  The Committee emphasizes the need to review these cases expeditiously.  In some cases even there is no
land allotted to the school; how the construction work will start.  The Committee hopes that the Department must be
making efforts on their own in this regard.  The Committee would like the Department to take up the matter at the
highest level to sort out the problem and submit a report to it within three months.
III.       PROJECT VIDYALAYAS
3.1       Committee’s attention was drawn towards the closure of a large number of project vidyalayas due to failure of
the sponsoring agencies in providing the required funds.  The Committee reiterates that the Department/and KVS,
besides approaching the project authorities for re-opening of closed vidyalayas. Those Project Vidyalayas which could
not be revived may be taken over by the Government and run as normal KVs.            
3.2       The Committee notes that there are 129 project sector KVs functioning at present.  Outstanding dues amounting
to Rs. 16.08 crores are to be paid by the sponsoring agencies.  These dues may be against both closed as well as running
project sector vidyalayas. The Committee understands that the Ministry is pursuing with the concerned agencies for
payment of dues/pending against them.  However, these efforts seem to have failed, as only three PSUs have responded
and these too have expressed their inability in liquidating their dues.  The Committee finds the situation quite
discouraging.  The Committee is of the view that this matter needs to be taken up at the highest level.  There is also a
need for evolving a mechanism for release of funds by project authorities in advance on yearly/half yearly basis.  Only
then, this problem is likely to be solved, otherwise, this financial burden on KV Sangathan could continue to persist or
may even increase.
IV.       KENDRIYA VIDYALAYA BUILDINGS
4.1       The Committee has made detailed observations in its earlier reports on the abnormal delay in the construction of
KV buildings.  The Committee had asked for a status report on the constructions indicating the year when projects were
cleared, funds allocated, and when the construction started; reasons for delay as also the revised estimate.   The
Committee found that 38 KVs were yet to be allotted land; construction work was going on in 65 KVs and in 28 KVs,
school buildings were at the planning stage.  A close scrutiny of the ongoing construction works in 65 KVs revealed that
11 different construction agencies were involved in constructing KV Buildings, with CPWD having the largest number
of 24 projects.  These included KVs sanctioned from January 2002 to December, 2005.  In as many as 40 KVs, work
was either at the planning stage or progress was very slow due to one reason or the other. Situation in this regard was
really bad in the N.E. Region.  Out of the 14 KVs buildings under construction in this region, status of the following
projects is self revealing:-

4.2       The Committee is concerned about the position in this regard in the NE Region and feels that special efforts
should be made to complete all the projects in a fixed time period.
4.3       The Committee observes that considerable time is taken in the various stages of construction including the delay,
sometimes, at the planning stage.  What is more disturbing is that a large number of these KVs, had been opened way
back in eighties.  The Committee understands that after a protracted procedure involving States/sponsoring agencies and
overcoming a number of hurdles, these KVs must have reached the stage when finally construction project could be
sanctioned.  However, it appears that series of other procedural formalities are yet to be fulfilled, before the students
could pursue their studies in a proper environment having required infrastructure.
4.4       The Committee found that construction of another 28 school buildings was at the planning stage.  The
Committee finds that these KVs are scattered in different States of the country, having various sponsoring agencies. 
The Committee is concerned to note that out of these 28 KVs, no progress is expected in 19 KVs, due to various reasons
beyond the control of KV Sangathan.  In some cases construction agencies have not submitted even preliminary
drawings and estimates. They are reminded from time to time to expedite it.  In such a situation the Committee is
constrained to conclude that the construction status of these KVs would continue to remain at the same stage.  It appears
that no agency is responsible and KV Sangathan itself seems to have abdicated its responsibility/duty.
4.5       The Committee made an attempt to understand the factors primarily responsible for such a dismal situation with
a view to find a solution to break this impasse. The Committee summoned the DG, CPWD to discuss this problem as
also to understand his constraints.  The Committee was given to understand that KV Sangathan had a well laid-out
monitoring mechanism functioning at different levels.  The Committee, however, feels that this monitoring mechanism
has not proved to be very effective so far.  The Committee observes that an initiative has been taken to simplify
procedural formalities.  Henceforth, all sanction orders issued by KVS are to be forwarded to the concerned CPWD
authorities by name.  This would result in eliminating undue delay occurring at various levels in KVS as well as in
CPWD. 
4.6       Another problem noticed by the Committee was lack of co-ordination between the civil and electrical wings of
CPWD.  This also, the Committee found, leads to unnecessary delays in this regard.  The Committee is happy to note
that CPWD has since introduced a composite tendering system, whereunder electrical works inside the building are to
be made part of the main contract.
4.7       Committee’s attention was also drawn towards another problem being faced by CPWD with regard to time taken
in handing over of works by CPWD to KV authorities, which varied from state to state. The Committee is of the view
that there is an urgent need for a complete review of existing procedure at every stage---pre-construction, construction
and post-construction of KV buildings. Although some initiative has been taken by KVS and CPWD, the Committee
feels that this would not serve the purpose.  The Committee, therefore, would like to emphasize that all unnecessary
procedural formalities need to be done away with urgently.  A regular and effective monitoring mechanism involving all
the concerned authorities, the Committee feels needs to be put in place urgently.  The Committee would like to impress
upon KV Sangathan, CPWD and other construction agencies to complete all the pending construction works in a pre-
approved fixed schedule so that there is no further cost escalation as also there was no inconvenience caused to the
students and teachers.
V.        ADMISSION CRITERIA FOR STUDENTS
5.1       The Committee notes that the present admission policy results in overcrowding of certain KVs in different parts
of the country and it therefore, feels that this problem needs to be tackled without any further delay. In this regard,
Committee’s attention has been drawn by the Report of the Baldev Mahajan Committee given in 2000. One of the main
recommendations of the Mahajan Committee, the Committee was informed was that freezing of sections was neither
academically sound nor administratively feasible.   The Committee is also of the view that problem of increasing
number of students cannot be solved by the freezing of sections.  The Committee was also informed that the Board of
Governors of KV Sangathan was in agreement with the recommendation of the Baldev Mahajan Committee that the
Commissioner, KVS should have full powers of opening new sections and sanctioning additional staff.  The Board of
Governors had, accordingly, decided to recommend the same to the Government.   The Committee, however, finds that
as per the latest response received from the Department, the recommendations of the Baldev Mahajan Committee have
since been rejected in principle.   The Committee fails to comprehend the reasons for the change in the stand of the
Government.    The Committee would like to point out that number of students in a class/section being more than the
prescribed ratio, does affect the quality of education adversely; it needs to be avoided. The Committee is also in favour
of more and more students getting admitted to the KVs.   But overcrowding is certainly not conducive for focused
attention on students performance. KVs cannot be an exception to this. The Committee, therefore, feels that all efforts

183rd Report of Human Resourse Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/183rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:28:50]
need to be made to avoid overcrowding in KVs by opening additional sections with all the infrastructure wherever
needed.
VI.       VACANCY POSITION
6.1       In its 162 nd Report, the Committee had dealt with the problem of vacancies existing in different categories of
teaching staff in KVS.   The Committee found that the position remained very discouraging for a long time.   The
Committee notes that the selection of 1571 teachers in December 2003, in which certain procedural irregularities were
alleged to have been committed, continued to remain undecided till September 2006.  As a result, the appointment of the
teachers was withheld. In the meantime, a Satyam Committee was appointed to look into the issues and the selected
teachers were given conditional appointment on ad hoc basis, till the Committee submitted its report. Thus, the teachers
remained ad-hoc for more than three years. In the meanwhile, the Committee learnt that the report of the Satyam
Committee has since been submitted to the Government. The Committee notes with serious concern that the process of
selection of teachers that had started in February 2003, could not be completed till the time of the writing of this Report.
The Committee is at a loss to see that 1571 posts of teachers continued to remain vacant for several years.  The
Committee, while appreciating the move for giving the ad hoc appointment to the selected teachers pending the inquiry,
demands strict action against those found responsible for this fiasco.  The Committee calls upon the government to
consider the recommendations of the Satyam Committee for an early implementation so that future of those teachers is
decided without further delay.  The Committee is also aware that on an average about 7.5% ad hoc teachers have
contractual appointment.  The Committee would like to point out that teachers appointed for a short period would have
no motivation to give good results, for obvious reasons.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that ad-hoc
appointment should be to the barest minimum and the vacancies must be filled as soon as possible.   The Committee
also has serious reservations about the prolonged recruitment procedure that goes on for years.   There is an urgent need
for having a review of the same for streamlining, decentralising and eliminating the unnecessary procedural formalities.
6.2       The Committee in its 162
nd Report had strongly advocated the need for having a decentralised - zone-wise
recruitment for KV teachers, instead of the existing centralized procedure.  The most obvious reason for having a
decentralised system is to avoid the inherent problems faced in a centralized recruitment system by the KVS and the
candidates coming from different parts of such a vast country. The Committee is of the firm view that centralized
recruitment system is one of the main reasons for continuance of vacancies for long time affecting the academic
environment of the Vidyalayas. The Committee therefore, reiterates its recommendations of decentralization of the
recruitment process for selection of candidates at zonal level so that it becomes convenient to people of different regions
to participate in the process which otherwise may not be possible for them.  It would also ensure proper representation
of the candidates from different parts of the country, particularly from NE States and J&K.
VII.     GRIEVANCES REDRESSAL
7.1       The Committee observes that some initiative has been taken by the KV Sangathan for strengthening the
Grievance Redressal Machinery.  Senior officers are visiting Regional Offices to attend to the grievances of employees. 
Every day, specific hours have been fixed at the KV Sangathan’s Headquarters when aggrieved employees can meet the
concerned officers including the Commissioner without prior appointment. While appreciating the initiative taken by
KV Sangathan, the Committee would like to point out that there should also be a mechanism whereby a track of efficacy
of such an outlet available to employees can be constantly monitored. The Committee feels that the ground reality in
this regard seem to be somewhat different. Even public representatives such as MPs sometimes, fail to contact the
concerned officers because most of the time they are not available. Details regarding number of Grievances received and
those dealt with also do not indicate a significant improvement.
            The Committee has learnt that teachers union in KVS has been derecognized. The Committee would like to have
a brief note on the issue for its consideration.
VIII.        SURVEY OF KVs
8.1       The Committee is of the firm view that this is the right time for making a comprehensive assessment of KVs
spread over different parts of the country.  Reason behind making such a suggestion is that Kendriya Vidyalayas having
evolved into a reputed educational system since its inception in 1960s have seen many ups and downs.  Inspite of the
best efforts put forth by all concerned, quite a few constraints continue to persist at the ground level.  Committee’s
specific recommendation for conducting a detailed survey was meant to take corrective measures based on its findings
so that KV Sangathan is better equipped in attaining its goals. Committee’s recommendations/observations on the
various aspects of functioning of KVS are also meant for this purpose only.  
8.2       The Committee is unhappy to note that the spirit of Committee’s suggestions have not been given the importance
that they deserved by the Department/KV Sangathan. The Committee is afraid that development of an Information

INTRODUCTION 
1.1       Sports and games not only help in the al l-round development of human personality but are also 
healthy means for recreation and relaxation. They work as elixir both for human body and mind.  Sports
also provides opportunities for personal and social  interaction fostering goodwill and peace amongst
different peoples. It instills values such as healthy competition, respect for rules,  team spirit, instinct o f
turning failure into success, leading to excellence in human endeavour and at tainment.  It enhances
sense of achievement, national pride and patriotism amongst individuals. 
1.2       Successive Five Year Plans in India ha ve laid emphasis on sports and physical education. The
National College of Physical Edu cation and National Institute of S ports were established during the
Second Plan and sports f acilities like stadia, sw imming pools and open-air th eatres were constructed. 
The National Coaching Scheme wa s launched during the Third plan , while allocations for physical
education, games and sports were in creased during the Fourth Plan. Fi fth Plan witnessed the expansion
of the Coaching faci lities. The Sixth Plan la id emphasis on spotting a nd nurturing young talent in
different sports and also setting up of facilities at different pl aces for promising sportspersons.
Adventure sports were pr omoted during the Seventh Plan with emphasis laid on deve lopment of sports
infrastructure at the grassroot level that included laying of synthetic tracks, etc. The growth of sports got
an added impetus, when Governme nt created a separate Departme nt of Sports in 1984. A National
Sports policy was adopted in 1984 on the basis of which, a Plan of Action was formulated in 1992.
Many rural schools thereafter, were assisted in developing playgrounds and buying sports equipments.
Schemes like Special Area Games (SAG) and SPDA were launched with a view to locating and
nurturing children having potential for sports and to provide special training to sportspersons. Ninth Plan
also attempted to develop excellen ce in sports, provide modern & sc ientific facilities including sports
physiology and sports medicine etc.  Modern equipments relevant to the training needs of sportspersons
were also sought to be provided.  During this plan period, Department of Sports was converted into a
full-fledged Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports in May 2000.  
1.3       Despite these efforts made after Independence, performance of the country in international sports
has all along been very dismal in comparison to ma ny other countries.  It is  ironical that despite ou r
large size and huge population, we have not been able to achieve a respectable status in the world sports
scenario.  Instead, there has been  a continuous deterioration in In dia’s performance over the years, 
despite spending considerable amount of mone y and creatin g some basic infrastructure in the countr y.

Our supremacy in hockey during the early decades of last century notwith standing, we have had
generally cloudy landscape of Indian  Sports.  For example, India ha s won 7 Olympic Gold (six from
1928-1956 and two in 1964 and 1980) a Silver (1960) and two Bronze (1968 and 1972).  The only other
medals in Olympics won by India are: Bronze by K.D Jadha v (1952), Leander Paes (1996), K
Mallesweri (2000) and latest bei ng a Silver by R.V.S. Rathore ( 2004). Although the achievements of
India in the Commonwealth Games 2002 and Asian Games, 2002 have shown some improvement, yet
we have a long way to go in this regard.  After every debacle in international sports, there starts a blame
game amongst various agencies responsible for pr omoting sports and then forgetting everything
afterwards. Such a poor performance by a country of more than 100 million people should be a matter of
debate and close introspection for not only the sports  administrators, policy-makers, Sports Federations, 
sportspersons but also amongst the people at large.  There is a need to sensitize everyone in this respect. 
Previous Studies & Reports 
1.4       Attempts have been made earlier to study and analyze the reasons for India’s dismal performance 
in international sports. Several co mmittees have so far been cons tituted by the Government for this
purpose. These Committees, no doubt, have come out with useful and practical
suggestions/recommendations, but it appears that these reports have remained on paper only, as there is
no perceptible change in the sports  scenario in the country.  The Committee would like to especially
mention its 34 th and 77 th Reports on the subject pres ented to both Houses of Parliament in the years 
1995 and 1998 respectively.  Most of the problems and issues identified by this Committee in these
Reports still remain the same; and very few of it s recommendations have ac tually been implemented. 
The Committee believes that it is probably the general inertia and re sistance inherent within the system
against any attempt to bring a bout change of any kind. The Comm ittee deprecates this tendency,
particularly in a system that is concerned with promoti ng sports and games. It emphasizes the need fo r
bringing about reforms in  sports management and governance ur gently to make it more dynamic,
responsive, responsible and result-oriented.      
1.5       It is in this backdrop that the Depa rtment-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human 
Resource Development decided to take  up the subject of promotion of  sports once again for a special
study with a view to providing so me broad guideline s for improving sports scenario.  Wide-ranging 
discussions were held by the Committe e with all those connected with s ports, official and non-official.  
It also made on-the-spot vi sits of the existing sports facilities/in frastructure at differ ent places in the
country.  It also invite d written memoranda by issu ing public notices in news papers/television, which
provided lot of inputs for this study.  
Main Issues/Problems 
1.6       The main problems that came to the noti ce of the Committee, during its visits and deliberations
were: lack of sports culture and consciousness in th e country; non-integration of sports with education; 
multiplicity of agencies involved in promotion of sports with no coordination and accountability, lack of
proper cooperation amongst th e Centre, States, Federations/Associa tions and various private and public
sector undertakings; lack of infrastr ucture in the rural areas and its concentration in urban areas; under-
utilisation of available infrastructure and its poor maintena nce and upkeep; lack of good quality and
affordable sports equipments; absence of adequate incentives for the yout h to take up spor ts as a career;
need for effective schemes for  identification of talents; unfair selection procedure and last minute
finalisation of teams; lack of adequate exposure and specialised training/coaching of international
standard; non-availability of nutritious diet for sportspersons; inadequate participation of women in
sports, lack of com mitted administrators with love and knowledge about s ports; and that of modern
facilities for sports me dicines, psychology, etc.   And last but not least, inad equate allocation for sports
for a country of continental dimension is also one of the major factors for the existing state of affairs. 
  
Sports Organisations in India 
Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports 
1.7       A Department of Sports was set up in 1982 at the time of the 9 th Asian Games held in New 
Delhi.  It led to various develo pments such as establishment of S ports Authorit y of India and the
Page 6 of 41185th Report of Human Resourse Development
7/16/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/HRD/185threport.htm

formulation of National Youth Policy in 1984.  A fu rther impetus to these activities was given by the
creation of a separate Department of Youth Affairs and Sports in 1985, the International Youth Year.  In
the same year, initiative was also taken to form ulate the National Youth Policy which was adopted in
1988.  In the year 2000, this Department was upgraded as the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports.  The
Ministry works under the overall supervision and guidance of the a Union Minister of Youth Affairs and
Sports who is assisted by the Secretary of the Ministry.  Two officers in the rank of Joint Secretary head
the two Bureaus of the Mini stry, namely (i) Youth A ffairs and (ii) Sports.  There the Joint Secretary
(Sports), there are Director (Sports ) and Deputy Secretary (Sports).  There are four Under Secretaries
and other Officers and staff looking after the sports and physical education in the Ministry. 
  
Sports Authority of India 
  
1.8       Sports Authority of India, a society under Societies Registration Act, is an apex body responsible
for implementing a number of schemes for spotting and nurturing of sports talent, promotion of sports in
special areas, women’s sports, rural sports etc. in the country.  SAI is  also responsible for maintaining 
and utilizing stadia in Delhi. Its primary objective is to develop excellence in and broad basing of sports
at different levels.  It also coordi nates with NSFs in various discipli nes. It has six Regional Centres and
four Sub-Centres, some of which are yet to beco me operational. SAI, in addition has two academic 
wings - one for training coaches and research and development in sports  at the Netaji Subhash National
Institute of Sports, Patiala and th e other for Physical Education a nd Research & Development at the
Lakshmibai National College of Physical Education, Thiruvana nthapuram. SAI is managed by a
Governing Body under the Chairmanship  of the Union Minister, Youth Af fairs and Sports.  DG is the
Chief Executive Officer of the SAI.  SAI follows three fold approach for fulfilling its responsibilities:- 
Training of elite sportspersons;  
Talent scouting and training them (Junior, Sub-junior); and 
Adoption and excellence development (Senior level) 
  
Indian Olympic Association  
  
1.9       Indian Olympic Associat ion (IOA) supervises, as  well as coordinates, the functioning of the
State Olympic Associations and also guides the Na tional Sports Federations (NSF). Each NFS has its
affiliated State Sports Associations . Each State Sports Association, in turn, is supposed to have district
level associations, though at  present, very few such district le vel sports associa tions are functioning
effectively.  
National Sports Federations  
1.10     Individual disciplines are looked after by th e concerned National Sports  Federations recognized
by the Government. Financial assistance is give n to these Federations  for conducting national
championships and international tournaments in the country, organising co aching camps, procuring
equipments and sponsorships, enforcing the rules of the game, promoting th e game in general and
participation in international tour naments abroad. Federations are al so supposed to continuously scout
and nurture fresh talents. The sche me is implemented with the help of Sports Authority of India unde r
its relevant schemes.  
State Level Organisations  
1.11     Almost all State Government s have their Directorates of Sports . Besides, some States have also
set up Sports Authorities/Councils. Each State has a State Sports Association fo r each discipline and
they perform responsibilities simila r to those of NSFs. Every State is  also supposed to have a State

Generating sports consciousness 
2.1       One of the major factors leading to such a dismal scenario in sports  and games is the lack o f
sports culture in the country at every level.  There is a general lack of sports consciousness in our society
- the parents, teachers, policy-makers, administrators, peoples’ representatives, etc.  General perception 
is that sports is a digression fr om academics.  Sports and games, in fact, help children in thei r
development – physical and mental.   This can be attained by bringing about a change in the parental and 
societal attitude towards the sports. 
2.2       For this, the Committee feels, that all out effort will have to be made  by everyone of us at every
level in every walk of life;  gove rnment alone would not be able to do this.  A national campaign fo r
generating consciousness about spor ts will have to be launched.  NGOs and local elected bodies, the
Committee believes, could play an ef fective role in this regard.  Such  a campaign may start, of course,
with Government patronage at the grassroot level, say from Aanganwadi Centres, primary schools, local
clubs, Mahila Mandals of NYKS, Re sident Welfare Associations, Gram  Panchayats, Municipal Bodies,
etc.  
Integrating sports with educational curriculum 
2.3       Another important aspect of such a campa ign/effort would be to i nvolve the parents in a big
way.  This can be done only when the sports and phys ical education are integr ated with educational
curriculum making it a co mpulsory subject upto secondary leve l and incorporating sports in the
evaluation system of the students.  Lack of social recognition and econo mic security in sports, in fact,
dissuades students and parents from opting sports as  a career.  Stories about penury of some of ou r
former sportspersons deter them to take to sports.  The Committee feels, that unless the sports becomes a
premier category in job mark et - government and private, parents/students will  not be attracted to it at 
all.  Industry and private corporations alongwith the government will have to give adequate weightage to
sports and physical  education, while making recruitments fo r them.  Sportspers ons are known to have
been successful managers/employees due to obvious reasons.  
2.4       Participation in games and sports fosters qualities like sportsmanship, fairness, team spirit, etc. in
the children that makes them ideal citizens.  The Co mmittee finds that integrating sports with education
is an old demand; even this Committee it self had underlined this point in its 34 th report submitted in the 
year 1995.  The Committee is of the view that this needs to be done  urgently.  The Committee strongly
recommends that immediate effort s be made with the help of De partment of Secondary and Highe r
Education, CBSE, State Boards of Education and th e Ministry of Yout h Affairs and Sports.  If the need
be, the matter could be put before the CABE also. 
2.5       The Committee feels that sports and games should be made comp ulsory from the primary
school.  The watchwords, in fact, s hould be “Catch them young and take sports to the gr assroot level”. 
The Committee is of the view that  by making physical education an in tegral part of the educational
curriculum, broad-basing of sports would be done automati cally. A physical fitness programme shoul d
be drawn and implemente d in the schools and colleges across th e country to sensitize every child/youth
about the value of fitnes s and good health, so that they become more disciplined as well as productive
human beings.

III        INADEQUATE INCENTIVES AND AWARDS  
3.1       Incentives and awards, financial and othe rs, not only provide recogniti on and social security to
sportspersons, but also motivate others to take up sports with intere st and seriousness.  At present, there
are very few incentives/rewards even for our talented and outst anding sportspersons including the
former sportspersons. The Central Government, the State Governments and the Public Secto r
Undertakings do not offer good job opportunities for our sportspersons. Corporate sector also does not
have attractive offers for them.  It is shameful to find some of  our former sports person who have
brought laurels to the country, selli ng tea/chat, etc on roadside stalls  to earn their daily bread.  The
Committee feels that in order to pr omote sports in the country we ne ed to provide adequate incentives,
good job opportunities, economic security and social  recognition to our budding, as well as existing
sportspersons, so that the youth – our greatest asset is attracted to sports. 
            Incentives and their support to our fo rmer sportspersons including pension is highly inadequate. 
The Committee is of the opinion th at former sportspersons particul arly the aged ones need to be
supported in a big way for which government must put a proper system in place at the earliest. 
In Academics 
3.2       As has been said elsewhere, students, w ho have inclination for sports , are put to disadvantage in
academics, as they have to spar e more time for sports. This af fects their academic performance
adversely.  Sometimes they are unable to get admission in educational in stitutions.  As a result, children
desist from taking up sports.  The Committee feels that to make up for this loss, the students who
perform well in sports should be given some compensatory marks in academics. Similarly, certain
percentage of seats for admission in  professional and other institutions /colleges should be reserved fo r
students who have achieved a certain level in sports. 
In Government jobs 
3.3       As regards, employing sportspersons in government, semi-government and private bodies and 
institutions, existing position is quite disheartening. There are no sp ecific rules/guidelines for this
purpose and even where these exist, there is a gene ral lack of will to imp lement those guidelines (o f
employing sportspersons) by the Government. For ex ample, the existing guidelines of the Central
Government to employ 5 percent of group C&D employees from amongst the outstanding sportspersons
are not being observed by the various  Ministries and Departments.  It is disheartening to note that
neither the Ministry of Sports nor  the Ministry of Pers onnel had a ready database , Ministry-wise, to

Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry/D epartment-wise position ma y be obtained and given 
to the Committee within three m onths for its consideration.  The Committee disapproves the idea o f
making reservation for eminent sportspersons in onl y group C and D and not in A&B groups also.  It is
insensitive to employ eminent/international sportspersons as class three and class four employees.

V.                    NEED FOR ADEQUATE  INFRASTRUCTURE 
5.1       The issue of sports infrastructure receiv ed focused attention of th e Committee during this study.
Given the current level of high demand, we need to build-up a country-wide world class infrastructure to 
attract and groom the potential s portspersons.  The Committee could get an overview of infrastructure
and facilities – existing and upcomi ng during its on-the-spot visits to the various centres run by the SAI 
in different regions of the country.  The Committee did see not only the status of infrastructure, but also
interacted with eminent sportspersons, former sportspersons coaches, s ports scientists, sports
administrators, etc. officials of Sports Association/Federation, the Ministry and SAI on this issue.  Based
on the feedback received during its visits and deliberations, the Co mmittee found that the issue o f
infrastructure has three aspects: (i) need for new and modern infras tructure (ii) maintenance/upkeep o f
the existing infrastructure and facili ties; and (iii) optimum utilization of  the infrastructure. In fact the
issue of sports infrastructure in the country revolves around these basic parameters. 
Lack of modern infrastructure 
5.2       Availability of modern infrastructure for sports is vital both for ma ss participation as well as
development of excellence in sports.  The Co mmittee found that the infrastructure of international
standards was not available in India even to the elite sportspersons.  The Government of India has
sought to provide f acilities and infrastructure in various parts of the c ountry through its different
schemes, namely, centres of excell ence, special area games,  SAI training centres,  National sports talent
contest, Army Boys Sports Company, etc.  But their geographical spread is highly inadequate for a huge
country like India.  Even the existing infrastructu re at these places were poorly maintained and many o f
these required immediate replacemen t/upgradation.  Several of these did not have s ynthetic track fo r
athletics or the surface for hocke y or indoor multi-pur pose halls or swimmi ng pool.  The regional 
centres of the Sports Authority of India, which are the centres of excellence also were found to be
lacking in many regards as far as infrastructure is c oncerned.  This aspect has been dealt with separately
in Part-II of this Report.  
5.3       We need to prioritize the games/sports fo r this purpose in coming year s. To begin with, we may
patronize games such as kho-kho, kabaddi, football, volleyball, basketball, etc, that do not require much
infrastructure and expenditure. S econd priority can be the discip lines like boxing, wrestling, shooting
etc. in which our sportspersons have been gi ving good performance. Disc iplines like athletics,
swimming and gymnastics provide majority of medals in inte rnational events and participation of ou r

sportspersons in such events could enlarge the scope of our medal tally. Our best  athletes must be given
maximum exposure to these even ts at international level. Our infrastructure needs to be
expanded/strengthened on the basis of such priorities decided by ourselves. 
5.4       The Committee feels that Government should plan the development of sports in a phased manner
so that scarce resources earmarked for the pur pose are optimally utilized  and necessary basic

Lack of sports infrastructure in Rural Areas 
5.5       The Committee found that the existing sports  infrastructure, was mainly  confined to urban area
like big cities, industrial townships, defence cantonm ents, etc. that catered to the needs of the people
living in the big cities and urban ar eas.  The organized sports is, ther efore, generally limited to urban
areas.  As a result, around 80 per cent of the popul ation, which lives in the rural and tribal areas,
generally remains deprived of even the basic sports facilities. In fact , most of our efforts to develop
sports, the Committee notice d, have so far been concentrated in  urban areas only, and the rural areas
have remained altogether neglected. We have also not been able to provide even simple play fields in all
our schools and residential locations, not to speak of more. The children in rural areas use the dry fields
as playground and tree branch as hockey stick and cricket bat.  We ha ve, thus, failed to encourage the
rural children/youth to ensure mass participation in sports. There is no dearth of potential in rural areas;
what we require today is a concer ted approach for creating at least basic facilities a nd providing basic
sports equipments in the rural areas.  
5.6       With the decentralization of powers and resources to panchayats an d Nagarpalikas, Government
should not find it difficult to pr ovide sports facilities at Gram Panchayat, Block, smaller towns and
District levels.  Sports competitio ns and championships can also be held periodically at these levels. 
Such a broad- basing of sports facilities wo uld automatically help in scou ting talent at an early age
because it is easier to train the young ones.  Panchayat and Nagarpalikas should be mandated and
encouraged to take up this responsibility. 
5.7       As regards, infrastructure, a pyramidical approach needs to be adopted. First the base has to be
enlarged. Major initiatives will have to be taken in creating playgrounds in rural and tribal areas at Block
and District levels instead of building huge stadia in  big cities. It is equally  important that the rural
population is encouraged to participat e in sports and use th e facilities provided to them to acquire skills
of modern games and sports. We must  endeavour to ensure that millio ns of children were not deprived
of opportunity to participate in sports due to lack of infrastructure.  Victor s come out of participants
only. We need to convert our huge  youth manpower (around 40 per cent  of total population) as ou r
greatest strength. 
5.8       It has also been observed that State Governments want to organi ze national or State level
competitions in the State capitals only. Generally, th is results in the construction of huge stadia and
concentration of sporting activiti es at the State headquarters. Th e Committee feels that instead o f
organizing the games at the State capitals, many of th e games could be held in other places in the State,
so that the sports infrastructure is not concentrated in one particul ar area. This would bring about the
much-needed distribution of infrastructures all over the State. Thus, more a nd more people would have 
easy access to these infrastructures within their own State.

VI.       TRAINING OF SPORTSPERSONS 
Need for modern training 
6.1       During its interaction with sportspersons , the Committee found that one  of the major reasons fo r
India’s poor performance in sports  was the lack of modern and tim ely training to our sportspersons.
Sportspersons in India, the Committee was informe d, are given training ba rely a couple of months
before the commencement of the competitions. In c ountries like China and Japan, the teams are trained
all through the year. In Germ any, sportspersons are scie ntifically selected betw een 6 to 8 years of age.
Initial years are devoted to general training to develop their athleticism.  Later, they are assessed to find
out in which particular discipline they are likely to excel and are pr ovided specific training for a period
of 8 to 10 years before they start representing their country in vari ous international tournaments. The
training system in the country, the Committee feels, needs to be re-oriented in keeping with our growing 
demand and fast changing techniques with adequate scientific back- up.  All sports have become high-
tech today; not depending only on stamina and strength.  The new traini ng system will have to take all
such concern into notice. 
6.2       The Committee is of the opinion that training forms the core of  good performance. Champions
cannot be produced by training the sportspersons just  for few months before the actual competition. 
Sports training is a systematic process extending over a long period of time.  
Dietary Allowance 
6.3       Availability of nutriti ous diet and food is one of the basi c requirements of any sportsperson to
gain strength and stamina, without which, it is not possible to excel in sports. Sportspersons should get
the diet that has necessary calor ific requirements for different games and sports in which they
participate.  The Committee is happy to note that it has been decide d to increase the dietary amount in
the SAI Schemes of STC, SAG to Rs. 100 per day a nd Rs.150 for the inmates of the scheme of Centre
for Excellence.  The Committee, however, feels that in view of recent price hike of food items, even this
enhanced amount would not be sufficient for world-class sportspersons.    
6.4       The Committee is of the firm opinion that  the Government should still consider raising dietary
amount substantially so that players can get a rich  and nutritious diet. The amount of diet allowance
should be periodically reviewed in the light of price escalations from time to time.  It, therefore, needs to
be made to minimum Rs. 250/- per person/per day. The Committee would like the Government to devise
a system of evaluating the nature and quality of diet required to be given to our sportspersons.

Lack of modern equipments 
6.5       Availability of sports equipment is a nother important component of  training. Our sportspersons
have to suffer not only due to inad equate supply of equipments but al so delay in their availability on
account of various reasons. SAI has six Regional Ce ntres and five sub-centre s for preparing Indian

required to be imported, which is a time consuming process. The cust oms duty on such imports is also

competitions. Shooting has been worst affected due to these factors.  
6.6       The Committee recommends that Gove rnment should make effort s to arrange the latest
technology for manufacturing the equipments indi genously. The cost of s ports equipments, the
Committee was told are very high which makes them unaffordable.  Even those equipments
produced/manufactured in India beco me costly due to high excise dut y on those items.  Sports goods
industry in India has been demanding for reducti on of duties levied on goods produced indigenously. 
The Ministry of Finance, therefore, should be approached for rationalizing the excise and import duty on
sports equipments so that  not only quality of indige nous sports goods can be improved, their cost could
also be brought down upto an affordable level. 
  
VII.     PROBLEMS OF COACHING AND COACHES         
7.1       SAI presently has 1438 coaches as agai nst 1623 coaches in 1996. The shortfall of coaches was
due to death, retirement, superannuation, voluntary retirement, etc. The co aches are recruited by
advertising vacancies as per the cr iteria followed for selection of coaches by a Sele ction Committee as
provided in recruitment rule s. Ten per cent of the vacancies in Grade II coaches are filled by direct
recruitment of world championship and Olympic participants. Foreign coaches are also engaged on the
recommendation of the concerned National Sports Federation by a Committee constituted by the
Government. The Committee examines  the bio-data and previous ach ievements of foreign coaches an d
after due verification, recommends the names of identified /selected foreign coac hes to the Government
for approval. Foreign coaches have been recommended in the fields of Athletics, Football, Archery,
Table Tennis, Wrestling, Shooting, Volleyball and Badminton.  
7.2       On a query as to how the different kinds  of techniques were used by the coaches and whethe r
SAI provided any refresher course for them, DG, SAI informed the Committee that SAI was conducting
refresher courses and it made consis tent efforts to up-grade the skills  of the coaches. Coaches were also 
sent for training in institutions abroad. However, SA I was short of coaches as most of them were geared
to one or the other national camps . DG, SAI conceded that  there were 14 to 15 disciplines for which
Government was paying heavy amount  to the foreign coaches. Gove rnment was however committed to
optimally utilise their services and it has now been made mandatory th at foreign coaches will also hold
clinics for Indian coaches so that their skills were up-graded.  
Shortage of Coaches 
7.3       The Committee notes that about fifteen hundred coaches to cover the whole country is highly
inadequate. In the absence of any recruitment fo r coaches since 1992, the number of coaches has further
declined over years. The Committee feels that there is no dearth of coaching talent in our country.  Ou r
coaches, if given proper exposure and opportunities in terms of trai ning, can produce better results than
foreign coaches. There may have be en marginal improvement in our performance after engagement o f
foreign coaches but there have been  other areas of concer ns like language problem and increase in dope
cases. We need to depute our coach es for trainings at internationa l level. We can also improve the
standard of our coachi ng and ensure a better secured envi ronment for our coaching community by
providing healthy social security and better avenues of advancement.  This would not only enhance the
level of their coaching but also reduce our expenditure on fo reign coaches to some extent. The
Committee would like the government to urgently st art the recruitment proce ss for coaches in view o f
increased demand for the forthcoming Asian and Commonwealth Games. 
Transfer of Coaches 
7.4       The transfer of coaches has been one of  the most debatable issues  before the Committee. The

recommended for withdrawal of such  coaches from the DCCs in the St ates and it has since been done,

State List, States implem ent their own policies a nd programmes for promoting sports. The policy o f
posting SAI coaches with the States, therefore, w itnessed one or more of  the problems mentioned
above.  The Committee notes that  for these reasons, decision to withdraw coaches from District

Committee also feels that the SAI wa s not able to have an  effective control/monitoring of its coaches at

7.8       The Committee, after having seen the pe rformance/standards of our coaches, has come to the

at our academic centres. 
Working condition, etc. of coaches 
7.9       Performance of our coaches, the Committe e feels, depends upon many factors like their training,

Contract Coaches

Prioritisation of disciplines for Olympics 
9.10     Many developing countries have identified only a few games and concen trated their efforts on
the selected games only. The Committ ee notes that we participate in majority of events more as a
customary practice, irrespective of  our chances for medals in the international events. The result is
always poor and we start blami ng our sportspersons. The fault lies in our planning. We need to
concentrate on those sports in which India has shown potential and can do better. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that our participation in international events, particularly in Olympics, should be
restricted to those discip lines in which we have competence of  international level to bag medals. It

X.        SPORTS MANAGEMENT AND ADMINISTRATION 
10.1     Sports management and administration form s an integral part of sports promotion of any
country. Sports administrators he lp in shaping the policies and de vise suitable a nd strong delivery
mechanism for implementation of s ports policies and schemes. As pr ofessionals, they are supposed to
have the requisite vision and foresi ght to administer and effect necessary changes suited to the overall
interest of sports. They are expected to mana ge the operations of various sports schemes and
infrastructure throughout the country. In fact they n eed to evolve such a netw ork of management which
is sports-friendly and result-oriented. 
Sports Authority of India 
10.2     The Sports Authority of I ndia was basically created to look after the main tenance and utilisation
of stadia created/upgraded for th e Asian Games, 1982.  The main object ives of SAI are to promote and
broad base sports in the country; to development exce llence in sports at different levels; and to utilise
stadia in Delhi. SAI has a Genera l Body consisting of 43 Members with  Hon'ble Prime Minister as the
President, Hon'ble Union Minister for Youth Affairs and Sports as Vice-President and Secretary SAI as 
the Member Secretary. There is a Governing body consisting of 28 members with Union Sports Minister
as the Chairman, 8 eminent sports persons are represented in both th ese bodies. DG, SAI is assisted by
the Executive Directors and Regional Directors and other officials down the line. 
10.3     There are six Regional Centres located at Bhopal (Central Region), Northern Centre at
Chandigarh (being shifted to Sonepat), Western Ce ntre at Gandhinagar, East ern Centre at Kolkata,
North-Eastern Centre at Imphal and Southern Centre at Bangalore. SA I is also imparting education by 
awarding diplomas and degrees in the field of sports at NIS, Patiala and Bangalore. It also conducts the
national coaching camps for el ite sportspersons to participate in in ternational competitions. To achieve
its objectives, SAI stands and works to develop excellence for internati onal competitions in association
with National Sports Federations. 
10.4     The Committee finds that the Ministry with  its bureaucratic set up of Secretary, Joint Secretary,
Directors, etc. is busy in framing the schemes/ programmes, rules and re gulations on the basis o f
National Sports Policy 2001. There is an other tier of sports administrati on in Sports Authority of India
with Director-General, and Secret ary from All India Serv ices. There are two Ex ecutive Directors one 
dealing with Teams and th e other with Finance. Lo wer in the hierar chy are Regional Di rectors at five
Regional Centers and De puty Directors at Sub-Centers. The th ird kind of administrative set u p is the

Sports Federations/Associations deal ing with different disciplines of sports. While the first two setups
are directly answerable to Government, the Federations/Associations are autonomous bodies. 
10.5     The Committee was informed that the DG, Sports Authority of India was authorized to sanction
projects upto Rs 50 lakhs and works above Rs 3 lakh are done by CPWD, which require the concurrence
of the central government through DG, SAI. The Regional Directors are entitled to approve projects
costing below Rs 3 lakh. However dur ing its visit, the Committee gath ered that a number of projects
from Regional Centers were pending fo r approval either at SAI level or at the Ministry level. Regional

Headquarters. Even in administrative matters, th e problem remains same.  The system of delegated
authority appears to be missing, causing thereby inordinate delays in decision- making.  
10.6     Officers belonging to All I ndia services come to the SAI main ly as DG and Secretary for short
tenure. They being not necessarily from sports background take some time to get conversant with the
problems of sports and sportspersons .  Before they do so, they eith er go back or take up some othe r
assignments.  As a result, they are hardly in a position to make  any worthwhile and effective
contribution. Major problems, theref ore, remain unattended due to fre quent changes of key officials at
decision-making level. The Commit tee recommends that in the pres ent system of taking All India 
Service officers as DG a nd Secretary in Sports Au thority of India, there is need for inducing some
element of continuity in administrative, financial and other matters. For this, a post of Addl. DG must be
provided with distinct powers and authority in all matt ers, which should be an ex-cadre post to be fille d 
by the existing EDs.  Such a system will ensure th at Addl. DG will be s portsperson from within, not
liable to transfer. 
10.7     The Committee noted that the SAI’s Execu tive Directors were burdene d because there are only 
two posts.  As a result, they have  to look after several major disciplines. In such a scenario, the
important works remain unattended, which adversely affects the promotional aspects of sports.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends to increase the pos ts of EDs in SAI to have  a judicious distribution
of work.  
10.8     The Committee opines that present management and administrat ion is too complicated to effect
changes tuned to the requirements of  our sports. The old and traditiona l methods of administration in a
bureaucratic atmosphere has done mo re harm than good to our spor ts. It is high time to bring
professionalism in our approach and induct qualifi ed and experienced sports administrators/managers
for managing operations of our sports schemes and infrastruc ture throughout the country. Ou r
administrators have to be scientif ic, value based, progressive and recep tive to the changes. There is no
dearth of such professionals in our country. We need to decentralize our decision making process. 
10.9     The Committee endorses the view of a former  DG, SAI suggesting at least three years tenure fo r
the Secretary of Sports Ministry who could involve himself in the w hole gamut of sports administration
and feel free to take business like decisions. 
10.10   The Committee recommends that there could be a group of eminent sports persons including SAI
officials for final selection of t eams and in the monitoring of thei r performance. The Committee also
underlines the need for assigning of discipline wise responsibilities to  the sports managers in SAI fo r
ensuring a better coordination with Federations. This flexible approach  in administration would help in
overhauling the sports setup across the country. It is equally importa nt to empower the regional centers
of SAI by decentralizing the decision making process.  
10.11   The Committee observes that th e term of the General Body of SA I is for three years and the last
tenure of the General Body has expi red on 20.3.04.    Last informa tion received by the Committee was
that the reconstitution of General Body of SAI was in  process.   The Commi ttee is not happy with this
State of affairs.   Reasons for undue delay in the reconstitution of such an  important body which must
have been anticipated well in a dvance are not known  to the Committee.   The Committee would like to
be apprised about the latest position in this matter.   The Committee is also of  the opinion that a review
of existing procedure for constitu tion of General Body of SAI may be undertaken and corrective steps
initiated.

 XI.       WOMEN’S PARTICIPATION 
11.1     The Committee was informed that the S ports Authority of India has been implementing a
scheme of National Sports Festiv al for Women in which regular tournaments in 12 identified sports
disciplines are organized annuall y from Block level onwards. Th ese tournaments, exclusively fo r
women, are held to attract more a nd more women into sports activiti es at all levels. The scheme has
however not had the desired result as  there is not much enthusiastic participation, for want of adequate
publicity and incentives. The sche me, the Committee feels, deserv es wider publicity through radio,
Doordarshan and print media, in order to achieve the objectives of broad- basing the sports an d 
encouraging mass participation by women. There is a need to give good incentives in the form of cash
awards and medals so as to attract mass participation by women.  
11.2     The Committee was informed that all effo rts are made to attract greater number of women
trainees in various schemes impl emented by SAI for providing sports  training and exposure to improve
the level of their participation in the sports.  The Committee notes that during 2003-04, the percentage of 
female participation, in all the four SAI scheme s such as NSTC, SAG, STC & COX was 29.47% which
during 2004-05 slightly impr oved in comparision to last year. The women participation in All India
Rural Sports Tournament and North East S ports Festival during 2003-04 was 36.94% and 37.89% 
respectively. The Committee opines that at present women participation in th ese schemes is quite low
and needs to be enhanced to the optimum. 
            The Committee learnt that the Girls we re not getting time to use play  field particularly in certain
States.  As a result, they are not able to play/practice.  The Committee feels that such an attitude towards
our women sportsperson is deplorable.  It, therefore recommends that effo rts be made to ensure that thy
also get equal opportunity to use the existing infrastructure at all the places. 
11.3     Many parents like to send their daughters to play games but they are hesitant to do so because o f
security and safety reasons. The Co mmittee noticed that out of 18 spor ts hostels of SAI, there is only
one sports hostel for women and ther e is no exclusive SPDA hostel for girls. Therefore, the Committee
feels that, there is a need for proper planning to  develop sports amongst women, by opening more sports
hostels for them and adopting more girls’ sports schools. 
11.4     In our male dominated system, women’s part icipation in sports get neglected.  The Committee 
feels that Sports Associations/Fed erations must have a separate gr oup/unit exclusively for the women
and by the women.  Similarly, women coaches are also in state of neglect.  We must have more qualified
women coaches from amongst ex-sportswomen.   
XII.     DEVELOPMENT OF SPORTS SCIENCES 
12.1     The Committee found that th e scientific back-up to the devel opment of sports at most of the 
places was in a rudimentary stage and at others, it was virtually non-existent. Sports psychology also 
was not very much in vogue.  Sports psychology and sports sciences, in fact, were indispensable fo r
improving/testing physical as well as mental capabilities of the sportspe rsons.  In the present era of stif f
competitions, sports has turned into more of a psyc hological war. Today, the ga mes are won or lost just
by a fraction of seconds or millimeters. There is a very narrow margin between the winner and loser.
Role of psychologists and sports medical experts can, therefore,  do wonders in such a situation. A good
psychologist working with a medical e xpert can, in fact, influence, to a large extent, the outcome of the
game, as well as the performance of  sportspersons. The Committee noticed that the sports medicine was
also not being given any priority  in India. The Committee emphasize s that due attention and priority
must be given to these discipli nes by all concerned. Th e Committee recommends that the services o f
good sports physiologists, psychologists and sports medical experts be made ava ilable to our players all
the times at all the centres.  
12.2     Advance in technology has come into each and every sphere a nd sports is no exception to this.
We need to acce pt s ports as a science. S ports science s ystem in the countr y needs to be develo ped

XIII.    SCHEME FOR ANTI-DOPING 
13.1     The scheme for dope test is being im plemented by SAI through the ‘Dope Control Centre’
located at the Nehru Stadium, New Delhi.  The Committee during its visit to the Center found that it was
still in the process of being set up and efforts were on to obtain permanent accreditation of its laboratory
by the International Olympic Committee and Worl d Anti-Doping Agency (WADA).  The Committee 
found that the pace of work at the Dope Control Centre was slow that needs to be expedited.   
13.2     The Committee shares the concern of the countrymen on the increasing instances of ou r
sportspersons, particularly the weightlifters and the athletes testing positive for the banned drugs.  These
instances raise serious questions not only about the facilities for dope testing in the country but also
about the manner in which various sports agencies/authorities are ignoring such a serious problem,
which brings shame instead of fa me to the nation.  Dope tests ar e done every time before Indian
contingent leaves the country for participating in international s ports events, and surprisingly some
sportspersons fail the dope tests outside even after having been cleared in the country.    This means that
either our test facilities and procedures are faulty or  there is a possibility of  some sportspersons taking
banned drugs after being cleared in the country.  If the drug is taken after they have been cleared, the
sportspersons should also be held responsible for testing positiv e during the international events.  Apart
from individual sportsperson, their Coaches also needs to be made accountable and they need to be more
vigilant about this.   
13.3     What surprised the Committee most was that nobody seems to take the responsibility for ou r
sportspersons testing positive for dr ugs.  The Ministry and the SAI argue  that it was basically not their 
duty/responsibility to get the athletes dope tested because they are under the control of IOA and various
sports federations.  Federations have ready excuse about the high cost of these tests and the lack of latest
sophisticated facilities for this purpose in the country.  T hus, at the end of the day, nobody was ready to
own the responsibility for the bad name that such in cidents bring to the nation.  The Committee at the
same time wishes to appreciate the efforts of the IOA in getting some of our sp ortspersons cleared after
they tested positive.   
13.4     The Committee feels extrem ely unhappy about the continuing indifference shown by all sports
bodies – Ministry, SAI, IOA, Federa tions to such a serious malaise.  Involving many ag encies in this, 
the Committee feels, has only complicated the matter.  They appear to be passing the buck to each other
with no serious efforts being made by any of them to clean the mess that plagued our sports.   
13.5     The Committee recommends to augment the testing facilities and a dopting foolproof procedure
for dope testing.  We should evolve  a mechanism with least possibility  of tempering with the samples. 
The entire procedure should be strictly as per the norms laid by WADA  and the punishment has to be as
per the World Anti-Doping Code. The Ministry should make efforts fo r employing experts in the area 
for making the test results authentic.   
13.6     The Committee also emphasizes an urgent need for educating our at hletes, coaches and othe r
supporting personnel about the harmful effects of doping on their health as well as to the prestige of the
nation.

14.2     The Committee feels that there is a need to increase the e quipments and other facilities available

XV.      PUTTING SPORTS IN CONCURRENT LIST 
15.1     The Committee was gi ven to understand that ‘sports’ being a State subject the primary 
responsibility of developing sports in the country re sted with the State Governments and the respective
State Sports Councils. The Committe e notes that at present there is a plethora of agencies working in
different directions towards pr omotion of sports. These agencies are working without any
coordination/liaison amongs t themselves. Such approach towards sports has not yielded any tangible
results so far.   Instead it has resulted in utter confusion and wastage of scarce resources.  
15.2     The Committee appreciates the limitations  of Central Government  in fixing accountability
amongst multiple agencies in the backdrop of present constitutional arrangements regarding division o f
subjects under different lists. There is hardly any law or regulation de fining the roles of such agencies
and as such there is a lot of dupli cation of efforts. Sports being in  state list, the Central Government
lacks legislative powers required for strict enforcement of Government guidelines.   
15.3     Besides, the Committee during its delibera tions with some State governments found that sports
hardly was a priority for them mainly due to the se vere resource crunch with them.  In some of the
States (like Gujarat and Karnataka), resources spared for sports were not increasing or were going down
over the years.  In such a situation, Centre’s role and contribution has to increase manifold in promoting
sports at national level.  
15.4     The Committee also notes that while ‘Sports ’ figure in the ‘State Li st’ of the Constitution, 
‘Education’ figured in the ‘Concur rent List’. Both the activities viz Education and Sports are inter-
related; in fact they are two f acets of the same coin. The Commi ttee while underlining the need fo r
bringing sports under the ‘Concurrent  List’ wishes to emphasise that it should be done only with the
consent of the States.  While Sports in the country could be developed in an effective and coordinated
manner only with Center and States as equal partners.  
15.5     The Committee was informed that legislati on for including ‘Sports’ in the Concurrent List was 
introduced in the Rajya Sabha in 1988, which could not  be discussed in the Pa rliament. The Committee
was informed that in 1996 a meeting of representatives of all politi cal parties to discuss the subject
remained inconclusive. Again in 2005, the matter wa s placed before the conf erence of State Sports
Ministers.  Many of the participating representa tives of the State Governments reported that thei r
Governments had not firmed up their views on the subject. Written communi cation regarding views o f
some State Governments have been received while communication from some State Governments is still
awaited. The Committee recommends that the views of the State Gove rnments may be once again taken
before taking a decision in this regard. 
15.6     In view of the greater responsibility of  the Union for encouraging sports, the Committee
recommends that Union has to play a pro-active role with regard to bringing sports under the Concurrent
list.  States’ fears in this regard will have to be  removed to convince them ab out the utilit y of such a 
move by citing the example of education.  It wa s only after education was brought to the Concurrent
List, popular schemes like SSA and MDM could be sponsored by the Unio n at all India level.  All the
States are being benefite d immensely by these scheme s.  A legislation may al so be enacted to provide
for an effective coordinating mechanism in the spor ts arena without impairi ng the autonomy of various
agencies. Such legislations have greatly improved the spor ts scenario in countri es like USA, Germany,
Thailand, Sri Lanka and China.

-           Regarding under utilisation of funds by the LNCPE, the Committee was informed that it was due
to delay in the project approval for the swimmi ng pool. The Committee was a ssured that the swimming
pool would be completed by June 2005. The Committee notes that many of the projects envisaged in the
LNCPE master plan are yet to be implemented.  This may be done immediately.  It hopes that
swimming pool would have started by now. 
-           The Committee was informed by th e SAI that centralized purch asing for LNCPE was done to
maintain very stringent quality specifications for which global tenders were invited. 
-           The DG SAI submitted before the Co mmittee that the State Govern ment should chart out a plan
to utilize all the facilities available in LNCPE, Trivandrum. The Committee desires that steps be taken to 
propagate the schemes of LNCPE so  that the aspiring sportspersons  and students could utilize the
various facilities. 
-           The Committee suggested that LNCP E might start training coache s also.  The DG, SAI replie d
that NIC, Patiala was already suppl ying sufficient number of coaches.  There was no study made for the
requirement of additional coaches.  If there was any necessity of Coaches, SAI was willing to start a
course for training coaches in LNCPE. The Comm ittee recommends that LN CPE must be  assigned a
larger role and developed as another academic wing of  SAI to cater to all the South Indian States.  It
could be developed on the same pattern as that of NIC Patiala. 
-           At present advanced training facilities for athletes were not availabl e in Kerala.  The prominent
sportspersons who were given adva nced training in other parts of India were finding it difficult to
continue their practice when they co me back to Kerala.  That adversely affected the capabilities of the
sportspersons. A centre might be started to give advance training to selected athletes. 
-           The Committee feels that regarding the construction of synthetic track rate contract may be
invited instead of the present system of contract. 
-           In Kerala there were specific geogr aphic areas wherefrom a large number of sportspersons in
particular sport were comin g from.  Those areas ma y be identified and trainin g Centres ma y be started
