2.6       The Committee expresses its serious reservation on the trend of Utilisation of allocated funds during 2006-07. About
38 per cent of fund utilization during the last quarter of the financial year with 15 per cent to be spent during the last month,
i.e. March  goes against the prescribed norms of only 33 per cent utilization during the last quarter. The Committee would,
therefore, like to emphasise that every conceivable attempt should be made for strict compliance of financial norms.
 
2.7       The Committee   has been voicing its concern about the declining trend in both allocation and utilization of funds for
women welfare schemes. For 2006-07, also, inspite of enhanced allocation of Rs. 130.70 crore, expenditure reported upto 16
th
March, 2007 is only Rs. 91.40 crores. Not only this, the Committee notes that it was only in the last quarter that utilization
picked up as expenditure reported upto 31st December, 2006 was only Rs. 58.75 crore.  
 
2.8            Pendency of Utilisation Certificates   under the various schemes handled by the Ministry continues to be an area of
concern for the Committee. The Committee was informed that a total of 6765 UCs have been pending as on date.   The year-
wise position is as under : -
Period No. of UCs pending
1986-87 to 2001-02 4697
2002 -03 to 2004-05 1089
2005-06 to 2006-07 979 (recent UCs)
Total: - 6765
           
The Committee is deeply disturbed by the status of outstanding Utilisation Certificates. As many as 4697 UCs outstanding for
the period 1986-87 to 2001-02 compels the Committee to conclude that role of the Ministry is perhaps confined to only
disbursement of funds. Year after year, Central Funds are being released to State Govts./ implementing agencies.   Ministry’s
efforts for pursuing the matter with the State Governments as well as the State nodal agencies for submission of the pending
UCs on priority basis seem to have made no impact.   The Committee is also not inclined to believe the contention of the
Ministry that  no further grant is released to any NGO/ implementing agency where UCs are pending. This is borne out by the
pertinent  observations made in the  Audit Report No.3 of 2006 (Para No. 1.4) that
“the Certificates of utilization of grants were required to be furnished by the Ministries/Departments concerned
to the Controller General of Accounts in respect of grants released to statutory bodies, non-government
organizations etc. to ensure that grants had been properly utilized for the purpose for which they were
sanctioned. In the case of Ministry of Women and Child Development, 5934 Utilization certificates (UCs)
involving an amount of Rs. 316.04 crore in respect of grants released up to March 2004, which were due by
31st March 2005 are stated to be outstanding at the time of audit.
Audit has observed that the Ministries/Departments before releasing grants to statutory bodies and non-
government organizations did not satisfy themselves about utilization of grants in 85% cases involving 59% of
the total grant released.”

emphasize that this issue  should be taken up with the highest authorities at the State level so that old cases are cleared and
also for identification of  the inherent drawbacks/hindrances--systematic, procedural and others.  The Committee may be
furnished details of implementing agencies (state-wise, schemewise) who are yet to submit UCs and the steps taken to
minimise the pending UCs.

st December, 2006, these figures reached to Rs. 156.91 crore and Rs. 15.34 crores under the
two schemes respectively.   State-wise analysis about availability of unspent balances raises doubt about adherence of the

th August, 2006   issued by the Department of Expenditure, -
which inter-alia stipulate that the unspent balances available with the States and implementing agencies must be taken into
account before further releases are made, are always taken into account.

III.
             INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES SCHEME (ICDS)
 
3.1
              The ICDS scheme/launched in 1975 aims at holistic development of children below six years and pregnant and
lactating mothers from disadvantaged sections by providing a package of integrated services, comprising of supplementary
nutrition, immunization, health check-up, referral services, pre-school, non-formal education and nutrition and health
education.
 
3.2       Plan allocation under ICDS constituted about 80% of the budget of the Ministry in 2006-07.  Plan allocation of Rs.
4454.52 crore was made in BE 2006-07, reduced to Rs. 4331.48 crore at RE stage.  Against this, expenditure of Rs.3874.86
crore  has been incurred upto 16
th March, 2007. Funds amounting to Rs.123.04 crores from ICDS were reappropriated to the
World Bank assisted ICDS projects.   Against an approved outlay of Rs. 10391.75 crore for ICDS during the Tenth Plan, 
expenditure reported is Rs. 11,883.05 crore.  Trend of allocation indicates that major provision has been made during the last
two years of the Plan Period.  Enhanced Plan allocation of Rs. 5204.00 crores has been made during 2007-08, the first year of
the Eleventh Plan. While appreciating the trend of optimum utilization of allocated funds during the Tenth Plan, the
Committee observes that quantum of unspent balances has also been showing an upward trend.  Unspent balances of Rs. 61.00
crores were available with different States as on 1 st April, 2006 which have increased upto Rs. 156.91 crores by the end of 
December, 2006.

3.13     The Committee is aware that the ICDS was envisioned as a community participative programme and the components
of the scheme do not provide for the creation of infrastructural facilities.   However, in view of the present dismal status of
AWC buildings and also chronic problem of fund constraints being faced by majority of States, it is now time that providing
infrastructural facilities like construction of pucca building and other related aspects form part of the scheme so that over a
period of time all the AWCs must have pucca building to function.   If the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan can provide 30% of its
allocation for infrastructure development, the Committee does not find any reason why a particular percentage of the fund
could not be allocated for infrastructure creation under the ICDS. 
 
3.14     The Committee notes that Ministry is doing all out efforts to universalize the ICDS Scheme.  The Secretary submitted
before the Committee that there seems to be a lack of motivation at the grass-root level and there is a case for a much stronger
community participation.              The Committee feels that the Ministry should come forward to revamp, redesign and recast
the ICDS scheme in all possible ways.
 
3.15     It was submitted before the Committee that   delays  happen  in the allocation of funds due to the involvement of RBI,
State Governments and implementing agencies.  When the money is the released by the Central Government first it goes to the
State Government’s account in the RBI.  The State Government in turn takes its own time to send it down, and depending
upon its ways and means position they keep the money for a month or two or three, and then, further pass it down.
 
3.16     The Committee recommends that since the flow of money from the Centre to the Implementing agencies is taking lot
of time, efforts may be made for quicker and expeditious dispersal of money.  If need be, the ICDS scheme may be converted
into a Mission Mode Scheme so that intermediate agencies can be removed.
 
3.17            Supreme Court, vide its order dated 7.10.2004, had inter-alia, directed all the States/UTs that the contractors shall
not be used for supply of nutrition in Anganwadi Centres and funds shall be spent by making use of SHGs and Mahila
Mandals for buying of grains and preparation of meals.  The Committee was informed that 21 States/UTs have so far
furnished information on system of procurement, storage, distribution of supplementary nutrition, involvement of Corporates/
SHGs and duties/responsibilities thereof under ICDS Programme in their States/UTs.  The Committee may like to know
whether any assessment of the impact of the changeover is being studied. The Committee also recommends that the remaining
states should be directed to furnish their feedback at the earliest.

expenditure incurred by thereon for supplementary nutrition whichever is less. Financial norms for supplementary nutrition
fixed in 1991 have been revised in October, 2004, for children from 6 months to 6 years, Rs. 2.00 per day per child and for
severely malnourished children, Rs. 2.70 per child per day.  On  a specific query about the number of children covered under

V.        RAJIV GANDHI NATIONAL CRECHE SCHEME FOR THE CHILDREN OF WORKING MOTHERS
 
5.1       The scheme aims to provide day care services for children in the age group of 0-6 years, belonging to economically
weaker sections of society, whose family income does not exceed Rs. 12,000 per month.  The crèches running under the
scheme provide health care, supplementary nutrition, medical check-up and immunization, etc. to the children whose parents
are away at work sites or are incapacitated due to sickness and are unable to look after them. 
 
5.2       The Committee notes that Plan funds being released under the Scheme are being optimally utilized by the
implementing agencies. Allocation   of Rs. 90.00 crores for 2007-08 is at an enhanced level due to increase in the financial
norms from Rs. 18,480/- to Rs. 42,384/- per crèche per annum.  There has been increase in the honorarium for crèche workers
and  component of supplementary nutrition also.  Under the scheme, 90 per cent of the total expenditure is released as grant to
the implementing organization, except the honorarium of crèche workers.
 
5.3       The scheme is implemented through the Central Social Welfare Board and two other national level organizations, i.e.,
Indian Council for Child Welfare and Bhartiya Adim Jati Sevak Sangh. Out of total 30,902 creches running in the country,
24,101 creches are being maintained by the Central Social Welfare Board, 3279 creches by ICCW and 5137 by BAJSS.
 
5.4       The Committee was informed that all these three organizations have experience of implementing crèche programme
across the country for almost three decades and have a nation-wide presence and network for running crèches.   These
organizations are well equipped with field units and staff.  Hence no constraints are being faced for implementation of the
scheme through these organizations. The Committee recommends that to meet the growth in number of creches other
organization/NGOs may also be involved in the implementation of these projects. 
 
5.5       While not disputing the considerable experience of the three implementing agencies handling the Crèche Scheme, the
Committee would like to draw attention to two problem areas.  First is the uneven spread of Creches across the country. Out of
total 30,902 creches in the country, maximum concentration is in Andhra Pradesh (3902), M.P.(2740), Maharashtra (2292),
Tamil Nadu (1928), U.P.(1868) and West Bengal (2203). The Committee strongly feels that there is a need for conducting a
survey across the country so as to bring the uncovered cities under the scheme.   This task can be easily handled by the State
monitoring agencies like State Women Development Corporations, NIPCCD etc.
 
5.6       The other area of concern identified by the Committee is the pendency of settlement of accounts. The Committee notes
that Andhra Pradesh State Board having the maximum number of crèches (3902) has settled accounts upto 1995-96 only. For
States like Assam, Manipur, Rajasthan, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram and A&N Islands, accounts have been settled upto 2003-
04 only.  Very few States have settled accounts upto 2005-06.  Evidently, funds are released without settlement of previous
accounts thereby violating the financial rules.  Details about crèches being run by the two other implementing agencies are not
known to the Committee.   The Committee apprehends a similar status with regard to 8659 creches   being run by them.  The
Committee would like to point out that with the enhanced financial norms and levying of user charges, financial management
should be as per the prescribed norms. The Committee wonders about the factors behind non-settlement of accounts by an
experienced body like CSWB having a country-wide network of State Boards for running the crèches.
 
5.7       The Committee notes that the monitoring of crèches which is a continuing process has been assigned to States/Women
study centres of the Universities and State Women Development Corporations during the current financial year.  So far,
feedback has been received from monitoring             agencies in respect of 276 creches being run in the States of Delhi,
Haryana, Jammu & Kashmir, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Nagaland, Orissa, Tripura and Uttar Pradesh. The Committee may
be apprised about the feed back on the implementation of the scheme.
 
5.8       The Committee notes that there are a large number of working mothers in unorganized sector who are in great need of
creches to look after their children when they go to work.  The safety of the children is utterly neglected and they are prone to

5.9       The component of the crèche workers training has been added to the scheme to orient the crèche workers for providing

X.            CENTRAL ADOPTION RESOURCE AGENCY (CARA)
 
10.1     Central Adoption Resource Agency (CARA) was set up in 1990 and has been registered as an autonomous body under
the Registration of Societies Act, 1860. 
 
10.2     It is assigned the role of regulating inter-country adoptions from India and promoting domestic adoption.   For this
purpose, CARA at present has recognized 65  Indian Placement Agencies(RIPAs) to carry out in-country and inter-country
adoptions of children, who are either relinquished by biological parents/unwed mother/guardians or are abandoned/destitute
children and have been declared legally free for adoption by Juvenile Welfare Board/Child Welfare Committee.  There are 128
Enlisted Foreign Adoption Agencies (EFAAs) in over 24 countries including 46 Government Departments enlisted by CARA
for processing the application of foreign/NRI parents for adoption.  There are also 18 Adoption Coordinating agencies (ACAs)
recognized for promoting Indian adoption and to formulate, develop and execute programmes and activities for generating
awareness in this regard.  These agencies also coordinate the activities of its member placement agencies and assist them in
finding Indian parents for their children.  There are no regional offices of CARA at present.  CARA regulates inter-country
adoption through “Guidelines for Adoption from India-2006”.  CARA issued 867 NOCs in the year 2005 and 853 NOCs in the
year 2006 for inter-country adoption.
 
10.3     The Committee notes that in the year 2005, 3151 children were adopted. However, keeping in view large number of
children waiting for adoption, the Committee feels that the scheme should be revisited for simplifying procedures.  There is
also need for obtaining feedback from the parents to know their difficulties during adoption after adoption.    The Committee
may also be apprised about the procedure adopted by CARA to monitor the life of the adopted children for a few years after
adoption.

18.3            Committee’s attention has been drawn by a Study entitled ‘Poverty, Gender and Micro-Credit: A study of the
Experience of RMK’ sponsored by the Ministry and carried out by the Centre for Women’s Development Studies, New Delhi
in 2002. This study looks at the RMK experience of six years from March, 1993 to March, 1999.
            The following observations made in the above study are worth noting –
“RMK seeks to extend micro credit, with this over all objective, to women in poverty households.  However,
despite this mandate to focus on poor as defined/ accepted in public policy on cut off household income level,
only a small minority of the assisted borrowers is in BPL income level and only a small percentage (3.9%) is
of ST. Those with <Rs.11000 annual household income are in a minority (20%). The majority are middle and
upper poor.  This exclusion of the poorest, the hard-core poor, results in most of the intended target group
remaining outside the micro credit net.”
          
“The implementation of RMK credit delivery is so NGO specific in respect of the identification and location
details of the borrowers that unless the NGO and its staff are available and they cooperate and provide the
details of the borrowers including their location, it is almost impossible to contact the borrowers and
interview them. There is no visibility of RMK programme as such and the borrowers are quite often not
aware that the funds they have received are RMK funds.”
 
18.4     The Committee may be apprised of the follow-up action initiated on the recommendations of the above study. The
Committee also notes that another study is to be conducted to assess the impact of credit scheme on women beneficiaries
during the last five years. The Committee hopes that this study would be completed at the earliest so that benefits under RMK
reach maximum beneficiaries.

borrowing agency which in turn charges any rate on or above 8% on reducing balance from the ultimate beneficiaries subject
to maximum upto 18%.  Reports have been received by the Committee that there are instances of implementing agencies
charging 24% as interest rate from the beneficiaries. The Committee recommends that this issue need to be looked into and
check should be prevented from doing so and a cap should be put on the interest charged, under this scheme.

Committee  was not agreed to by the Governing Board. Board was of the view that the position may be reviewed after two
years when RMK may have expanded business.
 
18.7     The Committee is not inclined to agree with the view taken by the Governing Board of RMK.  The Committee

XXI.            GENDER BUDGETING
 
21.1     Gender Budgeting is understood as a dissection of the Government budget to establish its gender-differential impacts
and to translate gender commitments into budgetary commitments.Gender Budgeting lends itself to strengthening
administrative processes and actions to achieve the targets for improvement in the position of women.  It not only entails a
look at allocation of resources for women but goes beyond to cover tracking the utilization of allocated resources, impact
analysis and beneficiary incidence analysis of public expenditure and policy from a gender perspective.
 
21.2     The Committee was informed that the Sub-Group on Gender Budgeting was set-up as part of the Working Group on
Empowerment of Women for 11
th Five Year Plan.
Main recommendations of the Working group are:
-         Important National  macro-economic policies to be engendered
-                Review of and effective implementation of all legislations and
-                laws with a gender perspective to eliminate all forms of discrimination
-                and violence against women.
-                Gender mainstreaming to be extended to corporate sector and other
-                civil society organizations
-                Estimation of value addition by women in the unorganized, informal
-                and rural non farm sector and systemized mechanism in place to
               monetize the labour, efforts and output and include the same in the GDP
-                Gender Outcome Assessment
-                Strengthening of Gender Budget cells in all Ministries/ Departments.
 
21.3     So far  50 Ministries/Departments have set up Gender Budgeting (GB) Cells. Detailed training manuals were needed to
be prepared which can be used by the Trainers. These manuals will give the approach and the methodology to be taken in the
engendering policies, schemes, programmes and assessing their gender outcomes. The Committee was informed that a Task
Force for developing a Gender Budgeting Manual is being constituted by the Ministry.
 
21.4     To ensure Gender Budgeting in true sense, in 2006-07 the Ministry adopted a multi pronged strategy to effectively
wield gender budgeting as a tool for women’s empowerment. Initiatives ranged from advocacy, training and capacity building
to strengthening partnerships, supporting policy dialogues and strategy sessions. However, the Committee notes that more pro-
active action is required to be taken to effectively handle the concept of Gender Budgeting. Preparation of training manual
which is indispensable tool of the concept is under formulation by sub-committee. It seems it will take another 2-3 years to
finalise the things. The Committee recommends that immediate step should be taken to finalise the training manual in a time-
bound manner. The Ministry should evolve a monitoring mechanism to ensure that all the Government
Ministries/Departments/Undertakings are taking necessary action for resorting to Gender Budgeting.
 
21.5     It has come to the notice of the Committee that many expenditures being incurred by different Ministries/Departments,
which are not directly women specific were being shown in the Gender budgeting.  This, Committee notes, results in inflated
figures that does not reflect the actual allocation for women.  The Committee recommends that this practice should be stopped
immediately and the Gender budgeting should reflect only those expenditure/allocation that are cent percent women specific.

efforts for pursuing the matter with the State Governments as well as the State nodal agencies for submission of the pending
UCs on priority basis seem to have made no impact.   The Committee is also not inclined to believe the contention of the

Ideal position for a scheme would be judicious and optimum utilization of allocated funds and achievement of physical targets.

REPORT
 
I           INTRODUCTION
 
1.1       The Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports, Government of India owes its origin to the Department of Sports, which
was set up in 1982 at the time of the 9
th Asian Games in New Delhi.  During the International Youth Year 1985 it was
upgraded to the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports.  On 17th May, 2000 it became a full fledged Ministry.
 
1.2       The Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports (MoYAS) is entrusted with the responsibilities relating to the development
of Youth and Adolescents, and the functions of the Central Government with regard to Sports and Physical Education.
 
1.3       The MoYA&S is implementing a large number of schemes for youth and adolescents development.   These
schemes are proposed to be re-oriented as a part of an integrated framework comprising three key thrust areas viz.,
Personality Development, Preparation for Work Participation/Employability, and Empowerment.

1.4       In so far as the subject of Sports is concerned, this figures in the State List of the Constitution.   In view of this, it is
the State Governments who are primarily responsible for the development and promotion of sports.  The MoYA&S in its
effort to complement the State's efforts aims at development of a broad based sports culture throughout the country, and
significantly expanding the pool of talented sportspersons who can be groomed to bring laurels to the country in
international events.  With this in view, a major initiative proposed to be launched by the Ministry is a scheme with the
title 'Panchayat Yuva Khel Abhiyan', which is aimed at creating basic sports infrastructure, and promoting sports activities
at the village/sub-district level, both as a necessary ingredient of youth development and as a means to substantially widen
the catchment for spotting of talent.   The Committee desires that Pancayat Yuva Khel Abhiyan should be finalized at the
earliest and the details in this regard may be furnished to the Committee.
 
1.5       The Committee was informed that the population of the youth and adolescents is nearly 45% of the total
population, and that of the number of persons below the age of 35 is around 75%.   This creates, the Committee feels, a
unique opportunity to take advantage of this "demographic dividend" and also highlights the urgency of addressing the
needs of the youth and adolescents in a comprehensive manner with the objective of creating responsible citizen as well as
a healthy and productive work force.
II
          BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The Ministry was allocated Rs. 600 crore in BE 2006-07 that was reduced to Rs. 500 crore at RE stage.  It has been
given for the year 2007-08, Rs. 700 crore.  Out of this, Rs. 200 crore is for youth development and Rs 500 core for the
sports.  This allocation for sports bureau includes Rs. 150 crore for Commonwealth Games also.
 
Youth Bureau
 
2.2       The Ministry had projected a demand of Rs. 397.25 crore for its Youth Bureau, against which the Planning
Commission has provided Rs. 200.00 crore.
 
2.3       The scheme-wise projected demand and allocation provided for Youth related activities for 2007-08 are given in
the table below:-

2.4       The Plan allocation for youth development in 2007-08 (Rs.200 crores) is about 30 per cent higher than the BE of
2006-07.  The Youth Bureau proposes to utilise this additional allocation judiciously to achieve its objectives.   The Nehru
Yuva Kendra Sangthan (NYKS) will get additional Rs.23 crores towards programme funding.  New initiatives such a
Youth Leadership and Personality Development, training for rural youth, Shramdan shivirs, Panchayat Yuva Shakti

Abhiyan and Programmes for National Integration, communal harmony, sadbhavna and peace have been proposed under
the NYKS.   Further, NSS will get additional allocation of Rs.16.5 crores under which the volunteers' strength will be
increased from 26 lakhs to 29.16 lakhs.  And the number of villages adopted by NSS will increase from 11,000 to 12,000
in this coming financial year.  The allocation for the Rajiv Gandhi National Institute of Youth Development is going up
from Rs.3.6 crores to Rs.8 crores.  This additional allocation will be utilised to impart vocational and soft skills to
unemployed youth, training of young Panchayat leaders and youth exchanges and home-stay programmes for youth from
North-East.  Under adolescence scheme, a National Adolescence Quiz by NSS is proposed in 350 districts.
2.5       The Committee does not dispute the fact that there is need for higher allocation for Youth Welfare Schemes.  Plan
allocation of Rs. 200.00 crore for 2007-08 is almost half of the projected requirements of the Ministry, i.e. Rs. 397.25
crore.  The Committee would, however, like to draw the attention of the Ministry towards the level of Plan fund utilization
during 2006-07.  Plan allocation of Rs. 145.00 crore for Youth Welfare Schemes had to be reduced to Rs. 110.34 crore at
the RE stage and up to 31
st Januray, 2007 only Rs. 77.24 crore could be utilized.   The Committee is not inclined to accept
the Ministry's contention that allocation was reduced at the RE stage due to overall cut in its Plan allocation.   The
Committee would like to point out that position was similar during 2005-06, when Plan allocation of Rs. 132.00 crore had
to be reduced to Rs. 124.32 crore and actual expenditure figures at the end of the financial year stood at Rs. 108.70 crore. 
The Committee observes that major cut has been effected under NYKS and NSS.  As against a demand of Rs. 130.00
crore, an allocation of Rs. 68.50 crore has been provided for NYKS and for NSS, an allocation of Rs. 54.00 crore has been
provided against a demand of Rs. 129.74 crore.  The Committee, however, notes that under both the schemes, allocated
funds during 2006-07 had to be brought down at the RE stage, and as on 31
st January, 2007, shortfall in expenditure was
reported.
 
2.6       As regards Sports Bureau, against a projected demand of Rs. 1176.86 crore (including Rs. 355 crore for
Commonwealth games 2010), an amount of Rs. 500.00 crore has been allocated, which is again 30% more than that in the
last year.  The cut in the demand is mainly due to non-inclusion of the newly proposed flagship scheme of "Panchayat
Yuva Khel Abhiyan". Against projected demand of Rs. 355.00 crore during 2007-08 for the Commonwealth Games
(CWG), allocation of only Rs. 150.00 crore has been provided.  This additionality in Plan allocation will give major
impetus for the promotion of sports activity across the country.  The additional allocation of Rs. 26 crore will help in
strengthening sports infrastructure, procurement of state-of-the-art technical and scientific equipment and training of
20,000 sports persons compared to about 13000 only in the current fiscal year.  Similarly, Laxmibai National Institute of
Physical Education, Gwalior will get additional Plan allocation of Rs.7 crore which will be utilized for strengthening its
sports infrastructure, scheme for talent search and training. Assistance to National Sports Federations has also been
augmented to enable greater coverage in the light of the Commonwealth Games.
 
2.7       The Committee observes that allocation of Rs. 500.00 crore for Sports for 2007-08, although being less than half of
the projected requirements of the Ministry, is at an enhanced level when compared with provision of Rs. 410.71 crore in
2006-07.  The Committee also notes that trend of utilization of allocated funds is equally discouraging in sports schemes
also.  Plan allocation of Rs. 410.71 crore had to be brought down to Rs. 346.95 crore at RE stage and up to 31
st January,
2007, expenditure reported was only Rs. 249.34 crore.  The Committee is of the view that performance level of Sports
Authority of India, Schemes of Incentives for Promotion of Sports, Scheme relating to Talent Search and Training,
Assistance to Sports Federations needs to be monitored closely during 2007-08 in the light of under utilization of allocated
funds during 2006-07 and enhanced provision made in 2007-08. 
 
2.8       The Secretary in her presentation before the Committee informed that due to some difficulties pertaining to old
utilization certificates, the pace of releases had been adversely affected which ultimately led to reduction from Rs.600
crore to Rs.500 crore at RE.   Otherwise, the quantum of expenditure and utilization could have been substantially higher.

III        NATIONAL SERVICE SCHEME
 
3.1       National Service Scheme launched in 1969 has primary focus on the development of personality of students
through community service.   Since its inception, more than 2.8 crore students from Universities, Colleges and other
educational Institutions have participated in NSS activities as student volunteers.
 
3.2       The Scheme is implemented through the State Governments. The basic unit of NSS consists of 50 or 100
volunteers and is headed by a Programme Officer at faculty/institution level.  At the University level, the Programme
Officers of affiliated colleges of the concerned University work under the guidance of Programme Coordinators.  At the
State level, all the Universities in the State work under the guidance of a State Liaison Officer.  The State Liaison Cell at
the State headquarters is responsible for ensuring timely release of grants under its jurisdiction and timely submission of
accounts thereof.  The State level Liaison Cell is fully funded by the Central Government.  There are 15 NSS Regional
Centres in the country.  These Regional Centres maintain liaison with the State Governments, Universities, +2 Councils,
Training and Orientation Centres and Training Orientation and Research Centre, Coordinators and Programme Officers.
 
3.3       The Committee notes that every student cannot join NSS as there is a ceiling on the number of volunteers a State
can have. The cap on the number of NSS volunteers, the Committee feels, appears to be incongruous to the objectives of
NSS.   Our efforts should be to provide every student who is desirous of joining NSS, opportunity to do so.  The
Committee feels that finance should not be a problem in achieving this as funds usually remain under utilized.
 
3.4       The Scheme is jointly funded by the Union and State Governments in a ratio of 7:5 in all States, except North East
Region, including Sikkim, and hilly areas, where the ratio is 3:1.  In J&K and all the Union Territories, Kendriya
Vidyalayas and Navodaya Vidyalayas, the programme is entirely funded by Government of India.  The funding to the
State Government for regular activities is Rs. 160/- per volunteer per annum for normal areas and Rs. 200/- per volunteer
per annum for North Eastern States including Sikkim, Himachal Pradesh and other hilly states as notified by the Planning

195th Report of Connittee On Human Resource Development

Commission from time to time.   For special camping programme, the funding is at the rate of Rs. 300/- per volunteer for
normal areas and Rs. 400/- per volunteer for North Eastern States including sikkim, Himachal Pradesh and other hilly
areas.
 
3.5       The Committee notes that the Ministry projected a demand of Rs. 129.74 crore in the BE 2007-08 as against which
an allocation of Rs.54.00 crore has been provided to NSS.  The enhanced allocation was sought to increase the number of
volunteers from existing 26.00 lakh to 29.10 lakh during 2007-08.  It was proposed to enhance the programme funding
from the existing level of Rs. 160/- per volunteer to that of Rs. 300/- per volunteer and to include a diet component into it. 
The Ministry also proposed to rationalize the funding pattern of the scheme from 7:5 to 75:25 for Normal States and from
3:1 to 90:10 for NE & hilly States.
 
3.6       The Committee welcomes the proposals of the Ministry for increasing the number of volunteers, enhancing
programme funding and rationalizing sharing pattern under this scheme.  It, however, feels that it would not be possible to
achieve these, due to heavy cut in allocations by the Planning Commission form what the Ministry had demanded. The
Committee also welcomes the introduction of diet component into this programme.   The Committee advises the Ministry
to ensure that this allocation does not remain underutilized.
 
3.7       The Committee, at the same time, is worried to note the precious fund lying unspent under NSS.  The Committee is
at a loss to see the huge backlogs in settling the accounts.   For example, four States/UTs have settled account up to
2001/02 only; nine States/UTs up to 2002-03, seventeen States/UTs up to 2003-04 and only five States/UTs up to 2004-
05.  The non-settlement of accounts and the unspent balances, in Committee’s view, are indicative of the poor health of
this scheme.  The Committee recommends the Ministry to take up the settlement of accounts with all States/UTs on
priority to clear the backlog during this financial year itself.
 
3.8       The Committee has been informed that a proposal for expansion of National Service Scheme (NSS) to all
universities, Colleges and Schools as well as to enroll the student of classes IX and X also as NSS volunteers was sent to
the Planning Commission for seeking in-principle approval.   The Planning Commission had advised to obtain the view of
Ministry of HRD. In the meanwhile the issue was deliberated in the Working Group for the formulation of 11
th Five Year
Plan.  It has proposed that the NSS volunteer's strength currently at 2.6 million, be substantially increased in a phased
manner to 5.08 million by the end of the 11 th Five Year Plan.  In this regard first priority will be accorded to extend NSS
to uncovered Universities, Colleges, Technical Institutes and +2 Schools under Higher Secondary Councils/Boards,
followed by setting up more units in the existing NSS institutions, wherever required.  However, the feasibility of
extending NSS to classes IX & X will be examined separately in a larger context relating to the universal coverage of
educational institutions either through the NCC or NSS.  In the process of increasing the number of volunteers, emphasis
will be given to the State and regions where this is low.  Enrolment of women volunteers will be encouraged through a
targeted special drive in the 11
th Five Year Plan period. The Committee welcomes the proposal to increase the volunteer's
strength to 5.08 million by the end of the 11 th Five Year Plan.  It hopes that the target of 5.08 million NSS volunteers will
be achieved and proper planning will be done in this regard.

IV        NEHRU YUVA KENDRA SANGATHAN
 
4.1       Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan (NYKS) is an autonomous body of the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports and
has its presence in 500 districts of the country.  It is one of the largest grassroot level organizations in the world, catering
to more than eight million non-student rural youth enrolled through about 2.53 lakh village based Youth Clubs.  These
Youth Clubs work in areas like education and training, awareness generation, skill development and self-employment,
entrepreneurial development, thrift and co-operation, besides personality development through sports and adventure and
sustained exposure to new ideas and development strategies.   For implementation of the programmes, every district has a
trained cadre of District Youth Coordinator, National Service Volunteers and Youth leaders.  The strength of NYKS is its
vast network of Youth Clubs at the grassroots level.
 
4.2       NYKS accomplishes its task through three categories of programmes:
(1)
               Regular programmes such as Youth Leaders and Youth Club Development, Panchayat Yuva Shakti Abhiyan,
Employment and Income Generation Programme through Rural Business Hub, Cultural Programmes, Mahila
Sashaktikaran Abhiyan, Work Camp, Local Need Based Project, Adventure Promotion Programmes, etc.
(2)               Special Schemes of Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports like National Service Volunteers, Youth
Development Centres, Awards to Outstanding Youth Clubs, Financial Assistance to Youth Clubs, Rural Sports
Clubs, Rural Information Technology Youth Development Centre (RITYDC), Scheme for Development and
Empowerment of Adolescents, Rashtriya Sadbhawana Yojana.
(3)
               Special Programmes undertaken in collaboration with other Ministries and Organizations.  Here in specific
schemes pertaining to Health, Education, Environment, Poverty alleviation, etc. are  undertaken by NYKS,
from time to time, as one of the implementing agencies on behalf of the concerned Ministries/Departments,
including Ministry of YAS.  In this role, the NYKS is practically seen as any other NGO.
 
4.3       Besides, the programmes covered under the above broad categories, NYKS also plans to observe/celebrate
Important National & International Days & Weeks.

V         RASHTRIYA SADBHAVANA YOJANA
 
5.1       The Rashtriya Sadhbhavana Yojana was launched in 2005 in place of the erstwhile National Reconstruction Corps
Scheme.  The Scheme aims at encouraging leadership among the rural youth.  Under the scheme average of around 10-20
volunteers in each of the 500 districts having presence of NYKS are to be enrolled as Nehru Yuva Sathees (NYSs).   These
NYSs are to be nominated by the selected best Youth Clubs and Youth Development Centres in the block and district
respectively.  During 2006-07, 4925 NYSs were deployed through NYKS.
 
5.2       The Committee notes that the performance of the scheme of Rashtriya Sadbhavna Yojna has been uneven in
different states.  The Ministry has informed that this is mainly on account of a requirement that the Youth Clubs, for this
purpose, should be registered for at least three years. However, this requirement could not be fulfilled since many Youth
Clubs could not get registered in many States like UP, Bihar as there are difficulties in getting registration in these States. 
As a result, the scheme suffered.  The Ministry has also submitted that there were some practical difficulties in the actual
selection of Nehru Yuva Sathees (NYSs).   The Ministry has not furnished any information as to what steps it took to
persuade the States to simplify the registration process.  The Committee only hopes that the Ministry must have taken the
matter of slow registration of clubs with concerned States to resolve it.  The Committee, in view of practical problems
being faced in selection of NYSs, regrets to say that these problems still persist.  The Committee recommends the Ministry
to take urgent steps to remove the difficulties encountered in the actual selection of Nehru Yuva Sathees.
5.3       One of the measures taken by the Ministry to improve the situation is to raise the level of honorarium for Nehru
Yuva Sathees from Rs. 1000/- to Rs.1500/-.  The committee welcomes this raise but is afraid that in the face of rising
inflation and other factors, even this raise may not be sufficient to encourage the volunteers to come forth as Nehru Yuva
Sathis.  The Committee is of the opinion that Rs. 1500 may not be at all adequate for areas like J&K, North-East,
Himachal Pradesh and Uttrakhand.
 
5.4       The Committee also welcomes the fact that Rashtriya Sadhbhavana Yojana has been included as a monitorable
programme in the revised 20 Point Programme.   It hopes that this inclusion will ensure proper implementation of the
Scheme.
 
5.5       The Committee notes that BE 2007-08 for the Yojana is pegged at Rs. 8.00 crore which is an enhancement to Rs.
5.00 crore that the Yojana got in RE 2006-07.  The Committee is, however, surprised to see that not a single rupee has
been spent till 31.12.2006 against an allocation of Rs. 5.00 crore.  The Committee would like to know the reasons behind
this complete non-utilization of funds.  It further desires to know as to how the Ministry could reach an achievement of
4925 volunteers against a target of 5911 fixed for the year 2006-07, without spending a single rupee until 31.12.2006.  The
Committee requests the Ministry to throw more light on this.
 
VI        PROMOTION OF NATIONAL INTEGRATION PROGRAMME
 
6.1       The Scheme of Promotion of National Integration was launched as a Central Scheme to provide the youth from
different parts of the country, and from diverse cultural backgrounds, opportunities to interact with each other, know each
others' customs and lifestyles, to work together in community service projects and, in the process, make them aware of the
underlying unity amidst diversity in the country and promote the sprit of national and emotional integration among the
youth.             
 
6.2       The Committee notes that Plan allocation saw a reduction to Rs. 6.15 crore (including NE) in RE 2006-07 from BE
of Rs. 10.00 crore.  However BE 2007-08 provides for enhanced allocation of Rs. 11.50 crore (including NE Region).  As
per the Ministry, the higher allocation under National Integration Programme is due to its importance for youth in the
present context.  The Ministry has been organizing Home Stay Exchange programme for youth of north-eastern states and
J&K to other parts of the country.  This will be strengthened and made two way process in which the youth from other

VII
       NATIONAL SERVICE VOLUNTEERS SCHEME
 
7.1       The National Service Volunteer Scheme provides a platform for the youth to take up a leadership role in the

195th Report of Connittee On Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/195threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:42:38]
spheres of the social and community service at the grass roots level.
 
7.2       The Service Volunteer is a youth social worker who is willing to commit his/her energy and time to the service of
the community and the country. The National Service Volunteer Scheme provides for an opportunity for first work
experience after education and is aimed to inculcate leadership qualities in them.  During their deployment, the Volunteers
are paid Rs. 1000/- per month by way of honorarium.  The NSVs, together with the Nehru Yura Sathees (NYSs) under
Rsahtriya Sadhbhavana Yojana, are the backbone of the NYKS.
 
7.3       The Committee notes that the Plan allocation in BE 2007-08 for National Service Volunteers Scheme has been
increased to Rs. 13.50 crores as compared to Rs. 6.00 crores in 2006-07.  The Ministry has informed that the reasons for
seeking increase in allocation for 2007-08 is the proposal to enhance the stipends of the volunteers from the existing Rs.
1000/- per month to Rs. 2500/- per month.  The Committee welcomes the enhancement in the stipends of the volunteers
but it still feels that this enhancement is not sufficient, given the fact that as NSVs, they contribute significantly for social
work on a full time basis. The Committee recommends further enhancement in the stipend of the Volunteers. 
 
7.4       The Scheme aims at deploying 4400 NSVs during 2007-08.  Under the scheme, the volunteers are enrolled in the
beginning of the year and allotted to Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan and National Service Scheme.   The recruitment is
made by a District level Committee headed by the collectors. 
 
7.5       The Committee notes that there is a little awareness about the existence of such a scheme in the public.   The
Committee emphasizes the need for giving a wider publicity about the scheme, mode of recruitment of volunteers, etc.
 
7.6       The Committee further notes that 30 per cent of NSVs after the training remain unemployed and only 30 per cent
become social worker.  The Committee feels that with this achievement, the scheme has failed to create a desirable impact
on our youth particularly to join social sector in a big way.
 
7.7       The Committee notes that these NSVs are associated with NYKs.  However, given the fact that only 500 districts in
the country have NYKs, the youth of remaining districts are being deprived of the opportunity to become NSVs.   Further,
with the projection of only 4400 NSVs to be deployed during 2007-08, the number of volunteers for a district comes to
mere 8 volunteers per district.  The Committee feels that this is an inadequate number.  It only hopes that NSVs are being
selected from uncovered districts as well.
 
7.8       The Committee takes note of the fact that about 5% of NSVs leave midway for various reasons.  The Committee
would like the Ministry to inform it about the impact this drop out has on the scheme and the steps taken to control it.
 
VIII      YOUTH HOSTELS
 
8.1       Youth Hostels are built to promote youth travel within the country.  They have been conceived as a joint venture
between the Central and the State Government.   While the Central Government bears the cost of construction, the State
Government provides fully developed land free of cost with water, electricity, approach road and staff quarters.  After
completion, Youth Hostels are handed over to the State Government  for management.  Youth hostels are generally located
in areas of historical and cultural value, educational centre, tourist importance etc. where facilities for youth activities are
available.  As on 31
st December, 2006, 73 Youth Hotels have been constructed and 20 hostels are under construction and
32 have been approved in principle.   So far, 14 Youth Hostels have been constructed in the North Eastern Region, which
are functional.
 
8.2       The Committee notes that the budgetary allocation for Youth Hostels has decreased to Rs. 1.25 crore in BE 2007-
08 in comparison to Rs. 3.50 crore allocated in RE 2006-07.  This reduction has been made in view of lower actual
expenditure till September, 2006 under Youth Hostel Scheme.   The Committee notes with concern the continuously low
utilization of funds under this scheme.  Against an allocation of Rs. 4.50 crore in 2005-06, the Ministry could utilize only
1.49 crore.  Further in 2006-07, against an allocation of Rs. 3.50 crore, the Ministry could spend a mere 7 lakh only till
31.12.2006.  The extremely low utilization of funds has severely affected the construction of Youth Hostels.  The
Committee is perturbed over such a poor performance of an important scheme from its inception.   It recommends the
Ministry to make effort to improve the situation and devise specific measures to address various problems associated with
this scheme.

8.3       Despite repeated suggestion to take urgent steps to complete the construction of 18 Youth Hostels that has been
under construction for years now, in some cases even 20 years, the Committee finds that the situation has not improved at
all.  Rather, the status has become worse as 2 more Youth Hostels has been added to the list of Youth Hostels under
construction.  The Committee finds this situation disappointing and strongly recommends the Ministry to take remedial
steps in this regard.
 
8.4       In response to the Committee's recommendation that specific action be initiated to remedy the problem of non
construction in 176
th Report of the Committee, the Ministry informed that it has taken remedial action for improvement in
the system by stopping release of approved funds till the identified plot is developed by the State Government and handed
over to CPWD or any other construction agency.   The Ministry has also decided to cancel the approval if the information
is not received.  In this process, the approval of Navegaon Youth Hostel in Maharashtra which was approved in principle
has been cancelled.   Ministry has also decided to recover the funds, released for the construction work where the
construction has not started.  In this process, DG, CPWD, New Delhi has been requested to refund the amount of Rs. 20.00
lakhs released to CPWD, Manipur for construction of Youth  Hostel at Bishnupur in Manipur.  The Ministry has now
decided to give priority to the on-going projects, and only thereafter will other approved projects be taken up.  No further
proposals are being approved or considered at present.  The Outcome Budget 2007-08 of the Ministry states its projected
outcomes are to complete the ongoing Youth Hostels and to start new Youth Hostels as per availability of funds.  While
agreeing with the Ministry's decision to firstly complete the ongoing construction of Youth Hostels, it expresses concern
over the inadequacy of funds since the budget earmarked for the languishing projects must have become insufficient in
relation to prevailing price index.  The Committee strongly recommends the Ministry to complete the construction in a
time bound manner.  The Committee feels that the Ministry's target of completing the construction of six Youth Hostels
during this fiscal is quite low, it must be more.
 
8.5       The Committee's attention is drawn to the oft-repeated fact that failure to get a developed site from the State
Government is the main reason behind the delay.   However, the Committee has been informed that approval is given and
the funds under the Scheme is released only after examining a developed site which is handed over to the CPWD for
construction of Youth Hostel.  If it were so, the Committee fails to appreciate the problem of late or non-availability of
requisite site for the Hostels.  In this backdrop, the Committee desires the Ministry to furnish a note as to the factors that
have caused delay in construction of Youth Hostels, since such delays result in time and cost overruns.
 
8.6       The Ministry has informed that based on the deliberations in the Working Group for the XIth Plan, it has been
proposed to increase the number of Youth Hostels in the country from 72 to 200 during the 11
th Five Year Plan.  However,
the actual number of new hostels that can be constructed will depend on the outlay given to the Ministry of Youth Affairs
and Sports.  It is also mentioned that some structural changes regarding the management of so many Youth Hostels have
been proposed by the Working Group which, inter-alia  would include possible PPP bases module.   This suggestion is
being examined in the Ministry.  In the meanwhile the focus of attention will be on completion of the on-going projects. 
The Committee is of the view that the private participation should not be explored as the first option to overhaul and
correct the things. The Committee would like to have a copy of the proposals of the Working Group, particularly as
regards the suggestions on structural changes in the management of the Youth Hostels. 
 
8.7       The Committee takes note of the following assessment made by the Working Group for the Eleventh Plan-
-
         Areas of concern are selection of site, construction and actual functioning of the Hostels, many times sites are
selected without due consideration, resulting in hostels not being optimally utilised after construction.
-         Construction of Hostels takes an unduly long time due to cumbersome procedure.
-         Instances of hostels being used by other organisations for other purposes are also there.
-         Only a handful of Government owned Youth Hostels have got affiliation to the International Youth Hostel
Association as they fail to meet the prescribed standards on accommodation, reception, hygiene, security etc.
 
8.8       The Committee strongly feels that keeping in view the proposed expansion of Youth Hostels from 72 to 200 during
the Eleventh Plan, the above-mentioned shortcomings need serious attention.   The Committee accordingly recommends
that the Ministry should initiate corrective measures in respect of existing Hostels and also ensure that the proposed
Hostels do not have these problem areas.

9.6       The Committee expresses its unhappiness over the slow pace of utilization of funds under all the schemes, except
for National Coaching Scheme and Plan Scheme staff and other facilities.   The situation is more grim in the case of
schemes like National Sports Talent Contest, Special Area Games, Centres of Excellence, Sports Science/Medical Centre
& Research Scholarship, Central Pool of Technical sports Equipment, SAI Housing complex, Indira Gandhi Stadium,
Computerized Sports Data Band and infrastructure Development & Capital Works.  The Committee fails to understand
that in case of some of the Schemes, although the expenditure is less than 50 per cent, the physical targets have been either
achieved or are close to it.  This suggests that either the targets fixed were not realistic or allocation to the scheme were
more than what was required.  This is a serious lapse.  The Committee recommends the Ministry to enquire into it and take
corrective measures immediately.
 
9.7       The Committee feels that the existing system of financial management in the SAI is weak and that needs to be
strengthened.  It has been the experience of the Committee that due to inadequate supervision/monitoring of the financial
affairs, instances of irregularities as well as adverse audit reports have been reported during the recent years.  The officials
looking after finance in the SAI are either over-burdened or are given responsibilities about which they do not have
relevant experience.  As a result, they are not able to spare required time for their main responsibility.  In view of the
above, the Committee feels that the person looking after finance should be given other responsibilities only when they are
able to fulfil their primary responsibility in an  effective and comprehensive manner.

10.1     On the promotion of traditional/indigenous games, the Ministry informed the Committee that SAI has undertaken

are being looked after by SAGs and STC Centres.  Also there are few National Sports Federations that look after few

      COMMONWEALTH GAMES, 2010

XVI     GENERAL OBSERVATION
 
16.1     The Committee after going through the replies and other documents relating to Demands for Grants of various
years including that of 2007-08 arrives at conclusion that the financial performance/management of the Ministry leaves
much to be desired.  Importance of the mandate of the Ministry – development, empowerment of youth as well as
promotion of sports – can hardly be over-emphasized.  The Committee has all these years been pleading for more funds for
these purposes.  Rs. 200 crore for development of youth who constitute 45% of our population and on whom the country is
pinning all its hope for future, is just a peanut.   Similarly, sports development gets Rs. 350 crore + Rs. 150 crore for
Commonwealth Games, 2010.
 
16.2     On the other hand, the Committee regrets to say that even these meagre allocations are not being utilized
completely and properly.  Every year, crores of rupees are left as unspent balance or being allowed to lapse due to various
reasons-non-settlement of accounts and pending UCs being the two most important ones.  As a result, crores of rupees are
blocked every year and our schemes languish.  Another disturbing trend noticed in this regard is the quantum jump in
spending of allocations in March every year.  Such a position leads to a situation where we have plan, programmes and
targets but there is no performance.   Flow of funds from Centre to States and other implementing agencies take 8 to 10
months, at times more.  Some schemes are prepared/declared to be revised/redesigned before they actually take off.    The
Committee has no option but to conclude that our schemes are suffering not merely because of paucity of funds but also
because of problems in our delivery mechanism, the procedure we adopt and above all the attitude in the administrative
machinery.  Lack of effective mechanisms for monitoring, authentic feedback, objective evaluation, etc. make it difficult
to gauge the performance of a scheme. 
 
16.3     These are larger questions which need to be considered at various levels to evolve a system as well as culture in
which we work as facilitator/enabler also not only as a controller, which has an effective system of transparency and
accountability and enough scope for correction and improvement.
16.4     The Committee has been expressing its reservation about the transfer of Sports Infrastructure Scheme to the States. 
The Committee has noted the assurance of the Ministry to consider it in the ongoing exercises for the formulation of the
Eleventh Plan.  The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation in 176
th Report for strengthening of monitoring and
effective implementation rather than transferring the scheme to the States.

            The Committee expresses its unhappiness over the slow pace of utilization of funds under all the schemes, except
for National Coaching Scheme and Plan Scheme staff and other facilities.   The situation is more grim in the case of
schemes like National Sports Talent Contest, Special Area Games, Centres of Excellence, Sports Science/Medical Centre
& Research Scholarship, Central Pool of Technical sports Equipment, SAI Housing complex, Indira Gandhi Stadium,
Computerized Sports Data Band and infrastructure Development & Capital Works.  The Committee fails to understand
that in case of some of the Schemes, although the expenditure is less than 50 per cent, the physical targets have been either
achieved or are close to it.  This suggests that either the targets fixed were not realistic or allocation to the scheme were
more than what was required.  This is a serious lapse.  The Committee recommends the Ministry to enquire into it and take
corrective measures immediately.                                                                                                             (para 9.6)
 
            The Committee feels that the existing system of financial management in the SAI is weak and that needs to be
strengthened.  It has been the experience of the Committee that due to inadequate supervision/monitoring of the financial

X         TRADITIONAL/INDIGENOUS GAMES
 
            The Committee strongly feels that traditional/indigenous games have not been given due attention as there appears
to be no scheme specifically for this purpose.  The Committee is of the opinion that the traditional/indigenous games need
not only be preserved but be also promoted in a planned manner.   The Committee disapproves this piecemeal approach in
this regard.  The Committee, therefore, emphasizes the need for a focussed policy to promote traditional indigenous
games.  It is of the opinion that Ministry should take all necessary steps urgently with a clear vision to achieve the goal.
                                           (para 10.1)
 
            The Committee is of the opinion that the details of grants shown in the Table is self-revealing about the Ministry’s
attitude towards the traditional/indigenous sports.  The Committee is particularly perturbed over the quantum of assistance
for games like Kho-Kho and Kabaddi.  It recommends the Ministry to increase the financial assistance to these NSFs and
also to recognize more traditional/indigenous games.                                                                                                     (para
10.3)
XI
        ASSISTANCE TO NATIONAL SPORTS FEDERATIONS
            The Committee notes that the Ministry has deliberately tried to be evasive in its reply.  It advises the Ministry to
give complete replies to a Parliamentary Committee.  The Committee would like to have names of the NSFs who have not

             The Committee has not been informed about the pending utilization certificates of the central assistance given to

XIII      COMMONWEALTH GAMES, 2010
            The Committee recommends the Ministry to formulate the estimates at the earliest so that there can be adequate
time to examine and allocate the funds.(para 13.1)
 
            The Committee finds an ad-hocism in projections and formulation of estimates for hosting an international event
like this.  It seems that there exists no clear schematic guidelines in this regard.  The Committee strongly recommends the
Ministry to come out with a clear guideline in this regard so that the expenditure on bid process and other necessary
expenditure can be met.      (para 13.5)
 
            The Committee is surprised to know that funds have been projected/allocated for every other activity such as
construction of games village, stadia, roads, transport, etc. but not for the training of our sportspersons for the
Commonwealth Games.  The Committee in one of its previous reports had proposed that some percentage of total
allocation for the games should be kept for training of our sportspersons.  The Committee is of the opinion that the
Ministry must create a special corpus for the training of athletes for the Commonwealth Games and other such events.  The
Committee hopes that the Ministry appreciates the high expectations the country has about its performance at the Games. 
The good showing will also bring a change in perception towards sports in the country.  The Committee, therefore,
strongly recommends that every effort be made for a world-class training of our athletes on a regular basis.
                                         (para 13.6)
 
            The Committee notes that major works relating to the Games are yet to begin; these were expected, according to
the Ministry, to start from June-August, 2007.  The Committee expresses its apprehension about timely completion of
various stadia, games village and other facilities for this Game.  The Committee, therefore, recommends to start the civil
and other works at the earliest and be completed positively by the end of 2009 so that our sportspersons have the
opportunity to familiarize themselves with facilities/equipment/grounds much in advance.
(para 13.7)

XVI     GENERAL OBSERVATION
 
            The Committee after going through the replies and other documents relating to Demands for Grants of various
years including that of 2007-08 arrives at conclusion that the financial performance/management of the Ministry leaves
much to be desired.  Importance of the mandate of the Ministry – development, empowerment of youth as well as
promotion of sports – can hardly be over-emphasized.  The Committee has all these years been pleading for more funds for
these purposes.  Rs. 200 crore for development of youth who constitute 45% of our population and on whom the country is
pinning all its hope for future, is just a peanut.   Similarly, sports development gets Rs. 350 crore + Rs. 150 crore for
Commonwealth Games, 2010.                                                                         (para 16.1)
 
            On the other hand, the Committee regrets to say that even these meagre allocations are not being utilized

completely and properly.  Every year, crores of rupees are left as unspent balance or being allowed to lapse due to various
reasons-non-settlement of accounts and pending UCs being the two most important ones.  As a result, crores of rupees are
blocked every year and our schemes languish.  Another disturbing trend noticed in this regard is the quantum jump in
spending of allocations in March every year.  Such a position leads to a situation where we have plan, programmes and
targets but there is no performance.   Flow of funds from Centre to States and other implementing agencies take 8 to 10
months, at times more.  Some schemes are prepared/declared to be revised/redesigned before they actually take off.    The
Committee has no option but to conclude that our schemes are suffering not merely because of paucity of funds but also
because of problems in our delivery mechanism, the procedure we adopt and above all the attitude in the administrative
machinery.  Lack of effective mechanisms for monitoring, authentic feedback, objective evaluation, etc. make it difficult
to gauge the performance of a scheme.                                                                                                            (para 16.2)
 
            These are larger questions which need to be considered at various levels to evolve a system as well as culture in
which we work as facilitator/enabler also not only as a controller, which has an effective system of transparency and
accountability and enough scope for correction and improvement.       (para 16.3)
